My Linux system has an odd issue with the HDMI port (a known hardware issue with the graphics card model), and I want to see how well this hub addresses the conversion from USB-C to HDMI. If this solves the issue with that system’s HDMI connectivity when I try it, I’ll be buying another one. Once I have tried this I will update my review. If it doesn’t work with Linux it’s okay – the product description does not mention Linux as a supported platform, so if it does happen to work it’s a bonus. My experience with this hub/dock has been very positive and for me it has been worth the expense. It’s expensive when considering I just needed an external card reader, but when considering everything else it does it’s a good investment for my system.

title: Inexpensive, Basic Lens Protection
text: A UV filter on a lens can be a cheap and effective way to protect your expensive glass. Some of these filters are better than others, and this one is on the lower end of the scale. That said, it's worth its asking price. Most digital cameras already have decent UV filtering built in so there's not a lot of sense to getting a UV filter for that purpose. However, these filters do have a very important role - they provide very inexpensive protection for the lens, for both dirt and scratches. An inexpensive filter like this is a lot less expensive to replace than a lens that cost hundreds of dollars. My complaint with this filter is the same as with other inexpensive filters I have used. It's reflective, and in certain situations I can get reflections between the lens and the filter that can mess up an otherwise good image. A fine example is when photographing trains or oncoming cars that have turned on their headlamps. In those cases, this filter interferes and causes very noticeable reflections when the angle is just right. The majority of the time, this filter is fine protection for my lens and I shoot with it in place. However, there are times when it is a detriment and I remove it for those cases. A more expensive filter that cuts down reflections is a better choice for those situations. However, those filters cost a lot more in most cases. This is a decent UV filter for the price. It provides good basic protection for the lens on which it is attached and the price is reasonable. There are cases where it's more of a problem than a help, though, and for those cases it is easy enough to remove.

title: Fun Filter; Use Sparingly
text: I have a gold streak filter that I use occasionally with my main lens. This is the first blue streak filter I have used and I use it with my most versatile (and newer) lens, and so far I am pleased with it. It's a specialty filter that is useful in certain situations. The idea behind this filter is that it has grooves in the glass that trap light and the result is a long, blue streak in the image when a light source is bright enough or is in the frame. This kind of filter is very similar to star filters that create 4-, 6- and 8-point stars, though this one creates just straight lines. When used properly this can cause some very dramatic effects in images, such as when photographing street lights or approaching cars at night. I do need to say, though, that this kind of filter can easily be overused if not thoughtful. When used a lot, the effect can get dull and be more of an annoyance; however, when it is sparingly used it can evoke that "oh wow!" type of response for the unexpected effect. This is a screw-on filter that will fit most standard lenses with threads. Make sure you select a filter size that is matched to your lens. I like this lens filter and the effect it brings to the table. It is a niche product that should be used sparingly, but when used at the right time it can create an eye-popping streak effect.

title: Decent Encrypted Drive; No Linux Support
text: I have had good success with Kingston products (in particular their SSD storage) so I was pleased to have the opportunity to work with this encrypted thumb drive. It has a lot of promise and it works better than other encrypted drives I have used. There is one drawback, at least for me - it does not support Linux (if it does, I haven't figured out how yet). I have the 16GB version, and the thing is built like a tank. It has a metal casing around the inner workings and it can handle some abuse. That's good news if you keep these things in a briefcase or loose in a bookbag. Setup is easy. When it is plugged into a Windows machine (I do not have access to a Mac so I cannot speak to that use case), the software is available and can be used to set up the drive with a password. That's pretty straightforward. If you forget your password, you can wipe the drive and start over but you cannot recover your data. So, choose your password wisely. Copy rates seem to be decent - a little slower than similar-sized drives I have that aren't encrypted but not prohibitively so. It's a trade-off, and a small one at that. When I popped this drive into my Linux machine, the kernel saw it immediately. However, all it could see was the setup partition which is approximately 100mb, a far cry from 16 GB. The drive is smart enough to hide its data from foreign OS-based systems so your data is safe. Linux is gaining users though, and being able to access the data from a Linux system would be good, even if there was a tedious process to get to the partition but still requiring a password. This is better than other encrypted drives I have used in the past which made the data scrambled but was still accessible. However, not being able to use this drive under Linux is a problem for me. To be fair, it is not advertised as compatible with Linux. This is a good drive and from what testing I have done it works well. That said, it does not support Linux and that is a negative for me. Hopefully Kingston will release a Linux-based version (or a software layer) for it in the future; for now it's only usable for me under Windows.

title: Sticks to the Basics
text: I have had excellent results with SanDisk products in the past so I anticipated a good experience with this thumb drive. So far it has met my expectations. There is some room for improvement but in operation it is a solid performer. This is a very simple and straightforward thumb drive with no bells and whistles. It doesn't come with a cap, it doesn't extend/retract, and there isn't even an LED to indicate that it's working. However, it has been reliable up to this point and I have had no issues with transfers. The lack of an LED is mildly problematic because it is difficult to know when a transfer completes, but there are ways to work around that. Speed is excellent. This is the fastest thumb drive I have now. The lack of the LED, not including a cap or making the sleeve retract, and no lanyard are cut corners. All of these would make this a better product. I am not unhappy with this drive and will use it until I wear it out. It is fast and appears to be reliable. It would have been nice if SanDisk had done more than the basics, but what is here is solid.

title: Good OEM Cable Substitute
text: Lightning cables are something that we all need in the house. I selected this one with the thought of having it on the main level of the house, to be available to all of us when we want to charge our phones without hunting down a cable. So far it has worked out very well for us and is one of the better cables with which I have worked. This is a flat cable as opposed to round and I've found this has a couple of big advantages. First, it's a lot less likely get get tangled or kinked which is great. It can be tangled, of course, but it is a lot less likely. The other big plus is that flat cables seem a lot less likely to break near the connectors for some reason. As such, I expect this cable to last for a while and to be easily accessible as long as it's not tangled up with other cables. In use it works great. It charges my phone without issue and it also works just fine as a data cable. I did not see any mention of being it MFi certified anywhere, but it seems to be just fine regardless. So far I have no complaints with this cable. It works, and I like the design.

title: Solid and Inexpensive All-Manual Lens
text: This is my second TTartisan lens for my Fuji X-T3. I have been deeply impressed with my other lens, especially considering the price point, so I had high expectations for this one and it does not disappoint. It's a solid all-manual lens that performs well. Right out of the box, I can't help but notice that this little lens has some serious heft to it. It's a very small and compact lens but it is made of metal and glass, not plastic, so the materials make it more hefty than expected. I like this; I have an expectation that if I fumble this lens it has some chance of surviving a moderate drop. This is a fixed focal length lens with a fast F/2 aperture. It's an all manual lens that does not share data with the camera body, so if you are looking for a lens that autofocuses or sends exposure data to the camera, this is not the lens you want. If you like working with all manual lenses, or if you want to learn more about working with them, this is actually a good choice. Exposures with this lens are dependent on the skill of the photographer, of course, but with the lens set properly exposures come out sharp, bright and with nice bokeh. There is a small bit of vignetting at the corners which is not completely unexpected, and in my case it is actually welcomes as I happen to like mild vignetting in many cases. At the widest aperture setting images are not quite as crisp and sharp as when this lens is stopped down a little, which isn't completely unexpected either. For me, F/2.8 works better, though my "default" setting is F/5.6 (true on all of my manual lenses). The focus ring is tight and smooth and the aperture ring has a solid feel to it as well. It's an easy lens to work with and to "fine tune" when shooting. The focal length makes this a very good choice for portraits. I like this little lens and I will be working with it more in the coming weeks and months. For the price I have no complaints. It's not perfect, but it is better than the price suggests and it seems to be very well made.

title: Works Under Windows and Linux
text: I prefer trackballs like this one to regular mice, and I like the fact that this one is bigger than average so I decided to give it a try. So far I am pleased with it, though it isn't perfect. DELUX is not a brand with which I was previously familiar so I wasn't sure what to expect. My requirements are fairly simple - it has to work with a dongle and it needs to work under both Linux and Windows. It definitely meets both of those requirements nicely and it has not given me any issues. I usually do not use mice with Bluetooth connections so this feature, while useful for connecting to multiple systems, is wasted on me. The dongle, however, is immediately picked up by the Linux kernel as well as by Windows and I was able to plug this in and go with no delays and no effort. This is indeed a larger trackball and it fits my hands wonderfully. I have the hands of a gorilla and finding mice and trackballs that fit me is a challenge and I usually end up settling for something that is less than ideal for me. In this case, the trackball feels good in my hands and there is no strain on my thumbs as I don't have to stretch my hand in weird ways to reach the ball properly. Other reviewers have mentioned that this trackball tends to skip. I have not observed this issue, though I have not had it long and I have not tried to use it with the computer more than a foot away. I also have not tried connecting via Bluetooth, which is when I have had troubles in the past with pointing devices. One thing that would have made this trackball better would have been quiet clicking of the buttons. This is not a quiet device in use, and after using a more quiet trackball it is quite noticeable. One important oversight is that it does not come with a battery. It takes a single AA battery, and I expected one in the box. Every other non-rechargeable pointing device I have purchased has come with a battery in the package. I am not sure why the decision was made to not include one here. This is a nice trackball and I will be using it quite a bit, particularly on my Linux system. It's a good size for me and so far it has worked well. It would have been nice if it was quieter when clicking, and I don't know why there was no battery in the package, but these are smaller issues. I'm pleased with this trackball.

title: Stable and Versatile
text: I selected this clamp for working with my mirrorless camera. There are times when clamping to a surface or a pole is more practical than setting up a tripod or monopod, so this kind of solution is useful in those cases. It's a decent clamp system and it works well, though it does require some messing with it to get used to it if you've only worked with a tripod in the past. This idea is simple here. This is a clamp system that includes a couple of adapters for attaching cameras and accessories so that the camera can be held steady without having to set up a big, bulky tripod or having to hold the camera by hand. It comes with two clamps that can be connected via the ball joint adapter so that the system can convert to an anchor support for a pole as well (not the intended use, but practical nonetheless). Included in the kit is a 1/4" adapter that connects to a standard camera mount (like my mirrorless), and an adapter for connecting a GoPro. It can be used directly with a cell phone, but it is not ideal for that and does require being creative with the clamps (not recommended); better is using the clamp to hold a selfie stick which in turn holds the camera. The clamps hold tight as do the ball joints. It takes a little bit of fiddling but getting this set up exactly as desired is possible so that you can get the perfect angle. Further, the system can hold a little weight and has no trouble at all holding my mirrorless camera steady. It seems to be made well and so far I have not had any issues with loose screws, stripped components, wobbly connectors (when properly tightened) or slipping grips. It's still early on in working with this system but so far I see no red flags. I am happy with this clamp set-up and I will get some good use out of it. It's a practical solution when a tripod or other mount is not workable. It's not particularly expensive, either.

title: Plug and Play
text: I work in an environment where I cannot use wireless connectivity like Wifi or Bluetooth, but I can use my smartphone. This is a problem if I want to use my iPhone 13 for music since I can’t directly connect my earphones or speakers to it. I selected this adapter for this purpose and it has answered the mail for me. This adapter is as simple as it looks - it connects to the lightning port on an Apple device and allows for connecting a 3.5mm jack on the other. There’s no set-up required or anything - it just works. There’s a momentary initial lag as the device is recognized but that’s a very small price to pay for the functionality. It’s designed to present the 3.5mm port at a 90 degree angle from the base of the phone. This is a lot less likely to break or get caught on something which can damage the phone. And, it’s small enough to not add much bulk to the phone. Some real thought went into this little device. It works well and requires no real thought - just plug and play.

title: Decent Frame; Issues with the Clips
text: I have wanted a backdrop for photography for a while and chose this one based on the brand name. I have some experience with Powerextra products, in particular their replacement batteries for a digital camera I own. Based on that previous experience I thought this would be a decent frame for a backdrop. It’s mostly good and I do like it but I found an issue with the clips. This is a fairly simple frame - two tripods with cross braces on which to hang a backdrop. It assembles fairly quickly and also tears down just as quickly. I especially like that the whole things collapses down into a small package that is roughly the same size as a fishing rod carrier and is very portable. In a pinch the whole assembly can fit wholesale inside a duffel bag with other things too, though that somewhat defeats the purpose. This is not a heavy-duty rig which should be obvious from the price. It’s a set-up that I would say is ideal for travel as it’s relatively lightweight and easy to store, but sturdy enough to work in fairly static environments. The main issue I have with this set-up is the set of four clips that come with it. I opened one of them and one of the tips on the clamping end popped off and went flying. It was easy enough to replace it, and it happened again on another one of the clips. I realized two things about the clips - three of the four clips were assembled incorrectly which makes this much more likely to happen, and the tips can be lost fairly easily. The clips are the most easily replaceable part of the whole assembly so in the grand scheme of things this is not a showstopper but more thought could have been put into the clamp design (and assembly) without increasing costs appreciably. This is not a perfect rid for setting up backdrops but it works well enough and the cost is very reasonable. Pay attention to the clip assembly, though, and ensure that the tips are installed correctly.

title: Fun Special Effect Filter
text: I have gotten more into creative photography and I have enjoyed playing with lens filters like these. I have worked with star filters in the past and I thought it might be fun to experiment with this light streak filter as well. So far I have no complaints, though it is the type of filter that should be used sparingly. This is a gold streak filter that works in the same way as star filters, only it channels light in a straight line across the frame instead of in multiple directions. That is, it can make lights look smeared as if swept from one direction in a straight line. The color of the filter lines alters the light slightly and it has a mildly warming effect. Some thought went into this filter and it allows for turning the filter (similar to a CPL) so that it can channel light in any single direction. As with any filter like this, it should be used sparingly. It is possible to have too much of a good thing and as such this can easily be overdone. When used properly and used infrequently it can make some very striking and impactful photos. It seems to be well made. There are no hitches in the turn when making directional adjustments, and the glass does not rattle loosely in the metal frame. I have found no damage to the glass or metal right out of the package either. One question that might come up is, why should you use this kind of filter then it is easy to do the same thing in software? The answer is straightforward - it's fun! This is very much a fun and useful filter but it is a special-use thing that should be used with some restraint. It seems to be well made and it does generate the desired effects. It is not particularly expensive either which is a plus.

title: Excellent Replacement for the Fuji-Branded Battery
text: I needed a second battery for my Fuji X-T3 and I really wasn't excited by the price of the NP-W126S battery, so I looked for third-party replacements. After scraping user forums online and doing some additional research I settled on this one from Nitecore. It has proven to be every bit as good as Fuji brand batteries, and in some ways it's a little better. I knew Nitecore as a manufacturer of flashlights and other light sources in particular. I was previously unaware of their batteries, so I was pleasantly surprised to discover that they had a battery that was an exact fit for my camera. It does fit perfectly, too - pops in and out without fuss and fits the charger without issue. One of the issues with third-party batteries is that the camera will sometimes complain about it and throw up a message about a non-standard battery. I was initially concerned that this one would give me that issue but it has not - my camera accepts it without complaint and it just works. I have been working with it for several months now, and it seems to actually last longer than the original battery that came with my camera (an actual NP-W126S battery). I have fully charged it one time, and since then I have taken well over 200 pictures with my camera (probably closer to 450) and it still has roughly 80% of the charge which is a big improvement. The thing that seems to drain my Fuji battery fastest is powering the camera on and off; this Nitecore battery seems to handle those cycles better. It has overcharge protection and it stops charging when it reaches full capacity, even on the Fuji charger. I was concerned about using it on the original charger and considered getting the Nitecore charger to go with this battery, but it's perfectly happy on the Fuji charger. I like the harder shell on this battery as compared to the original Fuji battery, Eventually this battery will fail; when it does, I am optimistic that the hard shell will keep it from swelling quickly so I can get it out of the camera when it finally starts to fail. I am very happy with this replacement battery and based on my experience with it I can heartily recommend it. The camera doesn't complain about it, it has some built-in overcharge protection and it has a longer duty cycle than the original NP-W126S that came with my camera. When this one eventually fails, I'll get another one.

title: Sony's Midrange ANC Buds
text: I have worked a lot with active noise canceling (ANC) headphones and ear buds, and I was excited to try these as Sony has really come on strong in recent years in this area. I usually do not wear ear buds, favoring full-sized over-the-ear can, but sometimes ear buds are the right answer. I am not unhappy with these. There are two aspects of these that need discussion - the ANC function and the sound quality. I’ll cover each of these separately. The ANC function is good but is not top-notch. That is, it’s very effective at killing off ambient sound and it allows for listening to music at lower volumes without letting in surrounding sounds like fans and air handlers in an office or road noise in a car. It is not as aggressive as some of Sony’s other offerings, but still far and away better than cheaper headphones and ear buds available. I like the fact that I can touch one of the buds and the mode switches to allow more ambient noise through for conversation. This is a common feature for ANC phones of any type anymore, and this pair of buds implements this well. The default sound profile is good but not perfect. The bass is good and not overdriven which is a refreshing change from most phones I have used. The midrange is a little off, with sound being a little muddy and with the slightest of distortion if you’re looking for it. The highs are not sharp and also seem a bit muted like the midrange, though it is not severe enough to write these off by any means. I have worked with ear buds that have better balanced sound profiles, but I have also heard much worse. Now, all that said, with Sony’s application it’s easy to access an equalizer to better balance the sound as desired. I have had no trouble tweaking the active profile in the equalizer to get these to sound better depending on the kind of music I’m listening to. These are Sony’s midrange buds, and are sold at a midrange price point. If these were priced like their top-end buds I would be hesitant to recommend them. At the price point, though, they’re a good option and are better than most off-brand or cheap ear buds available.

title: Small and Fast Storage for PC and Android
text: I like SanDisk storage devices and have used a variety of their products with my electronic devices. I was intrigued by this one because of the small size relative to the capacity. The fact that it can talk to an Android phone as well as a PC is an interesting feature. So far, I am pleased with it. I have the 128GB version and it is more than large enough for my needs, though there is a 256GB version for those that need more space. 20 years ago this kind of space would have been on a large hard drive and cost hundreds if not thousands. This one fits in my pocket and costs less than $20. Times have changed. This device connects to my PC with a USB Type A connector but at 3.0 speeds, meaning I can transfer plenty of data quickly without waiting half the day for it all to transfer. This is handy for moving picture archives or movie files which tend to be large. Both my Windows and my Linux systems see this device and are able to communicate with it. The other interface to this device is a MicroUSB connector, which works for older Android phones. Newer phones have a USB-C connector so be sure that your phone can use this device if that is your intended purpose. It comes with an app for installing on your Android phone to make it easier to manage. I don't have an Android phone anymore but I do have a tablet that runs Android, and this device connects to it without issue. It is small enough that it can fit in the coin pocket of my jeans with plenty of room to spare. This is both good and bad. On one hand, it is very easy to find room for this device no matter how burdened and heavily packed you are but it also means it is easy to misplace. I'd suggest adding a lanyard. So far I am pleased with this device. It is reliable, it has plenty of storage and it works with my PC as well as Android phones. It would be more useful with a lanyard and a USB-C option would be welcome, even if sold as a separate product entirely.

title: Decent Basic Player; Minor Odd Behaviors
text: The last Blu-Ray player I owned bit the dust about a month after we got it and I have been quietly looking for another one to replace it. I was given the opportunity to try this one and I took it. It's not a bad player and it seems to work, but there are a couple of behaviors about it that I do not like. It is as simple a player as it gets. It's not fancy and it doesn't do a lot of extras beyond basic player functions - pause, play, eject, skip, etc. At the end of the day it's all that's needed. It connects via HDMI which is fine, and the resolution and picture size can be tweaked in the menu system which is good. Playback is fine and I have had no issues with picture quality. There are two things about this player that bother me, both of which are annoyances but neither are deal breakers. First, when the unit is powered on it asks for the user to set the language and voice prompting. That's fine the first time. But, this player does it every time it is powered on again and that gets irritating. Second, when a disc is put in and playback starts, there's a very brief hesitation in the sound within the first 10 seconds of playback. This hesitation is just enough to notice, and then it's gone, almost like it skips a quarter-second of sound or something. It doesn't happen again until an eject operation and a disc is inserted again. I have observed this with multiple discs. There is no HDMI cable in the box. Keep that in mind when you buy - you'll need to either have a cable already or you'll have to buy one separately. This is not a bad player and so far it is working better than our previous Blu-Ray player. It sticks to the basics and it gets them right. There are a couple of minor odd behaviors that bug me a little but at the asking price I can overlook those.

title: Excellent Value; Does Not Strobe
text: I do a lot with photography and I always keep my eyes open for good lighting solutions that will help me get the lighting effects I want or need for given situations. I saw this one at a reasonable price and decided to take a chance on it. So far I am very pleased with it. It meets the biggest requirement I have for lighting - it does not strobe. So many LED lights have an issue with strobing, especially when they’re low-cost. This light is not expensive when compared to a lot of others, so even though it is marketed as a video light I was only cautiously optimistic. To determine this for sure, I set my camera to use the electronic shutter only, sped up the shutter speed as high as I could and pointed directly at the light when it was powered on. Strobing lights always show banding in pictures with higher shutter speeds when using the electronic shutter; this one did not (though the display on the camera sure did but that’s a different problem). This test proved to me that this LED light does not strobe, at least not slow enough for my camera sensor to see it at high shutter speeds. This is a fairly large LED panel, designed for video use of course but I also can work just fine for photography or even general lighting in the right setting. It comes with a clamp mount and a pole so it can be attached to a desk or shelf, then the mounting head allows for angling the light as needed so it can light a surface at just the right angle desired. The mount is sturdy and there should be no issues with stability when it is set up properly. The light is super-easy to adjust. There are two dials on the back for tweaking the brightness and the temperature range, and there is a remote included that does the same. The temperature can be adjusted from a warm 2800K to a blistering white 8000K and everywhere in between so you can get the lighting just right. Power is via an AC adapter and there is no battery. So, this is not a travel light by any means, If you need a light to use in the field, unless you have a power generator with you then this light isn’t it. For a static setting in a studio or room, this light is very good. One design decision that would have been nice would have been a detachable mount so it could be used with a standard tripod instead of a clamp mount. That’s not a big deal, especially at the price point, but it would have made this light so much more versatile. I have other lights that I can mount on a tripod, so I am not too concerned. This is a very good video light, especially when considering the price point. It has excellent temperature range, it has a solid mount for stability, and it does not strobe. If you’re looking for a solid video LED light that won’t cost a fortune, this one is better than could be reasonably expected at the asking price. It’s an easy one to recommend.

title: Very Fine Light Stick for Photography
text: I have a strong interest in photography and I always keep an eye open for lights and equipment that will help me take more creative or impactful pictures. I selected this light with the intent of using it for creative photography and so far I am pleased with it. I have other LED lights that have similar functions, but this one is different in a few ways that set it apart. This is a wand light as opposed to a square LED bank. As such, the light distribution is a bit different. It can directly cover a longer (wider) area which is handy when putting together a mock-up with miniatures. It has a couple of mounting options too, utilizing either a miniature tripod (included) or magnetically attaching to a metal surface. I do wish a clamp was included such that it could attach to the tripod horizontally, but such clamps are available if they're needed. This light is VERY bright and can easily light a small room when at full brightness. It can be dimmed to cast a soft light too which is good. It's not exactly the most ideal light source but it will work for general lighting in a pinch. The temperature range goes from 2500k (very warm and orange-y) to 9900k (blistering cold white) and everywhere in between. Getting the color just right is relatively easy though it does take a little patience and experimentation to get it right. Do keep in mind that because this is an LED-based light, the temperature band setting is quite narrow and presents a different light profile, one that the camera can see but the human eye cannot. In addition to "natural lighting" modes it can be set for specific colors too such as purple, red, blue and so on. Charging is done via a USB-C port, and the charging cable is included. I have not tried using this as a power source to charge my phone though the documentation doesn't say much about that. A full charge on this light lasts a while, though I have not drained it all the way down to find out how long it will last. Obviously the runtime is variable based on mode and brightness, and what is interesting about this light in particular is that it displays the estimated runtime on the screen based on current settings - this is a nice feature that I have not seen on a lot of these lights. There are some creative modes for use with video or for special effects in a live setting, though the usefulness of these modes is dependent on the user. I personally will never use them. However, in the right hands these might be very useful for a project. There are several effects available, including police flashers, tube TV glow simulation, flickering candle and more. The light comes with a nice canvas carrying pouch that provides basic storage and protection. I really like this light and will be working with it more in the coming weeks and months. It has some nice features and it has good color and brightness ranges. It's not terribly expensive either.

title: Bass Boost that Can Be Turned Off!
text: I am usually not a big fan of on-ear headphones. I have learned through experience that Philips makes good headphones, though, and based on the brand name I selected this set of headphones to try out. So far I am pleased with them. As mentioned, these are on-ear phones. For me, I prefer over-the-ear phones which are more comfortable most of the time, and that is probably the only complaint I have with these. After wearing these for a while I need to take them off for a short time before I can put them back on and keep going. This is true with most on-ear phones I have tried. For on-ear phones, though, these aren't bad and the ear fatigue is less than many I have used. This particular set boasts an on-demand bass boost, and for me that's a huge plus. Most headphones have the bass boost baked right in and there's no way to turn it off. I don't care for heavy-handed bass (gives me headaches), so for me it is a feature I will leave turned off most of the time. However, there are times when the bass needs some help, and these deliver. When activated, there is a very noticeable increase in bass response that will certainly make some people happy. So, about the sound profile... A set of headphones isn't worth any amount of money if they sound bad. These are fairly balanced phones when the bass booster is turned off. The highs are bright and clear, the midrange is warm and the bass is present but not overwhelming. The bass becomes front and center when the boost is turned on. These connect via Bluetooth and they pair and establish connection quickly. I have no complaints. These are good on-ear phones that work well. They're reasonably comfortable, and they connect well. The most interesting feature, to me, is the on-demand bass booster which is better than having a continuous bass boost that's built in. For me, that's a major positive point and is the reason I will continue using these. These sound good.

title: Nice Smaller Bendy-Leg Tripod
text: This is marketed as a tripod designed for the Nest camera, but I didn’t get it for that particular use. Instead, I selected it for two purposes – first as a low-profile support for a video light and second as a tabletop tripod mount for my camera that will fit in my camera bag. It is a decent little tripod, not perfect but good for my purposes. This is a small-profile tripod, measuring about 12” (a little more) when folded up as it comes from the package. It is fully assembled and is completely ready to go. The legs are initially straight; they are bendy though and can be adjusted some to increase/decrease the height as well as wrap around things to secure the tripod in place. The head has a standard mounting screw so it will fit most cameras and similar accessories. My video light uses this size of screw so it attaches very easily and securely to the tripod. There is an adjustment ring on the mounting screw that allows for getting the mount tight against the device to which it is attached, even when the whole screw does not fit. The head also has a ball joint so that it can tilt the device in any direction and secure it without issue. It works a bit better than other bendy-leg tripods I have used. It seems to be more stable in most situations. In particular, when the legs are wrapped around something and it is suspended off the ground, it doesn’t slip quite as readily, though with enough weight it can be shifted which should be fairly obvious. The one area where this tripod could be improved is in the feet at the ends of the legs. These are smooth, rubber feet and most of the time they’re adequate for keeping the tripod stable and still. That said, on an modest incline they are not non-slip enough to keep the tripod from shifting, especially when on a moving surface (I know, this is an unusual circumstance, but it does happen occasionally). It’s easy enough to work around this with some tacky adhesive like you might find in a classroom, but it would be nice if this wasn’t necessary. On smoother inclined surfaces there are better solutions. This is a nice little tripod that works reasonably well. It is not perfect but it does work better than a lot of other small, bendy-leg tripods. It’s made well and it fits nicely in my camera bag. Consider this one if you are looking for a small tripod.

title: Fun Display Boards; Require Gentle Care and Cleaning
text: I enjoy photography as a serious hobby and I lean to the creative side of it. I selected this set of display boards with the thought of doing more creative things with my pictures and so far I am happy with them. I will say they're not ideal for all situations and environments, though, and they require some gentle care. In a nutshell, these are plastic round platters that are matte finished on one side and glossy on the other. In the right lighting, these can make a photo really pop, particularly when using the black reflective surface. The white disk is good for darker subjects, while the black disk is better for reflection in low light situations. There are a couple of things about these that merit mention. First, these are plastic platters and are susceptible to scratches. Once the glossy side is scratched, these are basically no longer useful in their intended roles (the black disk in particular), though they can be repurposed. More subtle though is the fact that the black disk shows dust easily and when used in dusty environments it is almost useless. I wiped the black glossy surface with a microfiber cloth, and I hit it with an air duster can, and I still had particles that required editing after the fact to remove from the final image after less than 30 seconds of set-up after cleaning. I do like these display boards and I will get some good use from them. That said, these are not perfect and require some gentle care to keep them useful.

title: MUCH Better than Expected
text: I have a Fuji X-T3 and I have not shied away from third-party lenses at all. I have been looking for good wide-angle lenses and I have been aware of TTArtisan for a while. I was curious how well this lens would perform and I decided to take a chance on it. So far I am very pleased with it though I am still working with it and learning that it can do. This lens is a brick! Right out of the box I was startled at the overall weight. It has a lot of glass in it, but it also is all metal - very little (if any) plastic. Even the front lens cap is metal. In spite of the price, this is a solid little lens. It is probably the tightest fit lens I have used. It requires a little pressure to get it to click into place and to remove it later when mounting on the camera body. I was a little concerned at first, thinking I could potentially damage the camera. However, it does fit and does not harm the camera in spite of how tightly it fits. Optical quality seems to be good, though that varies a little with the aperture setting. At the widest settings (and f/1.4 in particular) there is a little softness in the corners and a slight vignetting. As the aperture is closed more the image gets sharper at the edges. This is not unusual or unexpected for wide-angle large-aperture lenses, and it is actually slightly better than I was expecting. I have not yet had a chance to get out and determine the coma with this lens. I am waiting for a clear night so I can get a starry sky shot with the aperture wide open, which will highlight not only the coma but also the chromatic characteristics. If it is particularly bad I will come back and update. As a portrait or landscape lens this one works very well. Initial exposures have worked out well, but I am still learning what this lens can do. Are there better wide-angle lenses out there? Sure - and they cost a lot more too. For the price this lens is far better than expected and I am looking forward to working with it more. It is good enough that I am staring to look at other TTArtisan offerings.

title: Comfortable, Quiet Operation
text: I selected this mouse/keyboard combo to work with a laptop I use every day. I wanted a full-sized keyboard and I was less concerned about the mouse because I prefer trackballs anyway. So far I have no complaints at all about this combo set, though I am especially pleased with the keyboard. This is a basic mouse/keyboard combo that connects via an RF receiver. The keyboard is a full-sized US layout keyboard, and the mouse is a basic 3-button mouse. These are marketed as having silent keys and clicks, and that interested me in particular. The keyboard is indeed nearly silent. I love the quiet operation and I love the feel of the keys themselves - they have a soft-down feel when pressed. I read one of the other reviews that stated that the keys stick a little, and I have not found that to be the case for me. The mouse is also quiet and it seems to work well, though it is nothing special. This combo works well under Windows 10, Windows 11 and Linux. I have not tried it elsewhere though I have no reason to believe it wouldn't work on other platforms. I am very happy with this combo set and expect years of service from it. It does live up to the claim that operation is very quiet, the keys have a nice feel to them, and the combo is priced reasonably.

title: Interesting Approach to Noise Reduction
text: Most of the headphones with which I have worked have been active noise canceling (ANC) phones so I know a lot about those, but I also have other headphones too that I like. I was unaware that 3M even had headphones, and I was also unsure what their "Quiet Space" was all about. It's an interesting solution that works fairly well. Overall, these are good phones, though there's one area that could use some slight improvement and that's the sound profile. These are over-the-ear phones and they are actually quite comfortable. I like how they feel on my head - they fit snugly and I can tilt my head without losing these phones, but they don't clamp down super tight either. Build-wise, these are more substantial than the price suggests. I like the size adjustment in particular which is designed to last and should not fatigue with use. I powered these on and they quickly paired and connected to my laptop. The range is good and I was able to walk a fair distance away without losing the connection or having the sound get crackly or having it skip. With no feed coming to them they eventually powered themselves off, saving battery but potentially frustrating the wearer if this is unexpected. Just putting these on I was surprised by the amount of noise isolation. Without even turning these on they drastically reduced the ambient noise in the room, even effectively blocking out the sound of a running fan. I have had very few headphones that have as effective sound isolation as these, and that's a huge plus right out of the gate. The Quiet Space function adds to this, but not like ANC phones - it injects white noise into the cans so all you hear is a gentle but constant hiss that overrides most other noises. It's not deathly quiet with these on, but you won't hear most other sounds in the area when they're producing white noise. This is a very different approach to sound cancellation and it works. The sound profile is the one area where these phones could use a little improvement, though these are not terrible and are better than some big-name phones I have used. The bass is not overdriven but it is not muted either, and this is refreshing since most manufacturers overdrive the bass. The highs are clear, though not shrill. The midrange, however, is flat to the point that music can sound slightly hollow. It's an easy fix with an equalizer and is better than one particular big-name manufacturer's similar flaw. I like these phones and will be working with them more. They take a different approach to dealing with ambient noise and surrounding distractions than what ANC phones use, and they seem to work well. They're well made, comfortable and reasonably priced.

title: More Comfortable Than It Looks
text: I selected this mouse as much for the cool factor as for the function. I needed a wireless mouse to use with a laptop and this one looked like a good fit. So far I have no complaints, but I do offer one word of caution with it. The most obvious thing about this mouse is the strange appearance. It doesn't resemble any other mouse I have used and at first it looks like it might be uncomfortable on the hands. On the contrary, though, it is quite comfortable and I have had no issues with it being too small for my hands even though it is a typical-sized mouse. I used with with my Windows 10 system and it works just fine. I have not tested it against my Linux system though I have no reason to believe it won't work - every other wireless mouse I have tried has worked without any trouble at all so I expect this one to be no different. If it proves otherwise I will return here and update. I ran into an immediate issue with this mouse - I could not find the receiver and as such I was unable to get it to connect to the system. It does not have any Bluetooth capability so that is not an option. As it turns out, the receiver was packaged in the box but was in a small plastic baggie separate from the mouse and when the box was opened to remove the mouse the receiver fell out, unnoticed. I thought I had been sent a mouse without the receiver until I finally realized what had happened and located the receiver. So, use some caution when taking this mouse out of the box. Overall, I am pleased with this mouse. It works as expected and is more comfortable than it looks.

title: Large and Comfortable
text: I don't have a lot of experience with HP peripherals, particularly mice, so I was on unfamiliar ground when working with this one. This has proven to be a decent mouse and so far I am pleased with it. This is a big mouse so it is well-suited for people with large hands like me. I like the fact that it is comfortable to use for long periods of time and it doesn't cause my hands to cramp like some other mice. I have had many mice that have caused me some issues in use so it is something to which I pay attention. The buttons work as expected right out of the box. This is a 7-button mouse - more buttons than I'm used to - and the buttons work as you'd expect - left- and right-click, forward page, back page, scroll, etc. Finding the wireless dongle was a little frustrating at first. It is tucked underneath, hidden under a removable panel that is held in place magnetically. I did not understand that the panel came out, even though a graphic printed on the bottom showed where to push. Once I realized that I found the wireless dongle and was able to connect it just fine. Now that said, this mouse does not require the dongle but can use Bluetooth as well and can be used with three devices. The scroll wheel can be smooth or it can be stepped, and that is controlled through a single mechanical button on the top of the mouse. This button tends to be a little fussy and I have had some minor issues getting the button to work as expected. It does work, it just requires deliberate and focused attention, not a half-attentive push. I am not sure if this is just my mouse or is an issue with the design overall. It's minor but noticeable. And, this mouse works flawlessly under Linux as well as under Windows. I like this mouse and will use it on one of my laptops. It fits my hand very well and it works as expected.

title: Much Better than Expected
text: I usually do not use ear buds and favor over-ear headphones when I am listening to music or am traveling. I decided to take a chance on these ear buds based on the fact that they have active noise canceling. These are better than I expected. These bear a striking resemblance to Apple’s Air Pods which is no accident. Apple makes a great product and at a glance these are very similar. I popped these in and they immediately were available for pairing. Pairing took almost no time at all and they were ready to go. Some headphones and ear buds take a good bit of time to connect or are hard to discover; these were simple and straightforward. I can’t really ask much more than that. The ANC function is not on by default, and it turns on and off with a touch and hold on either bud. When it kicks on, the impact is dramatic and immediate. I have a fan that I use for testing ANC headphones, and with it on it faded out nearly completely when I activated ANC on these buds. It is not as aggressive as something like Sony or Bose ANC, but it is good enough to say it’s better than average. With the ANC engaged, listening at low volume levels is easy and background sounds are usually not an issue. The sound profile is fairly balanced, which is a neat trick for ear buds (particularly with ANC). The highs are very clear and bright, almost to the point of being piercing though not to the pain threshold. The midrange is surprisingly warm and full and music sounds balanced as a result. Bass is present and reasonable which is a rare find anymore since most manufacturers boost bass to uncomfortable levels and usually at the expense of the midrange. These are surprisingly comfortable for in-ear-canal buds. Usually I struggle with ear buds that fit inside the opening of the ear canal and they either start to hurt after a while or they make my ears itch. These are light and they almost don’t feel like they’re in my ears at all. I actually will wear these more then other buds I have used simply because of how comfortable they are in comparison. I like that these do not need an app to be adjusted. These are a pleasant surprise in ear buds for me. They work well, have good sound and the ANC is surprisingly effective. These are priced very competitively too which is a big plus.

title: Finding the Balance
text: I have worked with a lot of ANC headphones, and I have a different pair of JVC phones that have served me well. I looked to these phones as a possible replacement for a dead pair of Bose QC-15 phones that finally just wore out. These are good phones that balance sound quality and ANC nicely. The ANC function is what interested me most about these and I set about testing them. These work very well but they are not as aggressive as Bose or Sony when it comes to actively cancelling out low-frequency noise. This is a good thing in most cases as the aggressive ANC on Bose and Sony is actually uncomfortable when turned on. Where the two bigger players go all-out for maximum ANC function, these go for "good enough for most" and in terms of how they compare against other manufacturers such as Sennheiser, Philips, and other well-known brands they compare well. They cancel out the lion's share of low droning noises such as road noise and fans, enough so that turning on music at low volumes is still workable in noisy environments. The sound profile is another important consideration and I have seen a wide variance in sound quality, particularly among ANC phones. These get the sound profile fairly close to right which is a refreshing change. The bass is present and strong but isn't pushed forward as with so many other headphones. The midrange is warm and gives music a decent depth. The highs are clear and bright without being shrill. These aren't audiophile quality phones by any means, but they are better than many I have used. These are over-the-ear phones which is my preference. I also like that these fit snugly and don't slip off whern I look down which is also a personal preference but it's important to me. If you like a very light set of phones these probably are not quite the right fit for you; if you like a set that fits a bit more firmly, these are good in that regard. These are comfortable too. The ear cups are padded nicely and I can wear them for a couple of hours before I need to take them off for a few minutes. Most headphones I have worn get uncomfortable after a while, and these do also but it is not as quick as with many. My one complaint is the way these are powered on and off. Instead of a simple on/off button or switch, the cans swivel to power them on and off. I can see the potential for taking them off and leaving them powered on, resulting in reduced useful runtime. I like these phones and have been working with them quite a bit of late. They're not a complete replacement for more aggressive ANC phones but they get the sound profile right and they are comfortable enough to wear for a long flight. These strike a nice balance between comfort, ANC capability and sound quality.

title: Nice Video Light for Vloggers
text: I selected this light for working with my camera, though I have other lights that are good for the tasks I have in mind. I have had good experiences with Logitech products and I had good expectations for this light. For the most part I am pleased with it. This is a small LED-based light that is designed to attach to a flat screen monitor and be used for video lighting. The target audience is very clearly vloggers and video makers, though it can be adapted for other uses with some thought. The main feature of this light which is important enough to mention is that it is a non-strobing LED, meaning no striping when at high shutter speeds. The light has a couple of settings that can be adjusted by buttons on the back. It can be brightened or darkened, and the color temperature can be adjusted as needed. I personally like using a warm setting more than a cool setting, but that's a preference and it changes based on what I am doing. There is some graduation in the levels though they are granular enough for my needs. The head of the light can be tilted forward and backward, so there is some adjustment that can be made. It is not adjustable from side to side, though. Also, it must be mounted on a surface where it can hang, not placed on a desk stand-alone. As such, it is specifically designed for hanging on a monitor. The one thing about this light that I do not care for is that it does not have any battery capacity. That is, it must be plugged in to a USB outlet to work. That's probably again related to being marketed as a vlogging tool, but it does reduce portability when a USB port is unavailable for use. It can be rigged to work with a power bank which is a sloppy work-around, but this is simply a patch. This is a decent light for video work and it is very definitely a tool for vloggers and video makers. It has no battery capacity so it must be plugged in to work, but otherwise it is a nice light that works well.

title: Fine Black Diffusion Filter
text: I have worked with K&F Concept filters in the past and generally had good experiences with them. They're good, mid-range quality filters at (usually) a budget price. I haven't worked with any black diffusion filters prior to this one so I have no basis against which to compare, but so far it seems to work as designed and seems to be made very well. In a nutshell, this type of filter softens light a bit, causing some gentle halos around light sources, without impacting image sharpness or detail. Where I have seen the most noticeable impact is in images where there otherwise would be a lot of shadows and contrast; instead of stark contrast and strong shadows, the filter has the effect of brightening up the shadows somewhat and creating smoother color gradients. Sure, this can be done in software after the fact, but it is a lot easier to do this at the time the image is taken and it certainly is a lot less work. The filter is very easy to install. This is my first magnetic filter and it is as easy to attach to my camera as I could have hoped. The threaded ring attaches to the lens in the same manner as a step ring or another filter, and the filter itself just snaps securely into place due to the magnetics. Removing the filter is just as simple, especially if you choose to leave the magnetic ring in place on the lens. The assembly seems to be well made. I have had filters in the past that have been poorly constructed and rattle in the frames when shaken, or have been mildly blemished, or just felt cheap. This filter has none of those issues and appears to be well made. This is a nice black diffusion filter. It's easy to install and use, and it just works. I will be using it more in the coming weeks.

title: Inexpensive and Easy to Install; Reduces Camera Shake
text: I have wanted a soft-release button for my Fuji X-T3 for a while and finally decided to treat myself. I chose this one as it specifically names my camera as one model it supports. It seems to work well so far. This particular button does fit my camera as advertised. As a soft release button it works well. It’s a little smoother and easier to use that directly pushing the shutter button on the camera, and it saves a fraction of a second of effort which can make the difference between getting a shot and just missing. What makes it a worthwhile accessory though is the reduction in camera shake it offers when pressing down versus the effort needed without it. The reduced camera shake is what I think is meant in the description by “no wobbling”. The button itself exaggerates the play in the shutter button on the camera which is fairly loose (not firmly restrained from slight jiggling). There are two of these little buttons in the pack. Properly installed, I suspect the second will never be needed. Both come in individual pouches and include a rubber gasket. Because if the size of the gasket, I’d recommend using a pair of tweezers to put it on the post - if you drop it there’s a fair chance you’ll lose it. From the product listing’s photos this button looks convex. It is not - it is concave. So far I am not unhappy with this soft release button. It fits my camera properly and it looks nice. It speeds shooting and reduces camera shake when pressing the button which for me is a win.

title: Got it Working Under Linux
text: I am a little different when it comes to computer users. I use Windows for email and photo editing, but just about everything else I do on Linux. I selected this drive for use on my Linux laptop and so far I am happy with it. It's very fast and it works very well. Linux recognizes the drive straight away. Note that Windows sees it too but it's not readily usable. I took the time to repartition and rebuild the drive with a different file system in order to optimize it for use under Linux, but that was the plan from the beginning. Once rebuilt I plugged it into the USB-C port and away we went. This drive is FAST. I have been able to copy large ISO images (9GB) in short order and it doesn't miss a beat. So far it has been reliable too, so this has become my new backup drive. This drive might be designed around Mac users but it does work under Linux (and I presume Windows as well) with some coaxing. It's fast and seems to be reliable.

title: Good Improvements Over Older Smart Watch Models
text: I have used smart watches for a while now and I have seen a steady progression in the technology. This is my first Gen 6 watch. It is a big improvement from what I have used before (beyond just battery life) and so far I am pleased with it. This is an Android-based smart watch, and it is similar in interface to previous smart watches I have seen and used. If you have used any generation of smart watch before this one the experience is very similar. I won't get too deep into the nuts and bolts of that or the WearOS app. There are two big areas of improvement I have seen with this new watch. First, the battery life is much better than previous smart watches I have used which is very encouraging. I have a Gen 2 watch that I love but it lasts only about 3 days on a charge, and my Gen 5 is not much better. This one lasts several days before the battery runs out. The more important improvement to me, though, is the way it doesn't interfere with the Bluetooth in my car. Previous watches messed up my ability to stream to the car's sound system to the point that the sound would sputter and simply die. I did trace it to the watch by powering off the watch completely after which the problem went away and would come back when the watch was powered on. This watch does not interfere at all and my car's Bluetooth works whether the watch is on or not. This is a stylish watch, a bit more upscale than some of the others I have seen and used. The band is a non-stretch link band that is a little snug but not unworkable. So far this watch works well for me. I am pleased with the improved battery life and even more happy that it doesn't mess with my car's Bluetooth connectivity.

title: Works with Linux; Bright and Clear
text: I selected this monitor to work on a beefy laptop I use for building Linux virtual machines and testing software, so my use case is a little different than the target audience. I have been needing a larger monitor to go with said laptop and this one seemed to be a good one. So far I am pleased with it, though I have not pushed it to its full potential. This is a 27" display capable of 2560x1440 resolution, fast refresh rates and bright colors. In the box comes the panel itself, a stand, and a DisplayPort cable. I was a little surprised that there was no HDMI cable in the box but this is all right, I have a couple of them so I was not left wanting. My initial testing was disastrous, though the issue proved to be a fault with the laptop, not the monitor. My laptop has an HDMI output, and it does provide enough power to let the monitor know that something is there, but it intermittently sends a signal so I was not getting a consistent display. After a couple of hours, the monitor would display nothing at all. Thinking I had a dud, I connected a different system to verify and the monitor came right up. It did the same with a second system as well. After some research I determined that the issue was the graphics card in my main laptop which has known problems with HDMI. I bought an adapter to connect to the Thunderbolt port on the laptop and everything works fine now. The system connected to this monitor is a gaming laptop that is running Linux with VMs installed. The system properly reports the model number of the display which is a very good sign. The OS does not push the monitor like a Windows gaming system might when used for actual gaming. For me, the screen real estate is what I needed. The adapter I bought caps the resolution at 1920x1200, so I am not getting the full resolution from this monitor but it is more than enough for my purposes. The monitor responds to signal on both HDMI ports. So far I have not had occasion to try using the DisplayPorts on the back. The display is very bright and clear, with no dead pixels. It seems to keep up very well with the system with no apparent lag, though again I am not pushing it as hard as I could. Because of the way I have it connected I can't bump up the refresh rate though it is happy at 60Hz. It doesn't appear to flicker to my eyes (though my camera disagrees), and it does not induce headaches. If I could make any changes at all, I would change the design of the stand/base. The base is not height-adjustible so I cannot raise or lower the monitor without getting an arm harness. That's a minor complaint and is not enough to get myself upset about but it is worth mentioning. Admittedly I am not the typical use case for a monitor like this, but I am happy with it nonetheless and it works well for me. The issues I have had with this monitor were related to other hardware, not the monitor itself. It seems to work very well, it is bright and clear and it gives me the screen real estate that I need. The fact that the Linux system recognizes its model number is a plus - it's supported.

title: Decent Slider, but Room for Improvement
text: I am primarily a stills shooter. That said, I do have an excellent camera that is very capable of shooting video and I do need it for such on occasion. I was interested in this camera slider as a way to get smooth shots and to reduce reliance on lens-based stabilization which is not included in my camera body. This has been a learning experience and while I like this slider there is definitely room for improvement. I will start with the basics. This is a large and fairly heavy animal, which is to be expected. It is roughly 3' long and in it’s most basic configuration rests on a flat surface with no issues. It does have some adjustments that can be made to the individual feet on the frame so it can be adjusted slightly for uneven but mostly level surfaces without using any other equipment. To get much more versatility out of it, though, it can be mounted on tripods on either end to raise it higher or to set up angular shots. The motor on the frame is controlled by a remote which comes with a battery pack. The remote is not wireless and has to be connected to the motor via the provided cabling. This is all right, but wireless functionality would make it much more versatile. It should be noted that the remote controls the slider, not the camera. I had some concern about this in the very beginning, thinking that the remote would be incompatible with my camera and that this unit would not work for me. I encountered some issues that bother me. First, when powered on and running the motor runs the slider down the track until it is either stopped or a stop point is set. If one is not set, it bumps into the end and keeps trying to go beyond, making an awful noise that will surely mess up any video that requires sound. In my mind, the motor should detect when it hits the end and stop, even if start and stop points are not set. When the motor is running and it is not near a stop point, it runs at constant speed and it is very smooth. When manually paused, it stops quickly but it doesn’t jerk to an abrupt stop like it hit something. But, if one of the end points are set and is reached, the motor slows down, then jerks to a stop, enough to notice in video footage. This is most obvious when the remote is set up to film in a loop as the issue can be observed repeatedly. The motor is not silent, though it is quiet. It is not loud enough to ruin a shot unless absolute quiet is needed, and the motor produces a low-volume, low-frequency hum that slightly resembles the sound of an electric trolling motor on a bass boat, but quieter. The point is that it is by no means silent, but it should be good enough in the majority of cases. This is out the window if the motor is allowed to reach the end of the track before it is stopped, in which case the noise is likely to be a serious issue. This is a decent slider and if used with some thought will serve nicely. There are definitely some places where it could be improved, particularly in the way it fails to handle reaching the end of tracks.

title: Words Fine in My Dash Cam
text: I selected this memory card because I needed one for a dash cam. When it comes to storage, name bands are usually the way to go when you need something really reliable, so I was a little hesitant at first to use a "store brand" card. So far, it has been fine and I have no complaints, though it will take time and more use to determine if it will hold up long-term. The card I received is a 128GB MicroSD with an adapter. The adapter makes it work in a camera like my mirrorless, but I would not recommend this kind of set-up unless pressed. The adapter is really most useful when pulling data from the card in a machine that does not have a slot for a MicroSD, so the adapter does have its place. The card fit in my dash cam with no issues and the cam seems to be happy with it. It detects the presence of the card and the full capacity of it which is good. Being a class 10 card it is fast enough to keep up with the recording and in a 45 minute trip it did not skip or stutter once. Quality seems to be fine. Using the adapter, my PC has no trouble reading the card and reformatting when I want to quickly erase it. So far, this card has worked out just fine and I am pleased with it. It's priced well and it seems to work well in the way I need it to work. Time will tell if it will hold up, but so far all indicators are positive.

title: Made Well and Works Well
text: USB-C cables are the one cable type I usually have trouble putting my hands on in my house, and I need them for charging my tablet as well as my video lights. I selected this one because I like cables with braided insulation and so far this one has worked out well for me. This is a 6' cable which is just about right for my needs. It is long enough to reach my devices when I have it plugged into my USB brick on my desk without requiring rearrangement of everything on my desk just to make it fit. Longer would be handy but unnecessary, but shorter would make it a lot less useful for me. I have not used it for data transfer, just charging up devices, and so far it has worked out well in that capacity. The connection is snug and I have not noticed any particular difference in charging speeds between this cable and the OEM cables that came with my devices. I am especially pleased with the build quality. The cable is stiff (as to be expected) and it should hold up for a long time against kinks and twists. The junctions where the cable goes into the plastic casings for the connectors are tight and allow no play which is a big plus for me as these are the spots where I have had cables fail most often. Overall, I am not unhappy with the build quality. This is a decent third-party USB-C cable that works very well for me. It is made well and it does a fine job charging my devices. It isn’t too expensive either, making it easy to recommend.

title: Very Versatile LED Video Light; Priced Very Well
text: I do a lot of creative photography work and I look for tools and ideas that will help me along in that regard. I took a chance on this LED light, thinking it would be a good tool for adding color and light when I need it, and so far I am pleased with it. This is not a very big light, about the size of an iPhone. It's small enough that finding a place for it in my camera bag takes little effort and it is always at the ready when I need it without requiring a bunch of storage. It comes in a carrying case and even the case is small. If you need a small light, keep reading. This is advertised as a video light, so one of the most important things to consider is whether or not is strobes. A lot of cheap LEDs strobe which makes them inappropriate for video work (or high speed photography for that matter). This is not a super-cheap light, more expensive than many of the LED banks I have seen, so I assumed it would not strobe and this assumption was correct. When considering that it is a non-strobing LED that is priced around $70 (as I write this), this thing is a bargain - good video lights are often more than double the cost. This light is a very interesting tool. I have other LED video lights, and these typically have a brightness setting, a few effects, and gel plates that can be used to tweak the color. This particular LED bank is different in that it allows for adjusting not only the brightness but also the colors, with RGB broken out into components that can be adjusted individually. So, if you need a really bright yellow light, a pale green light or a cool blue, this light can do it. Whatever color/brightness you need, there's a way to get it out of this light. This light also has a number of effects that will suit a videographer. I spent some time playing with these and cycling through the different effect modes. There's lightning flash, police lights, faulty bulbs and more, and these can be adjusted like the solid modes can be. These modes are not really of any use to me at the moment, personally, as I do not do video work much at all, but I can see some things I can do with them for fun and I do like having them available should I decide to do any video work later. When I received this light it was mostly discharged and I needed to plug it in to charge. The documentation says it takes about 2 hours to fully charge and that's fairly accurate. The display shows the charging level and it doesn't take too long from almost dead to fully changed. Though I am unlikely to need it, I like that I can charge a USB device with this light, like it's a power bank. I have not tried charging/powering my camera with it yet, but I like the idea that I can do that. This light comes with a hot shoe mount and USB-C charging cables. While it can be mounted on a tripod, a selfie stick is more versatile and makes getting this light in the right position easy. This is a neat little light and it is worth more than the asking price in my opinion. It seems to work very well, it has a lot of neat creative modes and, most importantly, it does not strobe. If you need a well-priced LED light that works well for video and high-speed photography, this is a good one to consider.

title: Better than Average ANC Phones
text: I have worked with a lot of active noise canceling (ANC) headphones by a lot of manufacturers, including an older pair of Philips headphones. I’ve seen a wide variance in ANC implementation and sound profiles, and to be honest few manufacturers get theirs right. With this set of headphones, Philips comes close. These are over-ear phones which I prefer over on-ear phones. They fit snugly but not tight, and they actually do a good job of sound isolation. Even if you don’t like the ANC function (which would defeat the purpose of having these phones), these do a surprisingly good job of sound isolation. The pads are soft enough and comfortable enough that I can wear these for quite a while without discomfort. After a bit of time they do start to get a little warm but not to the point that I need to take them off. These connect via Bluetooth and they connect very quickly. The connectivity of these phones is absolutely amazing: this is the very first pair of Bluetooth headphones I have used that maintains a steady connection up two flights of stairs with closed doors in between the phones and the source. The connectivity alone makes these very much worth checking out. The ANC function is very good though it is not quite as aggressive as that of Bose or Sony. It is strong enough to mostly drown out a droning high-volume fan (my baseline for testing), such that music at a low volume while the ANC is turned on completely drowns out the fan. While Bose and Sony go to the extreme for noise cancellation, and other manufacturers often have ANC that’s barely there, Philips has implemented a system that is good enough for most. I am pleased with the ANC and will use these phones when I travel next. The ANC function on these phones can be turned off if desired. There is also a special “awareness mode” that is an in-between mode that doesn’t completely turn off ANC but allows more environmental noise in, and this mode is really designed for permitting conversation without having to turn everything off completely. It works fairly well though the noise this mode produces via the external microphone is slightly harsh and shrill. The default sound profile is not exactly perfect but it is better than many I have used and heard. These do boost the bass by default though not to an uncomfortable level. Bass boost is very common in headphones and it’s often too aggressive, but these actually give a modest boost. The midrange is a little soft though present. The highs sound bright and clear but not piercing. As a result, the sound profile is not quite perfectly balanced but it still good. The sound profile can be tweaked via an app. I found the Philips Headphones app, installed it and started messing with it. The app works better than the reviews have suggested and it does a decent job of adjusting the headphones on the fly. The mode can be changed as well as the sound profile to adjust for different could quality based on music type, and there is a custom setting so that the equalizer can be adjusted to taste. The only complaint I have with the app is that there is about a 1s pause when changing modes between ANC. Awareness mode and Off, though this gap does not occur when changing the mode via the button on the headphones. I like these ANC phones. They’re not perfect but they’re better than average with a good ANC function and decent sound. The have absolutely incredible connectivity, and they can be adjusted to taste via an app. This is a pair to keep on the short list if you need Bluethooth headphones that maintain a connection a long way from the source and provide ANC in the deal.

title: Love the Watch, the Software not so Much
text: I have a smartwatch that I have worn now for over a year and I have been pleased with it. I was unfamiliar with the idea of a "hybrid smartwatch" and was interested in this one from Skagen. It's an interesting concept and the watch itself seems to work well, but I have some frustrations with the software. This is basically a traditional analog watch with some smartwatch functions built into it. The smartwatches I have used usually have a full digital face with all manner of things on the display, and depending on the face chosen it may or may not be easy to read. This watch keeps things relatively simple and has the hour and minute displayed with moving hands, and around the center are displays for steps, heart rate and weather-at-a-glance. The whole is clean and easy on the eyes. Now, that said, if you cannot read an analog watch this one might not be the best choice. Charging requires the special cable that comes with it and it takes a relatively short time to charge. The run time is much longer than most smartwatches I have used, getting well over a week on a single charge where a smartwatch is often 2-3 days or less. Skagen has a special app for interacting with the watch and it was easy to find in the repository. It installs quickly and guides through the setup without too much issue. It is good for activity tracking and limited health monitoring as well as limited customization of the face. However, I have had some difficulty with connectivity and staying connected through the app, such that it has been an annoyance. This is the biggest complaint I have so far. So far this watch has managed to keep good time, connected or not.
