Plan accordingly if you choose to transport this light. This is an adequate unit for its target audience but will leave the aspiring professional underwhelmed. If you are looking for something that will work sufficiently for making posts to social media this is a reasonable unit; if you need a serious ring light for photography, consider other options. The main problem with this light is the fact that it is designed for portability but comes with no carrying case; keep this in mind.

title: Bass Enhancement Done Right
text: I have worked with a lot of headphones, in particular active noise canceling (ANC) phones though I have several pairs of regular phones as well. One of the things that really bugs me about headphones these days is that there is a strong emphasis on bass, and most “bass enhanced” headphones overdrive the bass to the point that it destroys the rest of the sound profile in the process. This pair is one of the very few I have used that boosts the bass and gets it right. Well, let’s get right to it – the sound profile is the most important feature of any headphones. If the sound is off, music will sound terrible and even straight speech can sound weird. These headphones tout their bass response, and I was a little apprehensive at first. However, unlike most, the bass on these is not so overdriven that it gives me a headache or interferes with the midrange. This is very unusual. The bass is definitely strong, but what is interesting is that it is actually detailed and not just a pounding low-frequency noise. I can hear details in the bass range that I usually can’t hear. A bass guitar sounds like a bass guitar, not a heavy noise frequency that is lost in distortion even at lower volumes. Even more interesting is that the bass, while stronger than the midrange, does not overpower it and drown it out, and the midrange sounds right. The highs are nice and clear too, without being bitingly sharp. Overall, the manufacturer did a very good job getting the sound profile right. It’s not exactly balanced because of the enhanced bass, but the enhancement is done well enough to make music still sound very natural. Another area of surprise for me is that these are quite comfortable to wear for a little while even though they’re on-ear phones and not over-the-ear phones. I usually prefer over-the-ear phones that fit snugly, and these are the opposite of that. They’re on-ear and fit lightly, though tight enough to stay on when I tilt my head down and they do not pinch. These still have a little sound leakage when the volume is turned up a little, though it isn’t too bad at all. These are Bluetooth phones and I was able to get them to connect to my phone very quickly and easily. Reconnection is quick and effortless. Would I change anything? Yes – I would make these a tighter-fitting over-the-ear headphone. However, that’s a personal preference. Overall, I am hard-pressed to find much about which to complain with these headphones. They get the bass enhancement right and sound really good. If you like headphones with a good bass response but still sound good, these are a good choice to consider.

title: Decent Lower-Budget Camera
text: I prefer to use a camera that is separate from my smartphone in most cases (though having a camera on my phone does come in handy). My DSLR also has a video mode but again I’d rather keep that separate, in this case because of the SD card capacity. I was interested in this video camera, mainly because it has the features I need in a video camera and it is relatively inexpensive. So far it has proven to be worth its asking price. It is not a high-end camera by any means but it is fine for general use and it is priced reasonably. I’ll start with listing what’s in the box: the camera, a remote control for the camera, the microphone with foam wind guard, a cable to connect the microphone to the camera body, batteries for everything (3 different kinds), a carrying case, a 32GB SD card (not sure what class), a USB cable, an HDMI cable and a user’s manual for the camera as well as the microphone. Everything you need to get started is already in the box. The camera is very lightweight, more so than my Sony camera which is more solid and heavy. The Sony also cost several times more. The light weight and plastic housing makes this camera feel somewhat cheap, though that is more cosmetic. The weight is actually an advantage as it helps with one-handed filming where a heavier camera would cause fatigue faster. This is a 24MP digital camera and while that is not the best resolution available it is better than I would expect at this price point. Video comes out clear and smooth for the majority of projects. If you really need a higher resolution (in which case you’re probably doing more professional work) you likely will need to spend much more. One area of disappointment for me with this camera is the lack of optical zoom. The zoom is purely digital and in my experience a digital zoom solution is never as clear and accurate as an optical zoom. This camera is no exception and I find the digital zoom to be almost useless to me. It has some uses when not zoomed far, but when zooming in closer and closer it becomes clear that the image quality suffers. The camera does have a fairly comprehensive menu system and is easy to navigate. I did find the user manual mildly helpful in better understanding what the camera can do for me. Overall, this is a decent little camera, especially when considering that the cost is quite low. It is not a top of the line camera and it does lack an optical zoom, but for the price point it is a decent consideration if you need a video camera suitable for taking on vacation or for class projects.

title: Small Device, Performs Well
text: I have had good fortune with Verbatim products in the past, particularly blank CDs. I was excited to try this thumb drive and it has worked out well for me so far. The biggest plus is the size of the whole unit. This is a 32GB drive which is a good size for most things anymore. It is good as a mass storage device but it also is suitable as boot media if you need to use it for recovery media, OS replacement or other things. There are bigger thumbs drives out there, but this one is big enough for most. It comes preformatted with a FAT32 file system which makes it easy to read by practically all modern operating systems. My Linux system is able to mount it and read it, and Windows 10 opens it automatically. I likely will reformat it though for a better-performing file system to use primarily on my Linux system. I looked on the drive for hidden files and found only the system volume stuff. I did not make notes on the read/write speeds but it seems to perform on par with other name-brand drives I have. I have worked with drives that are quite slow when copying larger files like ISO images; this one seems about average when compared to Sandisk and PNY drives. Where this drive really distinguishes itself, though, is in the very small size, which is good but also could be a problem. It folds up to about the size of a nickel (approximately) and easily fits in a change pocket. This keeps it out of the way and makes it easy to toss in a bag, purse, pocket or backpack even when it’s full. However, it also means it can easily find its way into the laundry. So far, I have no complaints with this drive and am happy to recommend it. It performs well, it is easily recognized on different platforms and is small enough to go just about anywhere.

title: Sound Profile is Very Good, ANC is Ok
text: My experience with JVC up to this point has been with video equipment and televisions. My experiences have been positive so I hoped that this would be a good set of Active Noise Canceling (ANC) phones. I have worked with a lot of ANC phones – Bose, Sennheiser, Sony, Philips and more. Almost every set I have used has had some flaw, either in the ANC or in the sound profile. These JVC phones are interesting in that regard. The sound profile is nearly spot on, but the ANC is on the conservative side. I’ll go over the ANC first. This is not a real competitor for the high end Sony or Bose sets and if the main thing you want from a set of ANC phones is noise elimination then these are far from the strongest or most aggressive. I have a fan that I use as the main test for ANC phones, and with the most aggressive phones the fan is almost completely wiped out. The JVC phones do cancel a good bit of noise, but it leaves a good bit of sound behind that Bose in particular eliminates. Now, that said, ANC headphones that can cancel more than these are almost universally much more expensive, often by double the price. These are what can probably be called “good enough for most”. For me, I like a more aggressive headphone, but these cancel enough ambient noise that when I am listening to music I don’t hear much else. Many ANC phones fiddle with the sound profile to compensate for some of the lost frequency response, usually in the bass range and at the expense of the midrange. These phones are very unusual in that they don’t really seem to impact the sound profile much at all. And, the sound is very balanced. The bass is good, not overdriven (if you have ever used Dre Beats or Monster phones, you know exactly what I’m talking about). The midrange is warm and music sounds like it has the right depth as a result. The highs are clear and vocals sound very clean. The sound profile does not seem to be different between when the ANC function is on or off, though turning on the ANC does enhance the volume (which you can observe by having the headphones off when you activate the ANC in the middle of playback. The ear cups are comfortable and I can wear these for a while before I need to take them off for comfort reasons. They don’t seem to get too warm when wearing for a while which is good. They’re not the most comfortable phones I have used, but they are better than many. They connect via Bluetooth and I had no issues pairing and connecting them to my phone. My favorite feature is that there is an independent volume control on the headphones themselves that does not change the volume setting on the source device. This is a feature that is a bit unusual; often, when the phones have a volume control on them it impacts the system volume when adjusted. So, there is one thing about these phones that I think needs some improvement. Included with them is a cloth bag for protection, and that’s just not going to cut it, particularly in this price range. A bag prevents the contents from getting dirty but provides no damage protection. For the asking price (presently $149) these should have a hard case that at a minimum provides crush resistance. I am very pleased with these headphones, more than I expected to be. They sound great, though the ANC is passable. My biggest issue isn’t with the phones themselves but with the lack of a suitable protective case. Hopefully JVC will resolve that issue in the near future. If you want a good set of ANC phones without spending north of $300, these are worth a look.

title: Exceeds Expectations
text: I have worked with a lot of active noise canceling (ANC) headphones, from a large variety of manufacturers. Every set I have owned, from the top-of-the-line to the weakest and cheapest, has had its strengths and weaknesses. Until recently, Bose was the one to beat when it specifically came to the ANC function, though many others have a better sound profile. My favorite ANC phones are a set of Sony in-ear buds that rival Bose in ANC and trounce them in sound quality. When I found out that Microsoft had made an ANC headphone as well I did not have the highest of expectations – I expected mediocrity with the ANC and a reasonably good sound profile. I was dead wrong in both presuppositions – these are incredible headphones and are worth every penny of the asking price. They’re not absolutely perfect, but they’re better than one could reasonably expect. I’ll start by saying that I am sorry in advance for the lengthy review. I have a lot to say on these, and I would much rather give far too much information than not enough. The present asking price as I write this is $349 and that’s a lot of money to drop, so more information is better. Right out of the box these are relatively nondescript and don’t jump out as either flashy or gaudy. The controls that are visible and obvious are limited – a power button and a mute button, as well as the USB Type C power jack and a 3.5mm audio input jack. There are more controls, though, and it takes a quick glance at the documentation to get a feel for what’s there. There are two dials, one on each can, for controlling the level of ANC and for controlling the volume, L and R respectively. The flat portion of the cans facing outward are multi-function touch controls that allow you to play/pause, skip forward and backward, handle calls and also interact with your digital assistant. I will come back to that last point a little farther down. I powered these on and they immediately announced that they were ready to pair. I paired them to my iPhone and they connected and were usable quickly, faster than most Bluetooth devices I have used. I put them on, tapped once on the right ear and Pandora immediately started up. That was easy! The sound quality is very good though I will stop short of calling it audiophile level. The bass is good and not overdriven. I don’t care for deep, pounding bass and that is a problem with a lot of ANC phones I have used (Dre Beats being among the most aggressive in that regard). It softens as the volume level is dropped and that is very normal. The midrange is actually quite good with the proper amount of depth, so music sounds full and warm and not like it’s being piped through a tunnel. The highs are bright and clear though not piercing. Overall, these are among the most balanced ANC headphones when it comes to the sound profile. I cranked the volume and they don’t distort. The ability to adjust the ANC is not new; however, the way these headphones do it is very innovative and unlike anything else I have seen. The dial that controls it gradually lessens the amount of ANC that is applied when listening, in small but perceivable steps, until the ANC is turned off. With the central air on in the house, I gradually went from no ANC to maximum and it very gradually wiped out all of that sound. When at the maximum level the ANC is almost as aggressive as Bose, with a lot less of the the weird pressure sensation on the ears. A unique feature of these phones is integration with Cortana. When paired to a device running Cortana, simply saying “Hey, Cortana” gets its attention and you can interact with the same types of commands you use on the command line or the search window. It does require that Cortana be properly configured. I have Cortana installed on my iPhone (yes, you can do that and it works well), and the integration with the headphones when connected is good. I had a Windows Phone when they were still available and I would have liked to try this with that phone. There’s some debate on whether these are on-ear or over-the-ear phones. These are very definitely over-the-ear phones unless your ears are huge. The cups are buttery soft as is the head band, and these are very comfortable. I am able to wear them for long periods of time without fatigue. They do get warm after a while, so keep this in mind. One area a lot of headphones skimp on is the carrying case. The case with these phones is better than average. It is crush resistant and provides good protection for the phones. Included within is an audio cable for input as well as a USB charging cable. These headphones bring a lot to the table and were quite a shock for me. I had much lower expectations, for the ANC function in particular but also for the sound profile. Both exceeded my expectations and the comfort factor is the cherry on top. These are excellent phones and I am very pleased with them.

title: Works Better than Expected for the Price; Needs a Heavier Weighted Base
text: I have a teenage son who likes gaming on the PC and he has been wanting a new microphone for a while since his headset failed. I was given the opportunity to check this one out, and so far it has worked well. I do have complaint with it, though it’s not a deal breaker. This is a USB-based microphone so it does not take up the audio jack when plugged in. This is good as it does not preempt a standard headphone set when it’s plugged in. Windows 10 detects it and it is immediately available as an audio input device. No special set-up and no driver downloads are required – it’s plug and play. In use the sound quality has been good considering the price. In a two-way chat, those who have been on the other end of the discussion have told us that they can hear what is being said more clearly and there is less static than the previous microphone we were using, one that was quite a bit more expensive but still not high-end. That’s really all we could ask. The one issue I have with it is that the base is not weighted well at all and it is very easy to tip it over or knock the microphone from where it sits on the desk. It’s easy enough to fix by either attaching it to a heavier base, using double-sided tape or even Velcro to secure it to the desk, or some other rigging to anchor the microphone assembly to the workspace. In the grand scheme of things, this is a minor issue; that said, I would rather spend slightly more and have a weighted base that isn’t as easily toppled. For the price this is a good microphone that works better than could be reasonably expected. There is some room for improvement that would increase the cost slightly, but it would make the difference between being a good product and being a great one.

title: Great Clock, Mediocre (at best) Radio
text: I use my smart phone for an alarm clock and in that capacity it works well and is all I need. However, when I check the time in the night it requires fumbling with the phone, then being half-blinded by the screen when I turn it on long enough to check the time. I looked to this alarm clock to resolve this for me and in terms of timekeeping it’s exactly what I hoped. As a radio, though, it leaves much to be desired. The main feature of this clock that makes it worth the cost is the tremendous display. The numbers are huge and are red which does not ruin night vision. And, being always on all I have to do it look at it and know the time without fumbling in the dark for my phone. The projection on the ceiling is also great and I like being able to flip it at the touch of a button. For me, this is all I need. However, where it fails is in the audio department. The speaker is sub-par and when listening to music to does not do well at all and sounds bad though not awful. I have heard worse. I would rather see this sell for $10 more and have a better speaker in it. If you choose this alarm clock, get it for the display which is great and is the main selling point. If you are looking for a good clock radio and the sound is important to you, this might not be the best choice. I don’t care about the audio so this is a minor point; others may feel differently.

title: Design Flaws and Overpriced
text: I have a couple of vertical mice that I use with my various computer systems, and they really do help with wrist fatigue and pressure. I also have a very nice Logitech MX Ergo trackball which is my go-to device for all of my systems. With Logitech releasing this vertical mouse, I was very optimistic that I would have the perfect solution. I was sorely disappointed. This is the worst Logitech device I have used and I can’t recommend it. I’ll start with the good aspects of it, and then I will get into what isn’t so good. This device can be connected via wireless USB or by Bluetooth. This is handy for when you want to use multiple systems and want to connect to them, in different ways. If you already have another wireless Logitech device, it can connect to the receiver for that device, reducing the number of wireless ports required. It connects well through either method and I have been able to move it between systems just with the press of the connection button on top. In operation, it seems to work well as a pointing device. I will say that if you are not used to working with a vertical mouse there is a learning curve that is involved and you will be very frustrated while you make the adjustment. The movement isn’t hard – it’s working with the buttons which even though are worked with the same fingers they feel unnatural at first. This is a problem with all vertical mice, not just this one. It is rechargeable, meaning no more batteries, and it holds a charge for a good while. I like mice and keyboards that don’t need batteries as in the very long term it saves money. (Logitech has a solar keyboard that is phenomenal and never needs to be plugged in at all – great device.) I have three main issues with this vertical mouse. The first is the build quality. It feels very lightweight and cheap, and I would call it fragile. It is supposed to be light and maneuverable so it’s easy to use, but it’s so much so that it has a very cheap feel to it that is unsettling. Second, this is a HUGE mouse which for me is great but for most people is unworkable. It fits my hand very well, but I have hands like a gorilla. My wife tried it and found it to be completely unusable because she couldn’t work the buttons well at all due to the size. Finally, this is a very expensive peripheral compared to other vertical mice I have used that I actually prefer. This vertical mouse presently sells here for about $100. I have one that cost around $25 at the time I bought it, feels more solid and is easier to use. My wife and I compared the Logitech vertical mouse with my cheaper one, and we both agreed that the less expensive one was easier to handle and worked just as well. The only thing I lose with the cheaper mouse is Bluetooth connectivity, which in my case is not a deal breaker. I wish I could rate this mouse more highly but I just can’t. It’s expensive, feels cheap and just isn’t made to fit smaller hands (and usually, it’s a challenge finding mice for larger hands). It’s worth consideration if you need a mouse that can be easily transitioned between wireless and Bluetooth, but if you just need to use it with one system I’d recommend researching other options before making a purchase.

title: Great Keyboard but Set-Up is Flawed
text: I use laptops at home instead of tower systems, but I still prefer a stand-alone keyboard for most things. I have had very good success with Microsoft peripherals in the past so I had high expectations for this keyboard. So far, it works well enough but I have encountered a couple of snags that make it less than perfect. This is a slim and efficiently designed keyboard and it is slightly wider than my 15.6” laptop. It’s the right size for me and I am happy with the dimensions when it comes to fitting it in my work space. No complaints there. Set-up is a little on the tricky side. I tried to set it up for Bluetooth use without following the instructions first and got nowhere. It does not appear in the list of available devices so it could not be paired right off the bat, though my system does handle the Bluetooth standard. The instructions say to connect it via USB first, then turn it on and follow the set-up when Windows detects it. However, the instructions do not say that you must use the cable that came with the keyboard; I used a different one and failed, though the keyboard did work as a USB keyboard with that 3rd-party cable connected. I’ll answer the very obvious question right now – I was able to get it working under Linux as a USB keyboard, but not as a Bluetooth keyboard. I am not sure if the problem is with the Bluetooth receiver in the system I tested or if the keyboard is just not compatible at all. I have an iPhone as well and it did not see the keyboard in the list of available devices. This is not a failure or a shortcoming of the keyboard – it operates very much in accordance with how it has been marketed, so getting it to work under Linux with Bluetooth would have been just a bonus. Interestingly, it says it can be set up to work under the Windows Phone platform which has been discontinued... When I set it up under Windows 10, it did not go as the documentation said it would go. I did get the toast notification and I clicked as directed. It set everything up and said it was ready to go. It never allowed me to set up the fingerprint configuration and I have been unable to find any setting within Windows to allow me to revisit. So, I have a fingerprint reader that I can’t configure. Considering that this is being used in a home with a private computer with password protection this really isn’t a show-stopper but it would have been nice to mess with this technology. In operation the keyboard is very responsive and so far I have been pleased with it except for one thing that I cannot seem to reconfigure. I prefer to have the function keys operate as function keys by default, instead of media keys. Without being able to find a keyboard configuration setting in the OS anywhere I have no way to reverse the default operation, which is to require pressing the Function key prior to hitting F1 – F12 to get them to default as function keys instead of media keys. I do like this keyboard and it works well for my needs. The set-up isn’t bullet-proof though, and there are some behaviors it would be nice to change or reconfigure.

title: No Setup Required - It Just Works
text: I recently purchased a new [Windows] laptop that has a Type C connector, and I selected this unit to get more USB ports as well as the card reader. So far it has worked out well for me and it seems to work as designed, and with no tweaks or software installation required. This little unit is small and it easily fits in a shirt pocket though the cord does impact the way it fits in said pocket. It’s a little bigger than a comb but smaller than a candy bar. It feels solid and well-made and so far has shown no signs of fatigue or weakness. I plugged it in and the fit was very snug so I had to work with it to get it plugged in properly. That’s actually a positive – it should not come unplugged unexpectedly when I move my laptop or plug something else into it, a problem I have had on occasion with MicroUSB devices. Windows recognized it immediately and it didn’t seem to need any extra device drivers or anything to make it work. It picked up the Ethernet interface as well as the USB hub, and that’s really all I would expect before plugging in anything else. The card reader works and I was able to read images off of the card I use in my camera through this device. I have not yet tried it under Linux but that’s coming shortly. I also have an Android tablet with a Type C port with which I will try this device as well. I have not yet tried the HDMI adapter. I have a use for it as my laptop actually does not have an HDMI port on-board and I’d like to attach it to my television to stream video. Would I add anything? I would have liked to see an integrated wireless adapter or a Bluetooth receiver built in, though I have those built in to my system and adding those to this unit would drive up the cost a bit. I would probably make the unit slightly larger too. So far, this device has been solid for me. It works right out of the box without any setup required – plug it in and you’re ready to go.

title: Works Great in an MX ERGO
text: I bought this replacement ball for my Logitech MX ERGO, which worked well for me before I accidentally dropped it and subsequently put a pock mark on the original ball. The ERGO still worked but would occasionally get stuck when the support pegs would catch the pock and cause the ball to resist - not enough to really hurt anything but just enough to make digital drawing difficult and just enough to annoy me. This replacement ball has taken care of that for me and has proven to be a worthwhile expense for me. The ERGO and the M570 have the same size ball, so this ball can be used in either (I was using the ball from my old M570 in the ERGO while I waited for this ball to arrive). Replacement is a 30-second procedure and requires no special tools, though a pencil does make getting the old ball out a lot easier. There are two different finish types available, glossy and matte. I chose the glossy in red. Operation has been absolutely smooth with no resistance at all and no catches. I haven’t noticed any operational differences between it and the original gray ball that came in my ERGO. And, in my opinion, the dark red of this ball actually looks a little nicer than the original silver ball as well as the blue M570 ball. This wasn’t an expensive replacement and so far it has worked out very well for me. It has restored operation of my trackball to what it was before I damaged the original ball, which is really all I needed. Based on my experience with it, this is an easy replacement ball to recommend if you need to replace the ball in either a Logitech M570 or an MX ERGO.

title: Much Better than the Cheap Clones
text: NOTE: There are several models of GoPro cameras attached to this listing. I am specifically reviewing the GoPro Hero. I have worked with a number of the cheap knock-off sport cameras available and up to this point I have been relatively satisfied with them. I have not worked with an actual GoPro before now, so I was interested in seeing how well this unit would compare to the cheap clones. There’s really no comparison – the GoPro is an order of magnitude better. Yes, it’s more expensive but it’s a higher quality product that works better. Of the GoPro models available, this is the most budget-friendly I have seen and it doesn’t come with a lot of frills and extras. It does come in a waterproof shell and it does have a clip so you can attach it to a helmet or handle bars, but that’s really about all that comes in the package. There’s no memory card with it, either, so plan on picking up a MicroSD card with the camera. The usability when compared to the cheap clones is about the same. The menus are a bit different but they do perform the same general functions. That said, where the GoPro Hero sets itself apart from all of those cheaper cameras is in the quality of the product and the resulting pictures and recordings. This little camera is solid and so is the waterproof shell; it will stand up to some abuse and should just keep right on going without batting an eye. It also produces better-quality video than every clone I have tried, which is saying something because some of the cheap cameras actually do a decent job of producing good video. The size and weight are nice features that make it very highly portable. I have seen motorcyclists on the highways with cameras similar to this one mounted on their helmets, and while that looks funny to the observer it makes for some great videos online and it does give the motorcyclist some backing when there is a traffic incident. For the younger crowd, it’s great for capturing skateboarding tricks in the first person as well as that wild ride down a water tube. I have not worked with this camera a whole lot yet but I have seen enough to know it’s a big upgrade from the cheaper clones that are available in abundance. The Hero is a budget-friendly option for the user who wants quality results without breaking the bank, in exchange for giving up some of the less critical features like Bluetooth and WiFi connectivity. If you need those features, but you still want the best-quality, you’ll need to look at one of the more advanced and expensive models.

title: Does Not Retain DPI Setting Reliably; Slightly Smaller Than Average
text: I selected this mouse to be a spare for when I am on the go. Amazon-branded things are often of good quality so I was hopeful for this mouse. I came away a bit disappointed due to a couple of issues I have had with it. This is a basic wireless mouse, suitable for surfing the web, working on documents or similar tasks. It’s not particularly good for gaming as it is not designed for such. If the goal is to have something that will allow you to casually use the computer for basic tasks, this one will serve. If you need a heavy-duty mouse for frequent use or you need a gaming mouse, spend a little more and get a more solid mouse. One of the issues I have with mice is that I have huge hands and finding a mouse that fits my hand properly is a challenge. This is a smaller than average mouse, so it really doesn’t work for me. That’s not a big deal; it was designed for the large majority of people with smaller hands, so I can’t criticize this mouse for its size. It’s in that weird in-between size - smaller than the average desktop mouse but larger than a travel mouse. The real issue I have seen with this mouse, though, is with the DPI setting. After idling for a little while, the mouse has a very nasty and predictable habit of resetting the DPI mode automatically. This is the only mouse I have used that has exhibited the problem. This impacts me when I am doing photo editing or using a graphics program and I need fine control. Sure, I can hit the DPI setting and get it to where I need it to be easily enough, but I should not have to do this over and over, particularly when I need the same setting all the time. Other than the DPI setting, this mouse works exactly as expected. It is a decent mouse if you do not need predictable DPI settings. If you need a mouse that retains your settings, or if you need a larger mouse, or if you need a heavy-duty device, this is not the right choice for you. It’s fine for travel or casual use.

title: Good Sound and Comfort; A Couple of Areas for Improvement
text: I use active noise canceling (ANC) headphones all the time and prefer them to normal headphones as I tend to work in noisy environments and I’ve found that with ANC engaged I can play music at lower volumes. I like Sony headphones so I was excited to try these ANC ear buds. They’re a bit unusual in a few ways but they work well and are worth their asking price. These are truly wireless and have no physical connection between them. Power them both on and they find one another. They pair via Bluetooth to a phone, tablet or PC, and the connection is stable up to about 40’ around corners. This is a good start. There are several modes to these when it comes to the ANC function and each has its uses. I usually just use full ANC without any of the ambient sound modes turned on as it gives the best music experience. One of the two ambient modes is optimized for speech and voice, the other for more generalized noise. Neither completely cut off noise canceling, but rather they allow different bands of outside noise to come through. In full ANC mode, these are good noise cancellers, though not as aggressive as some others like Bose. These have proven to be comfortable, and they have the little wings on each bud for keeping them in place in your ear. I used them while working in the yard and never once did I have a problem with slipping or falling out, even though I have the wrong size silicone insert on one of them. The sound is very good but I would stop short of calling it outstanding. The bass is heavier than I like though not so bad that it gives me a headache unless I pump the volume up too much. The midrange is warm and full, and the highs are bright and crisp without being piercing. The sound can be adjusted a bit in the app that you can download, as it has an equalizer of sorts that lets you tweak the levels or choose a preset. Ah, the app… This is the primary downside of these. The method to adjust these is either an Android or iOS app, not a physical piece of hardware and there is no Windows equivalent (for those who want to use these with a PC). The app is a little clunky though fairly self-explanatory and it does do what it’s supposed to do. Given a choice between an app or an additional piece of hardware, I would choose the hardware. These charge up in the carrying case, which has leads that connect to each bud. Pay attention when you put these in the case – it is possible to reverse them, and while it hurts nothing the charging doesn’t work well… The case has some sort of battery in it and it charges the buds without being plugged in itself, though it does require occasional charging. Charging is fast – I charged them from empty to full in about an hour. One thing that could be improved, though: the buds can be popped in the charger while still powered on, and the act of charging them does not make them cut off. So, you can end up with dead buds and a dead charger too. These are decent wireless sport buds that have good sound and good ANC functions. They’re comfortable and not overpriced. There are a couple of areas for improvement, particularly in charging but also in the app control, that would make these even better.

title: Decent Unpowered USB Hub
text: One of the problems I have seen with the latest crop of notebooks and Ultrabooks that have come out is a lack of USB ports. There's usually a need for more ports than these systems have and it gets frustrating. A small USB hub like this is a good solution. That said, this particular hub does not have a separate power source so some consideration must be made when plugging in power-hungry devices. From a design stantpoint this is a solid unit, shaped to be accessible without being huge. It has a little weight to it and this is helpful for keeping it stable. The addition of Velcro strips in the package to secure it in one place is a welcome inclusion and makes securing the hub very simple no matter what your configuration is. The hub provides four USB 3.1 type A ports. Let me state what should be obvious - this will not convert a USB 1.1 or 2.0 port into a 3.1 port, so plug it into a 3.1 port if you want the speed across the hub. For my specific uses, it does not need to be a high-speed hub and I am find with using it as a 2.0 hub, but admittedly that's slightly wasteful. There is no power port on this hub and there is no DC adapter in the box. So, any power that the hub needs comes through the onboard port into which it is plugged. That's fine for low-power devices like mice, keyboards, memory sticks and so on, but if the intent is to plug in such things as USB hard drives with no external power supply this can cause some headaches. No, one drive isn't going to overload the hub, but if you have multiple drives attached there may be reliability issues when they starve one another for power. When the device plugged in has its own power supply (like a big backup drive), this has little impact on the hub. The point is, plan carefully how you intend to use the hub. I like this hub and it does a good job for what it is. It has given me three extra ports on an Ultrabook I use which is all I could ask for. The ability to power this hub with it's own power supply would be the only area for improvement I could find.

title: Works for Me
text: The Bluetooth adapter in my main system has failed so I have been looking for a replacement for it for some time. I am familiar with Sabrent as a brand so I was willing to give this little adapter a shot. It works for me, and so far it hasn’t given me any difficulties. First things first. This is a tiny little device, the size of a USB receiver for mice and keyboards. Be careful when you do not have this plugged in because it is easy to misplace. I don’t mention this as a fault but rather as a point of consideration. If your desk is cluttered like mine, be prepared to misplace this little guy once in a while if you ever unplug it. I didn’t have any issues setting this unit up. Others have reported that it’s not cooperative during setup and installation but that was not my experience. I plugged it in and Windows 10 saw the dongle right away. I loaded the drivers and it was good to go – simple as that. I have been able to pair keyboards, mice, and headphones through this adapter and all work like they should. I have observed, though, that the volume seems slightly low when using headphones when compared to the older adapter in the system. I am not sure if this is a function of the adapter or if there is some setting in Windows that I have not found. It’s not enough to bother me, but it is enough for me to notice. So far, so good with this adapter. It has given me Bluetooth connectivity again on a system where the interface had failed. No complaints from me.

title: Works Great Under Windows, Mac and Linux; Fast Switching Between Two Systems
text: I have worked with a number of trackballs, my most successful being a Logitech M570 which served me well for years. I finally wore it out and after some research I purchased the Logitech MX Ergo to replace it. I have had it about three days, and it has already proven to be exactly what I had hoped and more. It’s not perfect but it’s close. I was attracted to the fact that it works both as a wireless mouse with a USB receiver as well as a Bluetooth mouse. I have two computers on my desk, one being a Windows 10 system and the other being a Linux (Arch-based) system. My old trackball worked with both though I had to move the receiver between the systems, so I went with the assumption that this one would also work with both. I connected the trackball to my Windows system via Bluetooth and it has been flawless in operation. It connects without intervention and it works exactly as expected - all buttons work as they should and the operation is very smooth and predictable. I plugged the USB receiver into the Linux machine, pushed the channel button on the trackball and it immediately started working on the Linux machine, even though it was still paired to the Windows system via Bluetooth. It works exactly as it should and I have had absolutely no issues with the trackball on my Linux installation. So now, I can switch back and forth between the two systems with the push of the channel button and without having to connect or disconnect anything. It simply works, and the switch-over is fast. The take-away for me is that I no longer need two mice on the desk. I friend came over with his MacBook and there was no issue at all with connecting the trackball via USB. We did not try connecting via Bluetooth. The trackball has a metal plate on the bottom that is held in place with magnets, and depending on how the plate is attached the trackball can be tilted to ease wrist strain. The plate serves another purpose too - it adds a lot of weight to the trackball. Even without the plate, the trackball is hefty and has some mass to it, but the plate just makes it even more so. For me that’s a positive; others may dislike the added weight. One of the things I have missed has been a tilting scroll wheel. This trackball has one and I have been enjoying getting used to that feature again. One thing I did notice is that there is no CD/DVD in the package for loading drivers. This isn’t a big deal, and it’s easy enough to get the drivers from the net. That said, the trackball just seems to work when you attach it, without any issue. For me it has absolutely been plug-and-play, on every system I have tried. If I could change one thing - I would have made this trackball a little bigger. I have big hands and I struggle to find a trackball that’s an absolute perfect fit. This one is close. For the large majority of people it’s going to be spot on. I am very happy with this trackball and have no issue with recommending it. It works great, connects easily, when connected to two different systems it switches at the press of a button, it has a bit of heft to it and the tilt is adjustable for wrist comfort. It’s really all I could ask for.

title: Bluetooth Connectivity a Big Plus; Pen is Mediocre at Best
text: NOTE: This review is written for the Small, Bluetooth edition. I have been using Wacom Intuos and Bamboo tablets for years, not really for graphic arts but more for digital handwriting and for use as an alternative to traditional mice and trackballs. My present solution is an Intuos 5 medium which seems to be about the right fit for my hands and my work space. The one drawback has been that it’s a wired solution. This new Intuos is a Bluetooth solution and it is definitely a step forward. For me the challenge is downgrading to the small from the medium, but it’s a good fit for me when traveling and when working in cluttered spaces. To approximate the size, it is roughly equivalent to 7” tablet in size. It’s small enough to tuck away in a corner of a desk when not in use, and when it is being used it does not take up large amounts of real estate. The design itself makes it suitable for use just about anywhere it can be set down and kept stable - one of the reasons I like drawing tablets more than traditional mice. The Bluetooth connectivity is new to me, and I was pleasantly surprised to find that this unit can connect via USB as well. So, if your system is like one of mine and the Bluetooth doesn’t work, this drawing tablet still will work. I have it connected to my Windows 10 system. I have not yet made the effort to get it working with my Linux system, though I expect there will be some labor involved to make that work. I’ll revisit that later. In operation, this is a straightforward drawing tablet though it is an improvement over my Intuos 5 in some ways. Of course the Bluetooth is a step up, but I was surprised by the increased number of pressure levels which is effectively doubled over my old tablet - 4096 vs 2048. For someone like me, this is not a huge difference and I don’t take advantage, but for someone who is very serious about fine digital artwork this can be a huge benefit. For use in handwriting, it is not especially important as even 512 pressure levels (like my original Bamboo small) is more than sufficient. When you register, you get a choice between three Corel titles, of which you can select two (for the medium you get all three). Some may find the choice difficult - Painter Essentials 6, AfterShot 6 and Clip Studio Paint Pro (2 years) - but for me, having AfterShot is more than enough. There is a downside to this little tablet, though - the pen is mediocre. There is no comfort grip, changing the nib is a pain, and there’s a very limited number of replacement nibs for it. It’s the one weak spot in an otherwise nice product, and even then it’s not all that bad. The hardest part for me with this specific tablet is the move from a medium to a small, but this this counterbalanced by the Bluetooth connectivity and the inclusion of the Corel titles, specifically AfterShot. This is a very nice drawing solution and is it priced nicely. I’d recommend the small for anyone either just getting started or experimenting; the medium is a better fit for those more experienced or needing more real estate. I would choose a different pen if available, though.

title: Better Than Expected at the Price Point; Very Balanced Sound
text: I normally think of storage media and batteries when I think of Maxell. That said, this is my second pair of Maxell headphones. My first pair is an ANC set that isn’t perfect, but they’re far and away better than I would ever have expected. These phones are not ANC phones, they’re just wireless listening phones. I was hopeful that they would be as good as my ANC phones in terms of sound quality, and Maxell has not disappointed me. They’re not perfect but they’re better than you can reasonably expect from the asking price. Up front, let me say that I am not a big fan of on-ear headphones, and these fall into that category. I prefer an over-the-ear phone which to me is more comfortable. These aren’t bad for on-ear phones. This comes down to preference. If you are cool with on-ear phones, these will work for you, but if you have to have over-ear phones then you should consider other options. The pads are soft enough, though they aren’t super cushy like some others I have used. Being Bluetooth phones I immediately connected them to my phone. The connection went off without a hitch, though the phone was slower to find these than I had hoped. Once connected, they have been stable and reconnecting is much faster. The real test is the sound profile. On my ANC phones, Maxell worked a miracle and got the sound profile nearly perfect even when the noise canceling is turned on. With these phones, the sound profile is not precise but it’s very balanced and better than average. The bass is strong but not throbbing like most headphones made these days. I like bass, but I don’t appreciate the insistence on pumping it so heavily that it gives me a headache. The midrange is full and music sounds like it has some depth without sounding like it’s playing from the bottom of a well. The highs are bright and clear, though on specific frequency ranges there is the slightest hint of distortion if you really look for it (and since I’m reviewing these, I went looking for it). I cranked up the music as high as I could, and there was only a hint of distortion in the highs. And I had a headache when I was done. Build-wise, these are not too bad. I would not pack them in a gym bag or anything like that, but these should work fine for a long while as long as they’re cared for properly. There’s enough flex in them to make them durable enough to survive some rough handling, but at the end of the day they’re primarily plastic - a drop from the right height or being crushed in a book bag will break them. These phones are under $50 as I write this. What’s really distressing is that I have phones that are north of $200 that do not sound as good as these. Maxell knows how to make a good headphone that competes well with more expensive phones - I have two very different pairs to prove it. It begs the question - why are they only making budget headphones? I would rate these slightly lower if the asking price were above the $50 mark. But, at the asking price you’d be hard-pressed to find headphones that sound better.

title: Solid Performance; Slightly Pricier than Competitors
text: I have built systems with SSDs for the last several years and I have come to see where they have their strengths and weaknesses. Not all SSDs are the same, and some have distinct advantages over others though the gap is definitely narrowing. This is my first experience with Samsung’s SSDs, and so far it has been a very positive experience. It has given me no issues at all and has performed well. I installed the drive in a Dell Inspiron laptop which was running Windows 8. On the SSD, I installed Linux instead. Installation was very smooth, it was quick and I had a working system up and running in no time. I have now been running the system constantly for over a week (no powering off or hibernating) and the drive has shown no signs of trouble. I loaded up a virtual machine and ran it on top of the main installation. The VM and the host install both have performed admirably and have not suffered from any noticeable I/O lag. Running smartctl against the drive after the past week of testing, it has reported no errors and a very healthy drive across the board. Aside from the speed advantages of an SSD over a platter-based drive, this drive is absolutely silent (no surprise there) and so far I have not had any heat issues. It has given me no indications of any trouble in operation and my system is running as smoothly as should be expected. The one issue I have with this drive, and it’s not a performance or quality issue, is the pricing. It is a little more expensive than most, and so far I have not seen any real justification for it over the likes of Crucial, Kingston or other branded drives. There may be justifiable reasons that reveal themselves later (I do not know how long this drive will continue to work but it should literally last for several years, even under very heavy use), but for now it seems a tad expensive compared to competitors. Operationally I cannot find fault with this drive. It works well, it’s fast and quiet (as should be expected) and so far I’ve not had heat issues with it. Utilities I have run against it have shown that the drive is very healthy and has reported no problems out of the box. This is a good drive that will serve well. Time will tell, though, if it is worth the slightly higher asking price.

title: They Look Better Than They Sound
text: I have had several pairs of Panasonic headphones and I regard them as a budget-grade phone that is better than generic but leaves room for improvement. I was hopeful that these phones would be better and would distinguish themselves as better than average. Unfortunately they do not and they suffer from the same issues I have had with other Panasonic phones in the past. They're certainly not bad, but there is some room for improvement. First off, these look great, though I would stop short of calling them "retro" in appearance. They're styled to be retro-looking, but they betray their youth in the plastic details. That said, they have the cool factor that they are going for and the will stand out over most run-of-the-miss headphones than you'll find most people using. One of the problems I have with these is strictly a personal preference. When I use over-the-ear phones like these, I want a phone that clamps down tight over my ear and applies some pressure. This does two things for me - it cuts down on the chances that they'll slip off when I look down, and it cuts sound leakage when I am listening to something. These are a more relaxed, loose fit, and this is not to my tastes. There's a good number of users that will be very happy with the way these fit, and as I said this is a preference, so I cannot say this is a fault. It's something to keep in mind, though. Aside from the tightness (or lack thereof), the pads and band are soft and these can be worn for a long while without issue. These are Bluetooth phones, so I used them to connect to my Android tablet. They connected very quickly and without any real issues. I have no complaints there. They stay connected once paired and the range is good to at least 20-30 feet from the source which is good. Where these headphones fail, though, is in the most important area - the sound profile. The highs are slightly muddy though not unacceptably so. The bass is present and not overdriven which to me is a very good thing. But, the midrange is not right at all, and as a result the music sounds like it is coming out of a tunnel when I am listening. Yes, I could fix this with an equalizer, but many people will not think to do that or do not have access to one. This is a familiar issue I have had with Panasonic phones, and unfortunately these do not correct the issue. For speech, these sound just fine. These are interesting phones and they look good. For those liking a loose fit, they're going to be very comfortable. However, there is an issue in the sound profile that anyone serious about their music will not be able to help but notice, and at the price point it's a more serious issue than if these were inexpensive (budget) headphones.

title: Good Hardware, Not-So-Good Setup
text: I work a lot with smart watches but this is the first health monitor/GPS watch I have used. I was excited to have the opportunity to work with it, and I was hopeful that it would be a good unit. Epson is a brand I know well from their printers, so out of the gate I had some expectations. This watch has proven to be a mixed bag. I will start with what I believe are the strongest features. This watch has a much better-than-average charger. Many watches I have used have a magnetic charger that is either poorly constructed or will not stay on the device it'’s charging. This one, however, is a clamp-based charger that does a good job of holding the watch even under its own weight without letting it slip or shift. I would have liked to see other manufacturers adopt this kind of charging clamp. The battery lasts for a very long time. I charged it up completely and after taking it from the charger I deliberately left it on the shelf to drain. It's rated for 20 hours, and I assume that is for active use. Letting it sit idle, it lasted two weeks for me. It of course drains much faster when it is actively being used so once I started using it I had to charge it again. This is a handy data point if you're traveling - if you're going for a weekend, it holds enough charge to get through in most cases, and if you are an infrequent user it will retain a charge for a while. The display is very clear and easy to read. I have had no issues at all with the display and I am very pleased with how easy on the eyes it is. One of the issues I have with most wrist-wear of any kind is getting it to fit properly. I have large hands and wrists, and I found this watch to be a bit snug on even the loosest setting. This is par for the course for me. I was hopeful it would fit a bit better, but it wasn't to be. The aggravation started when I set up the software and paired the watch to my phone. The Bluetooth pairing did not go smoothly and I tried several times to get it straight. I finally switched over to setting it up through the watch instead of through the phone, and I was able to get it working and connected. While this is an acceptable work-around for someone with patience, it is an aggravation for someone who prefers things to just work the way they're supposed to. I will say I am not especially impressed with the software app. I think it is a little too overly complex and counter-intuitive, but it does work and it has a lot of features. It does a good job of tracking progress. So, aside from setup and fit, how does it work? It seems to work well. I am very familiar with sport GPS units so I assumed this one would work about the same, and it does. It acquires the satellites and uses those to report position back to the phone app so you can track yourself. This is useful when you want to see where you went and how far. The speed of acquisition of the satellites seems to be roughly the same as with my hand-held units. The heart rate monitor seems to be good and in measuring manually for comparison it appears to be accurate. The step feature is a good quick measurement and is sufficient to replace a dedicated pedometer. Overall this is a decent health watch, but there's some room for improvement. It looks great, it works well and it's easy to read. It is hampered by less-than-idea setup and software, and it would be nice if it fit a little better.

title: Flat Midrange
text: I will start by saying that I am typically not a fan of ear buds. I will also say that the very best headphones I have is a set of Sony active noise canceling ear buds. I have always had good success with Sony audio products and I regard the brand as an upper mid-range line. These buds are disappointing in that, while they’re comfortable for ear buds, the sound profile is lacking, specifically in the midrange. This is a basic set of ear buds that work as you might expect. They do not have ANC functionality, there is no battery or battery pack and there is no Bluetooth functionality. These are straight plug-in audio gear with no fancy features. These will work with just about any device that provides a 3.5mm audio jack. Most ear buds are uncomfortable to me, but these are surprisingly comfortable and I can wear these for a good bit of time. They come with several inserts of varying sizes so you can find the size that fits your ear canal just right. The included inserts are soft and do not irritate my ears as much as others have done in the past. I still very much prefer over-the-ear headphones which is a personal preference more than anything. So, where’s the problem? The problem lies in the sound profile which is unbalanced. Having used literally dozens of sets of ear buds and headphones over the past 3-5 years I have developed a good feel for what sounds right and what doesn’t. Most ear buds have one of two issues, either way too much bass or almost none at all. These are surprising in that they actually get the bass just about right, not too heavy and not too light. The highs are very bright and clear, perhaps a touch too piercing for my tastes but not to the point of being unacceptable. The midrange, though, is flat. The result is that music sounds somewhat sterile and lackluster. This is similar to the issue I have seen with my Bose headset. These still sound good, but they fall short of where they could and should be. Normally I would rate ear buds with a glitch in the sound profile a little higher, as they’re still quite usable and they sound decent. But, these are much more expensive than the average and I have heard less expensive buds with more balanced sound. Sony makes a number of sets of ear buds and headphones, but these are not among their best offerings.

title: Solid Replacement Lightning Cable
text: There are two of us in the house that use iPhones with the lightning port and as such we do need extra cables. Lightning cables are great but they do have a tendency to break. Also, not all third-party cables are the same and some are not worth the box they ship in. I was anxious to try this cable and I have found it to be a perfectly acceptable replacement for the one that came with my phone. Actually, it’s better. First things first - it is important to note that this cable is MFI-certified which is actually a big deal. I have worked with cables that are certified and those that are not. Those that carry certification are guaranteed to work properly with your device, while those that are not certified are a roll of the dice. This cable is certified so it means two things you can expect from it: it will allow you to charge your phone without worry, and it will allow you to connect your phone to your computer without complaining about the cable being unauthorized. It just works. The cable is shielded in a heavy nylon weave and that is a double-edged sword. On one hand it means the cable is very stiff and not very bendy which may or may not be an issue. More importantly, though, it means it is going to last longer than plastic coated cables which tend to flex and break. The ends are terminated well too, with a hard plastic sleeve at the end of each plug where the cable connects. This spot is where most cables fail, and it is nice to see that some thought was put into reinforcing the cable at this point. The weighted ball is interesting but to me it gets in the way. It can be slid up and down the cable which has its uses, but it is large enough and bulky enough to be more of a hindrance to me than a help. That said, if you are putting this cable in an area where it will not be moved and you intend to leave it there for the long term, it does prevent tangles and it allows for keeping gently tension on the cable. Overall, I am pleased with this cable. It’s a lot less expensive than Apple-branded cables and it definitely is more durable and should last a long time.

title: Great Sound; Feels Slightly Fragile
text: I am usually not a fan of ear bud-style headphones as I have trouble finding sets that are either comfortable or have good sound. More often than not, buds have been tuned to have the bass either too strong or too weak and they sound very unnatural. Sony did a good job with these and got them sounding very balanced. They’re not perfect when it comes to comfort but there are ways to remedy this. These are not active noise canceling (ANC) phones. Sony offers another model that is ANC-capable and they’re excellent but an order of magnitude more expensive. If you need ANC, this particular set of buds cannot do that so consider other options but be prepared to spend more. These are sport-style ear buds in that they come on a neck harness and they are wireless. They connect easily via Bluetooth though they come with an adapter so they can be corded and used with devices that cannot work with Bluetooth. One concern with this type of phone is that often the cord is a little short between the harness and the buds, meaning a turn of the head pulls the cord a bit and can dislodge the buds from your ears. This particular set has some extra play in the cord so I have not had this issue as of yet. The cord on either bud can be “shortened” on either side by pulling the slack through tensors on the harness to reduce play in the wire. In terms of use for sports and exercise, these feel a bit more fragile than most and I would caution against using them for doing anything much more active than running. They might hold up just fine, but these are a bit more pricey than most and are not ruggedized. This is probably my main complaint with these. Comfort-wise, these are not bad. I have had better success with these than most, though I still greatly prefer over-the-ear headphones most of the time. The inserts are relatively soft and pliable and they do fit well, and the set comes with multiple sizes so adjustments can be made to get them to fit just right. In researching, I found that there are plenty of replacement tips; so, they can be swapped out if need be to find something that fits better or is more comfortable. The main consideration about any set of phones, regardless of price, is the sound. In my mind, Sony has always had good quality products that do a fine job of balancing the sound. These ear buds are very much in line with my previous experiences. The sound profile is very balanced and even and the result is natural sounding playback. The tendency with the majority of manufacturers is to heavily push the bass. The bass in these is present and you can definitely hear it but it is not so pronounced as to dampen or overpower the rest of the profile. The midrange sounds good (particularly for ear buds) and had the right depth, meaning music sounds warm and not like it’s coming out of a tunnel or barrel. The highs are bright and clear but not piercing. I would stop short of saying these are audiophile quality, but the sound is much better than most bud-style earphones. These are not your typical, cheap set of ear buds. These are better than the average and they are designed to be more comfortable and useful in an active lifestyle. They sound great. My only complaint is the construction - the harness in particular feels fragile. If you don’t need ANC and you don’t anticipate using your phones for heavy physical activity, these are a great choice. If you need something a bit more rugged, you might consider other options.

title: Better Sound Than I Expected
text: Most of my experience with Logitech products has been with keyboards and mice, though the company has made products in other segments as well, such as video surveillance systems and Modula-2 compilers. This is the first set of Logitech speakers I have tried and used, and I was expecting them to be a solid mid-range offering. They’ve proven to be better than that. These speakers are not very large, about as big around as the lid on a container of oatmeal. They’re heavy, though, and in addition to the main speaker they have a bass subwoofer on each. They feel very solid and should hold up under some abuse shy of being dropped on a concrete surface. My first test was to connect them to my phone via Bluetooth. I plugged them in, turned them on and they immediately started broadcasting their ID. My phone immediately saw them and I was able to pair and connect them without any issue at all. Based on my experience there, the Bluetooth connectivity is excellent. I later tried to connect them to my computer by the audio cable – simple and easy as should be expected. The main question when using a set of speakers – how do they sound? In a word: excellent. The bass response is solid but not overdriven, the midrange is warm and has good depth, and the highs are sharp and clear without being shrill. I was expecting a more subdued sound profile, but Logitech did a good job with getting these to sound great. I would stop short of calling these audiophile quality, but the large majority of users should be happy. I bumped up the volume and tried to get these to distort and I was unsuccessful. They remained clear even through the full volume range. I set them in the kitchen, turned up the volume and went to the basement as I was still able to hear the sound clearly – through the ceiling. I do have speakers that sound better by a little bit, but they cost three times as much and they’re quite a bit larger. Considering the price point and the size of these speakers, these are much better than one could realistically expect.

title: Exactly What I Needed at a Good Price
text: I have a Samsung NX300 camera and so far the main problem I have had has been the battery life. I can get approximately 250-300 pictures between charges (assuming auto settings with average exposure times) which is very low and it has stranded me without battery power more than once. I was looking for extra batteries and an external charger when I found this one here on Amazon. I decided to take a chance on it and I purchased it, and that has paid off for me. First things first: the batteries in this pack work just fine in my camera. The size and footprint are the same as the manufacturer’s battery, but the capacity is actually higher. The original battery is 1130mA, but these are 1500mA which means more exposures per charge - in theory quite a bit more. I have not yet drained one of these so I do not know exactly how long they last but initial indicators are strong that I will get more than 300 exposures per charge. So, since there are two batteries in the package and I still have the original battery, I should be able to get 1,000 or more exposures per outing if I have all of them charged up when I start. The external charger is a big plus for me - no more plugging in the camera itself to charge the battery. It plugs into a standard outlet, but it also has an adapter so it can be plugged into the 12V outlet in the car. That’s handy for road trips. So far I have not used the adapter but I am pleased to have it and will use it at some point. The charger does a good job and I was able to charge up one of the batteries in 3-4 hours (I wasn’t paying attention so I am not sure of the exact time it took). If there’s anything at all I would add or improve: it would have been nice to have a USB cable to plug into the barrel adapter port, so it could be charged over USB too, even if it took a lot longer. That would be very convenient, but the package does not suffer from not having this. This is exactly what I was looking for and is exactly what I needed to eliminate my camera’s power issue. I have more than triple the battery power now, I don’t have to plug the camera in to charge the battery and I can even charge it in the car. The fact that the charger and both batteries together cost significantly less than a manufacturer’s replacement battery is just the cherry on top.

title: Fast, Quiet, and Works Great Under Windows and Linux
text: NOTE: I am writing this review for the 1TB platter-based Passport drive. I have a 250GB Passport I bought several years ago and it has served me well, though it has gotten close to full over time (I never imagined at the time that I would fill that thing up). I have had good fortune with it so I expected the same from this 1TB version, and so far I have been right. In addition to the larger capacity, it is very definitely a speed upgrade from my old Passport. This is a small drive in terms of physical footprint, approximately 4”x3”x0.5” in dimension. That’s a double-edged sword. On one hand, it is small enough to stuff in a shirt pocket which makes it an excellent on-the-go storage solution that’s almost as convenient as a thumb drive. But, that also means it is easy to misplace or lose (or have stolen if left unattended). It comes with software that allows you to password-protect the drive which is a nice deterrent in the event that the drive is taken. It’s certainly not foolproof, but it’s sufficient to keep the large majority of unauthorized access out. To be honest, since the drive does not leave my home I have not used the software at all. When you plug in the drive to a Windows or Linux system, the OS immediately recognizes the drive and it is available immediately for use. In the case of Windows, you can immediately explore the drive and read from it and write to it. For Linux, it depends on how you have configured automount and which desktop management software you use, but the kernel does register the presence of the drive and you can display the partition table. This is a USB 3.0 drive, making it a huge speed upgrade from my older 2.0-based Passport. This is a great solution for storing all of your pictures, movies, important documents, and as in my case large downloads and purchased software packages. With 1TB of space, I don’t think I am going to run out of space anytime soon. As a bonus, this is a very quiet drive. I put this drive on a USB power meter to see how much it draws from the USB port. At rest it pulls 0.17A. When actively reading, it peaks just under 0.6A which is surprisingly low. My concern was that this would add some strain on the USB port over a longer period of time but this seems to be an unjustified concern. That said, I am more likely to connect it to a USB hub instead of directly to a USB port. So far I have no complaints with this drive. It’s a big step up for me from my older Passport, being larger, faster and more quiet. It’s not cost prohibitive either which is just a bonus. If you need a decent backup drive with large capacity and a small footprint, this one is worth consideration.

title: Better for Business; Graphics Card is Mediocre
text: I have a Dell laptop that has served me well and I also have an older Dell workstation that has been great. I had high hoped for this tower system, and unfortunately it doesn’t quite meet expectations. If you are looking for an affordable gaming system, this one will work on the lower end. I’ll start with the positives. It comes with a 7th-generation core i7 processor and it is definitely fast. It is not one of the low power consumption processors, so when you look at the CPU in the device manager you see 8 of them reported - this is a good thing. Everything is integrated with this system and there are plenty of ports. You don’t need a separate graphics card (though you can add one - more on that in a minute), sound is built in, Bluetooth is built in too and it even has integrated wireless networking. This is a very attractive system too, and it’s quiet. If you don’t like a noisy system\, this one has you covered. It comes with 1TB storage. It’s disk-based so it’s slower than an SSD but with that amount of space you have more than enough space for most uses. And, it’s affordable. It will not break the bank if you already have a monitor and keyboard/mouse combo. And now for the bad news. I am not the least bit impressed with the graphics card. With modern games the more graphics memory you have the better, and having only 2GB video RAM is not enough to get it done anymore. My son is an avid gamer and has demonstrated to me that his business-grade laptop gets better frame rates. So, we are shopping for a better and more generous graphics card. Another area where we will be expanding is the system RAM. The RAM is DDR4 and it’s fast, but the system comes with only 8GB. Our present plan is to double it. No documentation? I know that the trend is to not include install/recovery media, but come on - there should be more than just a quick start in the box. This is a decent desktop system that would be find in a business environment, but it falls a little flat when it comes to gaming. It needs a better graphics card (well, at least more video RAM) and it needs more system RAM to be a respectable gaming system.

title: Outstanding Sound and Solid ANC Function
text: I have used active noise canceling (ANC) headphones for many years and I have come to expect - and look for - the subtle differences between them. I have worked with ANC phones from Bose, Sennheiser, Monster, Noontec and quite a few more. All of them have their strengths and weaknesses. This is my first experience with Sony ANC phones, and I anticipated good ANC functionality and a solid sound profile. At the price point ($300 as I write this) they need to be excellent to be worth any kind of consideration. These were a huge shock to me: the ANC is nearly on par with Bose and the sound profile is solid, giving better results than I imagined. I will address the ANC function first, then the sound profile, and afterward I will discuss design and features. I apologize ahead of time for being long-winded, but I’d rather give too much feedback than not enough. The ANC function is, in a single word, outstanding. Bose is the standard by which I compare others and very, very few headphones get anywhere near the same level of noise cancellation as my Bose sets (QC-15 and QC-20i, by the way). Those that get close usually have the same weird pressure sensation for which Bose is known. My primary test is a loud fan that I use for generating white noise when I want to drown out everything around me at night. I turned the fan on high speed, plugged the Sony’s buds into my ears and turned them on. I put them in ANC mode and the fan all but disappeared. All that remained of the noise was a faint, higher-frequency hiss (distinct from the ANC hiss which I will explain later). Of all the phones I have used, this set and the Bose are the only ones to wipe out that much noise. I also went into the bathroom and turned on the ventilation fan to test, and these phones again wiped out a large majority of the fan noise. For this fan, the Bose sets have a very slight edge but you have to be looking for it to notice. The main difference between the Bose sets and these is the utter lack of that weird pressure sensation with these. If you don’t like that sensation but you want very high ANC, these are simply excellent. Like a lot of ANC phones, these generate a faint hiss that you really won’t notice unless you’re not feeding any sound at all to them and you’re listening for it. The sound profile is also quite solid. Usually with ANC phones, because of the cancellation of certain bandwidths the phones compensate by twiddling the sound profile to fill in what was dropped, and usually this means overcompensation in the bass range (if you use Dre Beats, you know exactly what I mean). Heavy bass gives me headaches so I avoid headphones where the bass has been given too much boost. With these, Sony did not overdrive the bass at all but it’s still very solid and full - love it. The midrange is very warm and rich and music has the right depth. The highs are very bright and clear but not piercing. Overall, I am very pleased with the sound profile - not audiophile quality but closer than most. In terms of design, these are a wireless earbud product with a neck harness. So, these are neither on-ear or over-ear phones. The harness and slack but adjustable wiring to the actual earbuds ensures that they can be set up so they won’t tug or pull when you’re working out, running or otherwise doing physical activity. Being wireless, there’s no cord to tangle up either. And, one size really does fit all which is a problem with some regular phones. The neck assembly has a leatherette padding that is soft and will not chafe. The Bluetooth functionality works great. I paired these to my phone and they paired and connected in less than 5 seconds which is really all I could ask.
