Some text can be a bit fuzzy and images a little pixelated. They're not too much of a noticeable difference, but still noticeable. With my MiSTer gaming setup, the monitor was great too. With retro gaming, input latency is important. I noticed no added latency. I love that I can now move my gaming setup to wherever I please. The speakers are pretty darn good, too. The stand could use refinement. It doesn't stay up easily and requires a few attempts before it stays up.

title: Fine, though a bit tight.
text: Works well for my needs. The zippers aren't the best quality, but they haven't ripped nor snagged yet. The organizer is a bit slim; trying to fit a power brick, two wall adapters, and SD card case, and a phone stand proved a bit snug compared to my last organizer, which was only a bifold case. Still, everything fits and the color and feel are great.

title: Needed a miniUSB aviator cable, got a miniUSB aviator cable.
text: While miniUSB cables are phasing out, I have a couple of mechanical keyboards that use the connector type. I love the look of aviator cables, and hunted one down for my keyboard. The end connectors look like older miniUSB connector types, but the rest of the cable is braided. The end that connects to the keyboard is shorter; it's the perfect length for my setup. The aviator connections need a bit of fussing to get them screwed at first, but they screw fine after. The part that connects to the keyboard leads to the male end of the aviator connection. I wish it were the female end so I can use the other aviator cable I have; this way, the colors would match my keyboard. Alas, that is not so.

title: Wrong instructions and wobbly, but still fun to use.
text: Before ordering this telescope, I researched the difference between reflector and refractor telescopes. The last telescope I had was a hand-me-down (I forget which brand) refractor telescopes. I've developed a strong passion for everything beyond earth, so I looked forward to using this telescope--my first reflector telescope. Because the telescope requires assembly, I pulled out the instructions...and became very confused. While some of the parts looked similar to what was in the box, I quickly realized the instructions were for a completely different model. Even if these were the right instructions, the photographs provided were taken by a camera and not the clearest quality; good assembly instructions usually have computer-generated images or diagrams, not photographs taken by a camera. The rest of the instruction manual was a general guide on using telescopes, though a much better quick-start guide can be found easily online. So, with some trial and error, and a lot more time than I anticipated building the telescope, I finally got it assembled. And just in time too, because the moon had just crossed the window of the room I build the telescope in, and the moon was in great view. The opportunity also let me play around with the features of the telescope. It's not very easy to use because the stand is *very* wobbly. The counterweights are too much for the tripod, and the tripod should have used a better, more sturdy material. The dials and weights are easy to use, but the tripod makes everything longer to set up because the view won't always stay while moving. Despite all that, it's super fun to use. It comes with decent eyepieces to play around with; I didn't know how much of a difference eyepieces can make. With this telescope, I was able to view details of the moon for the first time. It really is just a big ball of rock spinning around.

title: Beefy but bombastic.
text: What a superb charger! I used this to replace my Amazon-brand brick, which, while it was great, needed to retire (I could hear rattling inside). This is about 1/3 larger than my previous charger, but still fits in my electronics organizer. The cable it comes with is also fantastic; it's the perfect length to keep my computer charged from the wall, and it's braided--yay for braids! There are two USB-C ports with different charging power. The weaker one won't charge if it's not powerful enough, which I realized when trying to charge my MacBook. That's pretty cool because I can charge two items at once, one with a bigger battery and one with a smaller. There's also a USB-A port that can be used at the same time. I notice a dip in charging power when all three ports are used, but that's kind of assumed considering it's used to charge three items at once.

title: Nice kit, but not for charging.
text: UPDATE LE DEUCE: Turns out the adapters can be used with other cables, but only if the USB-A adapter provided is linked to the other end. Plugging an adapter into the USB-C end of a cable with an USB-A port on the other end doesn't work. But if you have a cable with USB-C ports on both ends, then you can use any of the adapters as long as the included USB-A adapter is plugged into the other end. Now I know why they included it. Updated from 3 to 5 stars based on customer service and the fact that it just werks. UPDATE: With my first review, I thought it was the adapters that were the issue. However, I discovered that the adapters work only with the cable they come with. While I'm happy that they work, I'm disappointed that they work only with the cable provided because the cable is very short. This also means I can use only one adapter at a time. I hoped I could use these adapters to charge multiple devices at once. Unfortunately, that's not the case. Original review follows: Great little kit that gives me most adapters I need (the one missing is a miniUSB adapter) in an all-in-one kit. What I also like is that there are little compartments for microSD. I toss it in my electronics organizer. While I hoped it would eliminate the need for extra cables and my microSD case, I may need to get my other cables back. What I noticed immediately is that they're not meant for charging. I used the adapters to charge a copule devices and no power was drawn. At first I thought it was the cable, but the cables I've used are brand new, name-brand cables, and work fine without the adapters. So I tried other cables and there wasn't any power when charging. They work fine for data management, so I'll still keep the kit around.

title: As a backpack organizer, it fits my needs (currently).
text: I don't use this as a laptop sleeve. Instead, I got this because I thought I could use it as a backpack organizer. I carry various notebooks, writing, and drawing supplies with me. I'm not an artist by any means, but I like to journal using different media. Having them loose in my backpack didn't make it easy to find things or have everything in one organized location. This sleeve drastically reduced clutter and makes it faster and easier for me to journal. Currently, it holds my journal, a soft writing mat, my Sonnenleder pencil case, a few fountain pens, a whiteboard notebook, and some markers (dry-erase, Sakura, permanent). It's a tight squeeze, with the front pocket, but overall I have no worries of anything being damaged. In fact, I feel everything is more secure in this. I also love that there are pockets to tuck the handles; I use one only just to pull the sleeve out of my backpack. The front pocket sometimes gets caught in my backpack when I take it out. There's a bit of fabric on the cover of the front pocket so as to conceal the zipper; I wish there wasn't as much excess fabric, or at least some way to stick it closer to the sleeve (like some Velcro or something). But now, instead of looking for and taking out a bunch of things from my backpack, I just pull this out and everything is one, easy-to-locate space.

title: So far, so good!
text: These days I'm all about Thunderbolt 4 cables for as many devices as I can manage. I appreciate that I can use one cable for both data and power. This cable so far is great. I've used it as my main cable for the last several months. The cable has gotten looser (the covering isn't as rigid), but that's the only noticeable difference. It still delivers great power and data speed.

title: Charges devices quickly
text: My daughter has been using this as her charger to charge her iPad. It works quickly which is extremely convenient. She also loves the pink color! Perfect for a pre teen or teen (or adult!). The only drawback is the plug gets extremely hot so just be careful!

title: Very good, but slides are unstable.
text: The microscope is awesome, and the screen is super clear. We tested all the slides (some are more interesting than others) and the filters, which help a lot. I haven't used a microscope since high school many and plenty of moons ago, so it's awesome to see how technology has advanced. Even though this is considered a kid's set, it's an awesome kid's set and I use it just as much as my kids. The slides can be a pain sometimes because a slight bump on the table will move it. So long as there's no sudden jolt, though, it should be fine.

title: Mostly excellent, but does disconnect once in a while.
text: Having recently dug my music collection (odd how we go back into hobbies after years of stagnation), I took time to curate my setup (and by setup I mean my Note8 with a USB DAC) for optimal listening. Until recently, but "best" headphones were my Shure Aonic 4, which are excellent for the price range. The cable it comes with is okay, but preferably replaceable. It comes with an inline mic and makes a lot of feedback-noise when moved. I know cables are a mixed bag when it comes to audio equipment, so I shied away for years. But rather than place the emphasis on audio-quality improvement when looking at cables, I realized I'd rather get a cable if it looks and feels good. This one fit the ticket. This is the only cable I have that's meant to be swapped with MMCX in-ear headphones. They pair well with the Aonic 4. First, I'll get the problems I have out of the way. Since this cable is meant to connect with around-the-ear IEMs, there's a plastic wrap near each MMCX adapter. It makes wearing around the ears easier, but putting them on initially takes a few tries. They are easy to tangle, even if I use the "roadie wrap." Putting them on while on the go proved to be suboptimal; I have to be sitting or standing to put them on. Sometimes I get some feedback noise, but rarely. Definitely not the same as the stock cable that comes with the Aonic 4. The biggest problem I have is that the end connection disconnects nearly every time I use the cable. Having a modular cable is awesome, but the connection from the cable to the audio jack doesn't lock. I expected there to be a click, indicating it's on and snug, but no such thing. Since I use this cable while on the go, it's connected to my phone, which rests in my pocket. At least once the cable end will come loose. It's easy to press back in (just a little nudge will do), but it is rather annoying. Now for the good. The cable feels awesome. I get now why people prefer to upgrade certain cables. I care very little for how much the audio quality is "improved" (there's too much immeasurable subjectivity in that area), but having a cable that doesn't tangle easily and is very light makes enough of a difference to justify the upgrade. The cable is soft to the touch, though I don't doubt its ruggedness in the long term. The MMCX connectors snap satisfactorily into the Shure IEMs; at least those haven't come loose. The metal ends and Y-splitter are very nice and definitely attribute the cable with a premium look. This cable has sold me on the reasons to upgrade headphone cables.

title: Super handy.
text: Much better than what I had before. My previous case covered only a third of batteries I have. I have batteries in various sizes and shapes; this case covers them all (I do have a number of D-cell batteries that don't have spaces in the case, but I ordered too many anyway). The case even has slots for button batteries! It's made of durable plastic, akin to the plastic found in fishing tackle boxes. The latches close securely (for now).

title: Definitely dusts, but SUPER LOUD.
text: Outta the box, the duster is unbalanced. The weight is toward the nozzle, and the plastic feels brittle. Not sure how long this duster will last me. In any case, it works very well for what it's made: dusting my desk and other surfaces. The dust clears away far more than using compressed air. There are two settings, low and high. Usually low is enough. However, I can't stand using this for a while because it's sufferingly loud. My cat runs away whenever I turn this on. Honestly, it's almost as loud as my vacuum cleaner. I took it to my office and use it only for about 5 seconds. Also, because it's unbalanced, it becomes very heavy at the top and awkward to move when dusting.

title: Fun, but pricey.
text: It's an awesome ornament that definitely attracts attention. To work, it should be fully charged and hung on the tree; it works exactly as the description states.

title: Excellent charger.
text: Though we don't use this for data, the charging ability is great. We finally can fast-charge our devices, and the build quality feels like it should last a while.

title: Fine, but a bit weak.
text: This neck fan works well, but it's a bit weak. I still get sweaty in the areas it blows cool air. The neck fan fits our youngest daughter as well as me. The rotation of the fans isn't the best, but at least they reach where we'd like.

title: Work well.
text: The binoculars work well for everyday use. I've used it to see blocks away from my home, as well as for some stargazing. The binoculars aren't too heavy, but the angle can be a bit uncomfortable on my nose.

title: Chunky cable preferable for longer distances.
text: The cable itself works marvelously, and fits snug and secure in my TV. The only issue is that, because of the cable material, it's somewhat difficult to get into tight corners. I route cables from my mounted TV to an entertainment center on the floor, which has several holes for cable management. Getting the cable through the entertainment center was a bit of a hassle.

title: Works wunderbar!
text: Great cable and durably made. Has been used in various plugs, homes, and vehicles, and charges without issue.

title: A bit loose on the bud, but stays in the ear.
text: Wonderful replacement tips for my Shure Aonic 4. The sound is comfortable, and the feeling is soothing. They're not a perfect fit for the Shure, even though they're supposed to be compatible; the tips come off freely if pulled, but surprisingly they stay on when removing the earbuds from the within the ears.

title: Great, if a bit big.
text: These aren't just for consoles; we paired this with a computer, and it worked flawlessly. The comfort-level is very good; I didn't get fatigue after wearing it. The mic works well, and can be tucked in when not in use. They're bulky, so a bit distracting if you're using them to chat.

title: Fantastic system; so-so firmware.
text: This is the first mesh system I've used. I had a Linksys router and an Asus router before this, both installed with third-party firmware. After the Asus upgrade, I used the Linksys router as a repeater. The signal was okay; considering I had Xfinity 250Mbps, the Asus worked fantastically, while the Linksys trailed behind. We live in an old apartment building with thick, plaster walls, so signal can be very spotty. With this mesh system, I saw a huge upgrade the first week. Setup was very easy; quick instructions are provided. As soon as the setup was complete, I delved into the firmware. I recall being a little disappointed as I was used to the Asus custom firmware (Asuswrt-Merlin). The Asus firmware "just werqed." I run a small server, and setup was super easy with the Asus. With the Netgear, it was a lot more involved. Setting up outside ports was a pain; at the time, there was no simple way of forwarding ports. I recall a little workaround I was able to conduct with the server, but it took me days to figure out. The firmware also lacks time restrictions for devices (at least of this writing). Asuswrt-Merlin allows me to set specific times to shut off internet for devices, which comes in handy with a large family. As for the actual mesh system, so far so good. I can't tell when I'm using the main router or the satellite. The devices connect automatically without hiccup. I've since ditched Xfinity in favor of RCN 1Gbps; this mesh system works very well with the service. Once we have fiber, I can't wait to see the results.

title: Serious upgrade from Master 2.
text: Even after using both MX Master 2 and 3, my favorite mouse still is the Proteus Core G502. Does that mean I don't like the Master 2 or 3? Yes and no. Yes to 2, no to 3. I prefer wired mice (yes, I said "mice"). The additional tools I get from the software for the G502 allow me to customize the G502 far more than I can with either the Master 2 or 3 (both use the same software). With dual monitors, the G502 creates for a seamless work environment. I no longer game, and still the G502 reigns supreme in my hand. The Master 2 I received gratis from work. It was an arduous request to grant, but eventually my employer succumbed. However, I was far from impressed. I have small-ish hands for an adult, and found the Master 2 too large for comfort. I use a hybrid claw grip, and felt the Master 2 to be a ball in my hands. But the Master 3 is a worthy upgrade that I recommend to those who are in the similar boat as me. To me, the Master 3 leveled some of that bump; now it contours comfortably to the shape of my palm. The wheel is *excellent*; while I haven't given up on my G502 wheel, I became accustomed to the Master 3 wheel faster than I did to that of the Master 2. I love the mixture of textile plastics on the Master 3. The portions that touch the palm have a rubber-like feel, while the rest comprises a harder feel. My only qualm is the back and forward buttons. They aren't where my thumb seems to want to find them, and oftentimes I miss pressing them. Nevertheless, this is my go-to mouse at home.

title: Most excellent!
text: Works well for our use!

title: Wonderful "beater" speaker, though the bass drowns some of the detail.
text: Thus far we've used this speaker while working outside, bike-riding, and at home. It does get loud enough for the family to hear the music playing while on bike rides, and is very easy to use. We've paired it with both an Android and an iPhone, and the setup was a breeze on both. The quibble I have is that the bass can be a bit dominating. It drowns some detail in the music, even when tweaks are applied.

title: Excellent cable.
text: Works well and keeps our phones and tablets charged.

title: Very stiff, but works great.
text: Don't use this one in tight corners. It works well and I haven't noticed any drops in speed.

title: Pretty decent starter projector.
text: We've used this primarily during the lockdown. During the summer, we were able to bust this out for at-home theater. It's not a bad projector by the cost alone, but it's not good enough. This is my first personal projector, and my experience comes from working much more expensive projectors at work. The projector comes with a storing case, flimsy tripod, remote, and cables. The power cable is very short. If you're using this outside, be prepared to use an extension cable, even if you have an outdoor outlet near. The remote is fine, but most controls can be accessed on the projector. The tripod is very unstable. Even though it's metal, it feels very brittle and I never trust the tripod alone. With a bump, the project can move quite a bit. I therefore use a couple of books for stability. The projector's zoom features are nonexistent; to create a smaller or bigger picture, you need to manually move the device. Not too bad, but there's a lot of fiddling around. The focus is okay; it doesn't have wide range, but we usually can find a sweet spot pretty quickly. So far we've had success connecting a Chromecast and phones, and therefore are able to watch anything that streams. The picture quality is pretty good, and seems to be right around 1080p. We've never had trouble watching anything or felt that something from the picture was out of focus. Colors seem to be adequate. There are also speakers on this thing, but, as expected, they're not very loud. Thankfully there's a 3.5mm audio jack, which we've used for external speakers.

title: Very easy to assemble. A few quibbles.
text: This is our first projection screen, and we used it quite a bit this summer. It's very easy to assemble on the metal frame. It comes with legs, but we never used them; instead, we posted the screen on the back of the house. The instructions are straight-forward; after the second assembly and disassembly, we got the hang of it very quickly and didn't need the instructions. The bag it comes with fits everything snugly, and there's even a pouch just for the screen so that it doesn't mix with the metal. There is a very strong odor when we opened the box. Definitely has a marine smell, but it did go away after the third use. The screen latches onto the metal frame by buttons. However, the corners are very difficult to snap on, so much so that we decided to leave them unbuttoned. Thankfully there is a surplus of buttons, so the screen stayed straight and wrinkle-free. Even with the screen folded during storage, we didn't notice any creases while watching movies in the backyard. A great investment, especially during the quarantine.

title: Fantastic battery life.
text: These are my first wireless ear buds. I've got a couple of $100+ IEMs, the Sony WH-1000X M3, and Audio-Technica over-the-ear headphones. I think I've got a good sense of under-$500 sound quality, and these Technics are slightly overpriced in my opinion, but they still sound fanstastic. I have smaller ear canals than normal (as told by my audiologist), so I always opt for a size down when trying on tips. I followed the instructions to insert these Technics buds into my ear holes with the smaller tips, and they fit great. They don't come out with vigorous head-shaking, and haven't come out during my work commutes. I walk about half an hour a day, and so far so good. The ear buds pair easily, and they always connect to my phone when I take them out of the case. I tried the noise-canceling, but found it to be sub-par compared to my Sony headphones. Sony actually sucks out the volume outside; these Technics add a white noise filter, which to me obstructs the audio I'm listening to. There's an app you can download to your phone which turns off the white-noise filter, so I did that, and turned of equalizer settings. On my phone I use Poweramp v3, AntennaPod, and Amazon Prime HD. They all sound great, but, because the Technics don't slide all the way into my ear, some of the bass gets lost. Higher volumes help, but then you run into ear damage. Overall, I'm pleased with my first set of wireless ear buds. While they won't take over my Shure IEMs, they're super convenient to have during my work commutes.

title: Sound great, but maybe not perfect.
text: With the right tips, these sound fantastic. I can imagine with further "break-in" and maybe some customization, they will be phenomenal. They are a little bass-heavy, but nothing too detrimental. For reference, here's what I used: - Samsung Note8 - VE Odyssey HD DAC - Poweramp v3 - songs ripped from CD into FLAC using EAC Here's my previous experience: - 1More Quad - Audio Technica ATH-M50x - Sony WH-1000MX3 - Technics EAH-AZ70W These sound better than the Technics, but not nearly as good as the Sony. With that said, these wired headphones aren't exactly the best spokesperson for staying wired. I'm all for wired for both audio and video, but I admit that wireless options like the Sony and Technics make me a believer. With the right codecs and setup, you can achieve wonderful results. There is supreme comfort with these IEMs. With the right tips, I got them fitting snugly in my ear (but there is some trial with error), and there is a metal right around the ear to allow the wire to stay in place. But I question whether these IEMs are worth the price. For $300 you can get cheaper IEMs (imported) with better tips and cables and still have some change in your wallet. And with the push into wireless around the same price range, Shure really needs to push their technology and rely less on their name. Their name alone certainly commands attention, but the wallet is stronger.

title: Very good, inexpensive Thunderbolt 3 cables.
text: I'm trying to transition all my USB-C cables to Thunderbolt 3, and I'm finding some brands work better than others. Monoprice, Apple, and Amazon Basics make quality, inexpensive cables. I've heard of Cable Matters, but haven't used them before. This is my first cable from them and I'm overall pleased thus far. I ordered the short, 2.4ft since I planned on using this in the car. It's the perfect length. The plug is located just by the gear shift, and it reaches comfortably to the phone mount on the vent. It charges very quickly and stops once the phone reaches 100%. The material also seems pretty good, so I'm not worried leaving this in the car.

title: Quality is stellar. Limited usage, perhaps.
text: The qualit of this storage case is pretty darn good. The zippers are nice and thick, the fabric is thick (though I'm not sure if it will develop fuzz balls over time), and the interior is more than good. The upper half has a bumped, cushioned roof, most likely to protect anything the elastic strap hugs. The strap is also meaty and tight; I would trust the combination of the strap and cushioned roof with most electronics. There is an abundance of plastic pages for memory cards; they seem to fit up to normal SD size. Because of this, you have to move them to access anything you may store underneath. However, because of the length of the pages, you can also opt to store things on top of them. The shell is pretty stuff (probably because of enclosed cardboard or something similar).

title: Working good so far.
text: I haven't been able to test this cable's HDMI 2.0 capabilities yet, but for working with my Switch it works great. I've experienced no signal loss in the year-plus that I've been using it.

title: Basic mouse.
text: Basic mouse for general needs. Can come in handy during lockdown. Reminds me of the backup mice I'd purchase in my college bookstore during a night of late studying. It works well on most surfaces, but anything with too much texture can cause it some hassle. It's also super light; I'm used to Logitech mice with weight.

title: Vibrant cables.
text: These Cat7 cables work well and I haven't notice any drops in the Cat7 speeds. I like how they're very vibrant as they're easily distinguishable from other cables.

title: Decent for the price.
text: Not sure how "handmade" this laptop sleeve is, but it does the job handsomely, both functionally and aesthetically. It looks great housing my HP Pavilion in my backpack since I rarely use the sleeve by itself. It's slim but cushiony enough to provide some generous padding without taking up much space. It doesn't feel that premium, but it otherwise looks really good.

title: Lights are fine, but the cables get in the way.
text: Actual setup is pretty easy. But because there are so many parts I wouldn't recommend this as a pop-&-go solution. I'd recommend this if you want a more stable setup but easily moved to a different location. That said, once I got everything set the way I wanted, I found issues when plugging everything in. The cables are pretty thick and stiff (:wink:), which cause the connected devices to move unintentionally from their set places. So I'd suggest using lighter cables. Otherwise, it's a fantastic set of tools you can use from taking pictures of market items to hobbyist indulgences.

title: When it connects, it's great.
text: I have a love/hate relationship with this device. On the one hand, it works great when it actually connects, but on the other hand I hate when it doesn't. It comes with a USB 2.0 dongle, but the keyboard can be very fidgety when connecting to the dongle. I've used this on a DE-10 Nano and Raspberry Pi 4, and they both have given me connectivity issues with this keyboard. I also tested this on a MacBook Pro, but only the mouse feature was tested (which works great). I'm not sure if it's the battery or the keyboard, but it has a hard time staying connected. I'll lose key presses or the battery will die quickly. It becomes very upsetting when I'm resetting or entering a password and, on Raspbian, I can't see the password due to security measures, so I'll never tell if the keyboard entered the intended keys correctly until I get a success or failure. Usually when I miss a password it's due to user error, but when I'm using this keyboard it can be either user or device error. The size of it is comfortable in the hand, and the tactility of the buttons feel great. But I feel the size is too small for it to be used as a keyboard comfortably. Some keys aren't placed in standard US ANSI layouts, and the thumb has to do quite a stretch when entering some characters or commands.

title: Excellent general electronics organizer.
text: I carry around with me various cables and chargers, as well as adapters and SD cards. I used to use a roll-up organizer, but found them to be sub-optimal. I prefer book-style organizers, even though they take up more room; they're far better at organizing, and can hold more. They also tend to retain longevity of the devices since there's no stress from rolling them up. In this case, I house a few chargers, a handful of cables, a Pelican SD card case, a power brick, additional SD cards in the included slots, and a few USB devices. I also tossed in some cable ties, even though they don't really fit anywhere. But they haven't moved around despite my moving items in and out. The case isn't hard-shell by any means, but it does do a good job retaining its shape in my backpack. I feel it can protect my goods good enough; by adding smaller chargers in the inside spine, it helps give it a sturdier feel by adding a backbone to the spine.

title: Good, potent cable, but a little stiff with the braidng.
text: This is a pretty good cable in that it can charge up to 3A using USB-A and USB-C, but the braiding on it is super stiff. It's not that flexible, so it doesn't work well with tight areas or if you've got the cable connected to a narrow port. Still, for the actual charging and syncing it works well.

title: Very good, versatile SSD.
text: I've had Verbatim products since I was a wee lad in the '90s and my parents had Verbatim 3.5" disks. The name is a good name for easy-to-find computer storage options, and the name still does well today. I've used this 2.5" SATA SSD in myriad devices, from a hard drive bay to a Linux laptop, and it currently resides in my PS3 Slim where the OS boots a bit faster than the previous, stock HDD (though not much faster since the PS3 doesn't support SSD natively). No matter how many times I've wiped or used this SSD, the product works well. It's got a nice, satin shell that allows it to fit in all kinds of devices.

title: Short cable, slow to start, but still rocking.
text: I use this bay for two semi-permanent WD Blue drives, as well as the occasional SSD. I've never had the bay fail on me in over a year of use. The cable is pretty short, but then again I have the bay pretty far from the computer. Because I don't have a desktop, bays and enclosures come really handy for me. Sometimes the bay falls asleep after a period of inactivity; it can take up to 15 seconds for it to awake fully, but a minor issue considering how much use I've gotten out of it. Because of this as well as a Sabrent hub I have, I'm a fan of their products.

title: Stays cool. Slow at boot, but speeds up.
text: I'm currently using this with my NextcloudPi setup to store my own data over the network. The Raspberry Pi4 supports USB 3.0, which this SSD also does. That's one of the main things I look for when hounding an SSD: fast transfer rates, as well as large capacity. I know Samsung has a good reputation for SSD storage; I was very excited when this came in the mail. After re-installing NextcloudPi, I let the setup wizard reformat the Samsung T7 into Btrfs. The T7 formated flawlessly, and the storage shows up completely on both my web panel and my web settings. I had to restart my Pi4 a few times, and each time I shot some items to my SSD for testing. I noticed it was pretty slow on boot, but after a few hours it seemed to read and write almost as fast as my previous SSD. I supposed, over time, it will adjust to the Pi4. My previous drive was a Verbatim USB SSD, also 3.0. That thing got HOT. It was also made of aluminum on the outside, and I was afraid this T7 would be the same. So far so good; it remains much cooler than the Verbatim.

title: Fast memory ports, slow internet port.
text: I hope laptops don't go the way of phones where they try to get rid of as many features for the sake of thinness. Computers are tools and if you can't use a computer to its fullest then it's not made correctly. Unfortunately, our family as a newer MBP and I'm constantly attaching this hub just to plug in USB devices, SD cards, and now a LAN cable since I'm trying to set up hotspots around the home. The ports for the USB and cards are fast, and I like that there are both dedicated 2.0 and 3.0 ports. I also like that there's a dedicated microSD slot, since most of my SD cards nowadays are microSD; if I'm multi-taskin' then I can place two cards, one with an adapter and one without. The LAN port is a bit sluggish in comparison. It takes a while to detect internet via Ethernet cable, and sometimes it spots out.

title: Not as good as Velcro's original, but does the job.
text: I used these when my trusty Velcro-branded ties ran out. They're a bit too wide and thin for my taste, but they do the job. They haven't ripped at all!

title: Protects in style.
text: We got this to carry around our MBP. It works well and has great cushion. It is a bit bulky and takes up some room in bags, but by itself it works great and resists a lot of stains.

title: So smooth.
text: This is the first time I've considered a build, and I was fortunate to receive this to put in. It was very easy install, but as I mentioned I'm a newb and therefore am not sure if ease of installation is usually as simple. The lights are pretty easy to control as well. The lights are pretty unobtrusive, and it seems to work great overall. It's quiet and the lighting is subtle in my case.

title: Easy to set up; working well so far.
text: We had an Asus router that was working extremely well over the past couple of years, but for some reason it just went completely kaputt. Finally, it was time to set this one up. The installation was a breeze, and I love that there's an app to allow me to monitor it instead of having to use a web browser. However, the initial web page needs some updating! I'm pretty tech-savvy, but IT stuff always gets me hot and bothered. This one was one of the better experiences. So far so good, but I will update if I need to change my rating.

title: Excellent cable.
text: Love the bold red cable as it makes it easier to spot amongst the tangle of black and white cables we have. The first week I had it I carried it in my Switch case, and used it for both my Switch and Note8. Worked great. Tested it on our 2016 MBP as well and it worked fine; didn't charge as quickly as Apple's own charger, but for USB 3.1 it charged fast enough. Now I keep it in my car as my car charger for my phone while driving. The cable is long enough to reach the USB ports in the middle console, but I'm able to leave it in the adapter near the front console while the phone is held on by the vent mount. The included strap helps keep the braided cable in place. The ends seem to be made of very strong metal (aluminum?). There are Amazon Basics logos on them, but time will tell how long they last.

title: Very nice. The only missing feature I'd like is more preferential, really.
text: This is an extremely nice stand, and goes well with any desk setup and any laptop. I currently use it at work to prop my black Dell work laptop, and it still looks nice with a mostly black computer setup. The aluminum feels a bit on the cheap side, but still decent enough. It's very sturdy and gives me the assurance this will last some years, if not decades. You have to assemble it out of the box, but it comes with the hex key you need (as most assembly-required items do anyway these days). It rotates fine and doesn't swivel when it's not supposed to. I'm able to plug items in and out of the laptop and it doesn't move at all, but when I want to swivel it it has enough give when I push. The only nitpick I have is that I sometimes havce to move the laptop up a bit to open it as there no support in the back. I realize that's to accomodate laptops of many sizes, but if they implemented a back panel that could slide in and out of the support panel then that would've negated having to lift the laptop up. I tned to power off my computer during the weekends, so every Monday morning I have to stretch awkwardly over my desk, prop the laptop up to open it and power it on, then rest it back down. Again, not really a dealbreaker but it's the only thing from making this stand perfect in my eyes.

title: Works fine but gets HOT.
text: And I mean really hot! I can't even touch it when it's plugged in, let alone when data is being transferred. Still, it's super fast. My computer recognizes it and opens it immediately after plugging it in, and data transfers extremely quickly. Helps that my USB port is USB 3.0 as well. The color is nice, but the metal is a bit too glossy for being matte. The cable is very short but works fine enough for me. Just be warned that you can't touch this when it's being used!

title: Works. Super ugly, though.
text: A mixture of white and aluminum normally goes okay but doesn't really work here. The white color of the plastic doesn't seem to blend well with the aluminum pole of the stand. They do work well with my Sony noise-canceling headphones at work, but they do not look pleasant with my work setup. You have to assemble the base by placing the holder and the base into the pole, and that's pretty much it. I wouldn't choose these again if I had the choice, though.

title: Easy to set up, and very good picture quality.
text: We have a cable box in the living room, but it's costly to add smaller boxes, so we opted for this to use in the bedroom. Thankfully, our bedroom TV is a smart TV so we can stream most things, but it's still nice to have local channels to catch the news. Our building is an older building with plaster walls, so I was afraid this wasn't going to work as well. The bedroom TV is against a wall that's in the middle of the apartment; once I set everything up, however, I was shocked to find that it still worked well. It's not a simple plug-and-play; after everything is plugged in, you have to run an initialization through the TV's menu (which the antenanna insturctions dictate, but I chose to ignore the first time around). There are a lot more channels than I thought there'd be; after the first initialization process, all the channels stay there. I've had no issues with it getting a good signal. I think being on the very top level of my apartment building helps, even though the walls are plaster. The only downside is that the channel selection is backwards on my TV. I can't tell if it's my TV or the antenna. When changing channels and pressing up, the mini guide shows the channels going down. It's a bit confusing, even months after using this.

title: Powerful, flashy, and controllable.
text: This isn't the first time I've installed memory, but I was super excited to try these. The colors are vibrant but can be controlled easily, and they go very well with the Corsair RGB CPU cooler I have. The enhancement stronger RAM provides is always a must, and this is no exception. I know RGB may be a bit flashy for some people, but I embrace the vibrancy.

title: Cute wireless headphones
text: These wireless headphones were easy to set up with my iPhone. I usually use them while using the elliptical at the gym. The earbuds stay in my ear. One drawback is that they are not especially comfortable - the earbuds aren’t soft. I’m usually only using them for about 30 minutes at a time but I could see them becoming extremely uncomfortable with prolonged use - so I decreased my review by one star. The color of the earbuds is nice and the sound is clear. The batteries last a decent amount of time. I usually charge them prior to each time I use them though.

title: Decent "smart" remote, but finicky power buttons.
text: At the time I received this remote with my new X1 box, it was the first "smart" remote we had in the household; I was fiddling with the remote, box, and TV for a whole night to soak in all the features. My favorite to this day is how intelligent the lighting is on the buttons; lift them slightly and the lights turn on, but remain off when lying still for a while. I haven't used the voice features after the initial night, so I can't comment on that. Everything still works great, and overall I find the button configuration pretty intuitive. I still confuse the Exit and Last buttons sometimes, so maybe some tweaking could be used between those two (if there hasn't been yet). But the main issue I have is how the power buttons don't work properly. When turning on both box and TV, the TV will turn on but the X1 box won't. It's been like that with two TVs. And when powering them off the TV will turn off but the box won't. I have to manually turn it off, which is a step more than I'd like but I've adjusted.

title: Similar to the Tile locator
text: This is specifically made for iPhone 6/6s. It also comes with a case. You have to be within 150 feet of the item in order for it to be detected. In order for this to work, you have to use the case provided or the pixie needs to attach to your current case. I love my current case so I didn’t not opt to use the included case. The pixie that comes to attach to your current phone case is bulky and not very secretive. My phone paired easily. When opening the app, it shows the location of the item where the pixie was last updated. The pixie is very similar to the Tile locator, but I prefer the look of the Tile moreso.

title: Not sound-proof, but good enough for office use.
text: I knew right away that these would be my office headphones. I have a mechanical keyboard that I use at work, and the office I work in is semi-open. There's a *lot* of noise coming every-which-way. These are a much-needed accessory to my work productivity, as I'm easily distracted by things in my periphery, whether visually or auditory. The presentation is great. The box is very high quality, reminiscent of the recent Samsung Galaxy device boxes. A smooth matte feel with gloss--weirdly pristine. The box slides out of the slipcover and you get the headphones already in the case. What I like is that they're folded, and there's even a little sheet underneath the phones that always reminds you how to put them back in. Also included is a 3.5mm cable in case you don't want to use Bluetooth, a charging cable, and an adapter. The case is nice, but as I keep mine at work I can't testify to its durability. There's a thin mesh net on the backside in case anyone needs to store one or two thin headphone accessory/-ies along. The accent colors are a nice light copper/rose gold color. I love that color; I'm glad it's getting more attention in recent years. It didn't take long to charge the headphones, so they come with a little bit of juice. As soon as you turn them on, you get a soft beep along with a voice indicating they're turned on. Nice responsive feedback. Once I put them on I could hear the headphones working to drown out the sound; there was a thick veil of soundproofing that was draped over my ears as soon as the earpads touched them. The first thing I did was listen to podcasts through the Pocket Casts app and .flac music through Poweramp v3. With podcasts, the difference was phenomenal. Listening to "Wait, wait... Don't tell me!" made me feel as though I were in the audience. The music was fantastic...until I tried on my other headphones which I use for music only. I thought the bass might've been too strong with the Sony headphones, and I was right. After using even "cheaper" headphones like the Audio-Technica M50x, I could tell the Sony had too much bass. I'm not sure if that's partly because of the noise-canceling technology or what, but the bass can be toned down a bit, methinks. I then proceeded to download the supplementary app to get the fullest suite of attributes the headphones can get. The app works well, and I didn't experience any hiccups while actually using the app. The only hiccup was when I was trying to download the update. It took *forever*. Almost an hour and it was just halfway through. I decided to bring them to work the next day and let the app sit there while updating. Thankfully, it remembers the progress, even though the app kept crashing during the update process. There are some optimization tweaks in the app, some sound profiles to let you configure the noise cancelation level (yes, level; the noise cancelation is pure software; you can set it to drown out the most noise as possible or have no noise cancellation at all), and even a little snippet of what is currently playing through the headphones. A simple UI with all the features you need. The first few days I used it I was active, and I kept noticing that my ears sometimes would pop depending on whether I sat down or arose quickly. Another weird thing is that when I take the headphones off, my ears sometimes need a minute or two to adjust. There's so much noise in the world! After taking the headphones off I can hear HVAC activity and my loud work neighbor who's otherwise not that loud. I had some headphones with some touch controls before and always found them tacky. I used them once when I first got them and never again. But with these headphones, I'm always using the tap gesture to play/pause and the swipe gesture to raise or lower the volume. There are also swipe gestures to skip or go back a track, but since I never do that anyway I never use those gestures. You have to be careful with the tap; when it works, it works. But the whole surface isn't the active portion and you have to hit it right in the center. Sometimes I'm hitting my finger against my ears trying to find the spot and hurting myself in the process. I tested the gesture where you put your entire palm on the cup to turn off the noise canceling feature and let the mic allow incoming conversation, but not after the third try. I could hear the other people just fine, but I found the right hand over my ear felt awkward, and one person didn't realize I could even hear them. Putting your hand over your headphones isn't a gesture people immediately see as you paying attention to them. The headphones are extremely lightweight and comfortable to use; I left them on for about two hours once before having to take them off. I actually was surprised with how light they were; when I got the Amazon box I didn't believe it was my headphones. It was much lighter than expected. For my first noise-canceling headphones I'm pleased. The sound balance can be better (less bass), but they make for fantastic headphones to use at work. I wasn't sure what I was expecting with noise-canceling technology. I thought it would drown out all noises, but you still can hear the occasional mutter; it just won't be distinct. Oh, forgot to mention the battery life. I charged it only once and have been using it for a week, at about an hour or two each day. Still going well. If you press the power button once it will tell you the battery level. AFter the initial update the voice indicator might give the wrong battery level (it did for me), but give it about ten or fifteen minutes to adjust and it will go back to normal.

title: Very useful, but a bit bulky.
text: Have this plugged in in one of the main sockets in the kitchen. The wall outlet is the only one away from liquids, so it's the only one I felt safe plugging this into. Unfortunately, that outlet plate shares space with a switch, and this surge protector presses against the switch so that it bends it a bit. There's no damage, but I did have to force this a bit in there to get it situated. Would be nice if GE engineered it so that it was less than half the size of a square plate. The plugs work fine, however. We've used it for a few kitchen appliances and a vacuum cleaner, all plugged in at the same time, and about three running at once while charging a phone, and the power kept up fine. Very handy to have in a room where people constantly charge phones and tablets, but that also requires other plugged items like appliances.

title: Swell briefcase. Works fine with my 13" MBP.
text: Now that I'm transitioning to a more corporate world I figured it's about time I get a more "professional"-looking carrying satchel than my Osprey backpack. The only laptops I possess range around thirteen inches, as I find carrying anything heavier than that is far too large to be considered portable. This briefcase has it all. There are pockets galore; at times I feel there are too many as I keep unzipping the wrong pocket or can't remember in which pocket I put something, so I wish the tags would've been different somehow. Maybe have some lanyards on some or another. But inside the pockets you get even more pockets and sashes to separate compartments. The material is sturdy and has held up just fine in this insane Chicago spring weather. We've had temperatures ranging from 40-80 in just two weeks, as well as rainy and dry weathers. Chicago, I tell ya! My 2010 13" MBP fits fine in the main laptop sleeve without sliding around much, and I'm not able to feel much wait on my shoulder from carrying it around all day, along with a couple of books, a Hobonichi planner, and my pencil case. The main flaw I will say this has is the shoulder strap. It's not easily adjustable, and I still haven't fully figured it out. There is a buckle in the middle on either side--one static, and the other adjustable. But the adjustable buckle doesn't allow the strap easy give, and so I can't for the life of me get it to a comfortable length. The removable strap is sturdy otherwise. The other issue is the clasp holding the two handles together. It's not long enough, so instead of closing it with one hand I'm having to use both hands to squeeze the handles together before being able to snap the button together. All in all, it's a great briefcase usable even with 13" laptops, but the shoulder strap and the handle clasp need better, user-friendly improvements.

title: Headphones
text: Good sound quality but not the best for noise cancellation. It is inconvenient they are not foldable and, considering so, they should at least come with a case. Fit feels snug and they have not fallen off on accident. Bluetooth range is very good, I have been able to walk 3 floors down in my house and did not lose connection.

title: Extremely sturdy; threads could be tighter, though.
text: Nice lanyard to have on the backpack. Perfect for charging most mobile devices as we transition to USB-C as the standard. The plug ends are inserted into a cap with a thin lanyard. That then gets screwed in so the plugs don't fall out. I found that the thin lanyard attached to the cap was a bit too thin; not sure how it will be in the long run, but compared to the very thick strand at the bottom it seemed odd to have such a thin one at the top. Also, I cannot get the screw to tighten all the way; there's always a bit of looseness at the end, and I'm afraid it will defeat the purpose of having such a rugged lanyard when the screw will come undone and the plugs pop out. Great to have on a backpack, though. I just have it strapped to my backpack with the thicker lanyard.

title: Nice but finicky.
text: The headphones themselves are comfortable and easily adjustable, the range is nice, and the sound quality is great, but the controls themselves are frustrating. The pairing says that you hold until the light flashes blue then red, and I did this. But what happened to me is I held it and it flashed blue once then it would flash red repeatedly. The manual said nothing about repeated red flashing so I assumed it was in pairing mode and I was confused as to why it wouldn't appear on my phone. After a while, I realized that if I held the pairing button longer after it started flashing red then it would flash blue and red alternately and then I could pair. I still have no clue what the red flashing means. Also, the way the skip/volume is set up is weird and temperamental. You hold the button to change the volume and press once to skip or go to the previous song (depending on which volume buttons you press), but sometimes after letting go from holding the volume button the song will change anyway. I think it would be more efficient to switch to press to change volume and hold to change song to prevent accidental switches. I have yet to try a phone call but if the volume/song switch buttons weren't so annoying this would be a great product.

title: Sturdy cable. Fantastic for the price.
text: Amazingly sturdy cable. Monoprice rarely ever disappoints for the price, and that still is true in this case. Works great, too; most of the HDMI cables are similar. It all depends on the cabling with how they perform, in my experience. This one is definitely going to be the longest you'll need for a home living room setup. Monoprice, for the price, always delivers. This one is super thick, so if you prefer something with more manageable angles then I'd suggest Mediabridge.

title: Great.
text: Since we mounted our TV we like to use as few chords as possible. This way they are neatly tucked along the wall and down into the entertainment center where all our entertainment equipment is housed. So the main HDMI cable runs down but of course we have more components that require a cable than the one connected to the TV. Our solution? A signal splitter. Thankfully, we have only three output connections so this one seemed perfect. Plus, it touts 4k signal, even though most pre-4k HDMI boxes should be fine, but it's nice to have that in the title just in case. What I use this mostly for is the cable box and a couple of video game systems. As for the cable box, seems to work fine; no dropped signals that I've noticed, nor any degradation in quality. As for game consoles, I have the PS3 and the Wii U hooked up to it. SAme: no noticeable quality degradation nor input lag. Now, to put it to the real test, I hooked up some retro consoles that have been modded to output native HDMI; that means they'll be HDMI with no lag. Considering I have this and two HDMI cables connecting the console to the TV, I was curious to see if there truly was any lag. With older games, timing is everything, especially on the 8-bit consoles with platformers and fighters, like the NES. From what I could tell, there was absolutely no lag, not to mention signal loss. The buttons responded as though I were using a normal NES on a CRT. So yeah, I'm pretty satisfied. It's a bit light and doesn't have heavy pads on the bottom to prevent it from sliding around. With so many cables, and the ability to use the remote control, it should be a bit more stable on the surface. I haven't used the remote as the detections are instant. No need to manually switch the inputs, at least from my experience. Also, I didn't need to use the power adapter; the power from the HDMI cables seemed to be sufficient, and the detection was not complicated by the lack of adapter. Weird.

title: Basic mount. Tilt is very minimal. No instructions included.
text: Got this to mount a 42" Samsung TV onto our bedroom wall. It is very basic and doesn't require too much knowledge if you've mounted TVs before, but mine didn't come with instructions. I looked online and there are no available instructions, so I had to figure it out from similar mounts and reviews online. The only biggest problem I had was with the screws; I didn't know what width I needed to drill a pilot hole as many PDFs online had different numbers, but I found the right size and drilled away. Unfortunately, the drill I have wasn't strong enough to drill these all way, but I was able to use a socket wrench to finish putting them in by hand. The mount is decent, but, again, instructions would've been helpful. For instance, I couldn't tell if the spring-loaded bolts at the bottom of the mount, once the TV is hoisted up, were to be tightened after positioning the TV or left alone. I tried tightening them only to realize they were to be left alone. About five minutes wasted. I tilting the mount more but really you get about a half-inch's worth of movement. Otherwise, fine. Fantastic for the price, and more of a fixed mount if you need it.

title: Good watch; buttons a bit hard to press.
text: I run during the summer and run outside. I hate carrying heavy items with me, like water bottles and phones. I feel they sort of hinder my performance, though I realize it's probably more psychological than physical. Still, I'm not going to mess with a run I've been accustomed to for nearly twenty years, but I do wish, more often than not, that I had some way of tracking my run and how many miles I've done *exactly* while being outside. Sure, I can track the mileage by checking my phone before and after, but it would be nice to have a tracker on me without adding any psychological weight. I used to have a Polar watch that worked fine, but it died some time ago and I never bothered to get a replacement. But finally I did. With this one, I'm able to wear the watch without toting my phone along and it still carries all the features and tracking as if the phone were connected to any other tracking watch. While this watch is used for a number of cardio activities, I use it only for running. There are "pages" of exercises you can track, but for a quick run the default is set on the bottom left button--very nice to have, especially for me. Not sure if you can change the default on there to another exercise, but for me it's perfect and I haven't bothered looking up how to change it. But curious to check out the full features, I ventured into the different pages (or screens) the watch has to offer. During my course, I found that the buttons were *very* stiff. This might be to prevent accidental presses during exercise, but I found that I had to press almost twice has hard as other electronic watches for the watch to recognize my press. But, from my uses so far, I've pressed it mostly to view all the screens when testing out all the features. When actually running, I do no more than a few presses before and after each run. The network had trouble activating itself in the beginning, but that's because I was fiddling with it outside. It kept trying to set itself numerous times when I actually ran outside, but I always dismissed it. Once, however, I was under the open sky I let it connect and it has had no problem or delay connecting ever since. After every run I am able to sync it with the Epson app, as well as RunKeeper. People have complained about the Epson app but I find it neat and useful. Overall, it's a great little watch that accurately records my runs and uploads them without the use of the phone during the workout. I'm able to review it speedily on my phone right after, and I love that I can now track my progress without the burden of added weight. It's pricey for sure, but considering I don't need my phone and my previous watch lasted me ten years, I'm sure this watch will be a great investment that will last me hopefully for another decade or so.

title: Pricey, but fits and feels great.
text: We have had a couple of MBPs before getting this one, and those two have sustained minor injuries over the last 10+ years. But since this MBP will be used between two people this time, we decided to get some sort of protection for it besides the padded sleeve. This one was far more expensive than others, but I love the colors and that I could see a majority of MBP. It snaps-fit into the MBP. They're a bit stiff and the snap sounds like it damages the computer, but obviously it's supposed to protect it I guess that's normal. The kit comes with two filters that fit over the MBP as well, in case you're worried about having full coverage. Though I"m not sure if there are any films to remove from them; they come with tabs that you have to remove--like from phone screen protectors--but they remove nothing when I remove them. I lifted them up and out and just the tabs took off. Weird. It's very pricey for what it is, but it looks sleek and doesn't add much bulk. I like the blue accents in the inside, though they're barely noticeable when on the computer. The bump at the bottom where you rest your thumb when using the track pad takes some getting used to. I've been used to the groove of the MBP for years, which has been improved with each subsequent model, but this one tries to make it easier to find the notch but at the same time throws me off because I'm not used to it. It's a nice case; maybe a bit pricey, but I love the colors. Just wish the Thule logo was more subdued.

title: Nice, cheap Bluetooth sport earbuds.
text: I use this with my Note8 and so far have used Poweramp, Spotify, YouTube, and Audible through them. It worked wonderfully and I got no hiccups from the signal. I used it while running and stationary at my desk. No distortion and the sound is very good, considering the price. The clip works great and stays on my shirt while running. At this time, I have run on the treadmills. I don't like it, but it's much too cold at the moment to run outside in Chicago (I don't like layering). I don't expect it to differ much, though, when I start using it outside in the summer.

title: Great sunglasses; okay smartglasses.
text: As sunglasses, they are phenomenal. They even fit my slightly narrow face. I own a pair of Gascans that I've had for almost eight years and they are my favorite pair of sunnies. Wanted something now that I'm starting to run more and the sun can sometimes cause a harsh glare. So nice sunglasses with the ability to track my exercises? Sure; why not. As sunglasses they fit a bit loose on my head, but with the same material that I used on my Gascans I was able to make them tighter by fitting some foam on the hinges; this way they wouldn't (and didn't) loosen while running. They fit great and are an excellent addition to my running routine. The sun isn't as vibrant as of this writing, but I will continue to use these throughout the winter as the sun's glare on the snow will be an issue. I tried these on without the smart devices enabled at first to get an idea as to how the sunglasses were by themselves. The box comes with all the electronics apart from the glasses, and the glasses come in a nice semi-hard shell with the additional lens inside. I then equipped everything in one bout. The earphones fit okay, but they did tend to slide out at times during the few times I've used this so far while running. No issue in terms of when I'm in the gym, however. Syncing from my phone has never been an issue, though I hate carrying it with me. As smartglasses, they're okay; nothing revolutionary, and it's up to you if you want to pay the premium price for something your phone already can do, provided you take it with you. As the coach doesn't do as much as I'd like as of this writing, as I already have most of my workouts set. I suppose it may not be entirely geared for me as the only exercise I do outdoors is running; the rest is all in the gym. The music does tend to cut in and out, and I wound up just shutting it off completely after a while. I may look into more comfortable replacements, too. As sunglasses, these are phenomenal. The perfect sunnies for triathlons, methinks (when they're not wet). But as for smartglasses, a novel idea but needs improvement.

title: Great tablet for the price.
text: For $80, this tablet is actually pretty good. It's about the same height as my Note8, but almost double the width. Still, the tablet-exclusive apps on the Google Play Store work without issue on it, though of course you're going to sacrifice some viewing due to the smaller scale. When I got the tablet I knew it wasn't going to be anything spectacular. At $80, I knew it wasn't going to compete with the devices I was used to, but it still was nice to have to act as a tablet to play my tablet-exclusive games on and for the kids to use to play their games. The screen of course isn't the sharpest, and out of the box it isn't as sensitive in all areas. Two of the first games I installed were a couple of pinball apps, and the screen had a hard time detecting my presses on the left side. The screen is quite sharp considering it's a "low-end" tablet, and the feel is very solid. Has a nice textured back to it which makes me reconsider if I'll get a case. The screen does retain fingerprints easily but a quick wipe on a shirt resolves all issues. There is a microSD slot which is a nice addition; I can transfer any transferable games to that since this tablet has only 16 GB (less considering there's only 14.-something and some of that is taken up by the OS). Operating the OS is super sluggish. Takes four times as long to do something as it would on a beefier device. But actual in-app operations aren't as bad. A little more sluggish than on a beefier device, but not enough to notice that much. Since this tablet doesn't have a phone speaker at the top, the actual main speaker is located in its stead. As a result, you get a nice, loud, crisp sound whenever you watch a movie or play a game. All in all, a fantastic little tablet for the price; I hope the missing sensitivity spots are temporary. The screen isn't as smooth as others, but I'm willing to forgive that for the price.

title: Beautiful watch, but notifications don't always appear.
text: First time using a hybrid smartwatch. I have used fully fledged smartwatches before, but never a hybrid. I was curious as to how they worked. Did they have a mini screen? Did they play notifications? Or was it just a simple vibration gimmick and time and date were synced to the phone? (Answers: #3.) Anyway, when I got the watch I was impressed right as soon as I opened the box. It was and is beautiful. I love a rose gold tint when it's more copper than pink. Really, many of the rose gold colors geared for men is more of a copper color; not sure why companies are naming them "rose gold." It sounds nicer? Going with the Apple trend? I dunno. Either way, I like it. The strap is made of premium leather. I own many leather watch straps, and I love the way this one feels. Light, but solid and soft. The rose gold accentuates it handsomely. Now, on to the device itself, which, as I stated, is my first hybrid smartwatch. I have a Note8, and so I've used only an Android to pair with this watch. I don't recall if the box states it works with iOS (I've placed the watch in my drawer and the box is stored in the basement, so I don't feel much like fetching it), but with Android it works fine. I say fine because I did experience some small hiccups which I will discuss further. The instructions included were bare, but really you're to install the app on your phone and follow the instructions from there. In the quick-start menu you'll get the watch running in less than a minute. The hands move as you set the watch, and everything is synchronized correctly. The app does all the work for you; you can assign shortcuts to the buttons on either side of the crown, set the notification functions, and so on. For me, I set the upper one to check the alarm and the crown to check the date. The watch is beautiful on the wrist. I like to wear it with warmer, redder colors, and it fits beautiful with the entire ensemble. The time so far has always been synchronized, but I have noticed some slight hiccups while paired with my phone. The notifications don't always show. I have one contact set to my favorites, and that one always shoes (both hands move to 1 and the watch vibrates when I get a call or text from the favorite, and subsequent favorites will be moved to 2, 3, etc.). However, I do not always get notifications for texts from others. From my understanding, the watch is supposed to vibrate for texts and calls, even if they're not part of your favorites, but I get notifications almost always just for my favorite, and not the others. I don't recall any notification for an incoming call, whether from my favorite or others. As a hybrid smartwatch, I like that I can see my steps through the complication, and see the date and alarm settings (though I hate that the date isn't a complication; instead you have to assign on of the three buttons to check the date). However, because it doesn't always detect notifications I'm still perplexed as to utilizing its full functionality. I hope it's just some sort of glitch that will fix itself with...time.

title: Excellent headphones at this price point.
text: Got these for my daughter to use when she has screen time with the iPad or one of our phones. They come in a very nice box with a window display inside the front flap. Included inside were the micro-USB charging cable and the 3.5mm-3.5mm headphone jack--both made of threaded fabric. Very nice. The headphones didn't come pre-charged so we charged them right away. The sole LED on the 'phones turned red during the charge. Once they were done, we paired them first with my Galaxy S5--it was detected right away. Next we paired with our ancient iPad 2, which also detected the headphones immediately. My wife carried them to a doctor's visit and it paired flawlessly with her iPhone 7. They are very attractive as headphones; the sound is decent. About right for this price range. They fold for storage but ours didn't come with a carrying case of any kind (not sure if one is supposed to be included). The volume doesn't reach very high, but I guess since this is for our daughter anyway that's a non-issue for us, but still something to point out.

title: Amazing IEMs with a couple of noticeable drawbacks.
text: I am not an audiophile by any means. I have Rockbox installed on my iPod video classic with a FiiO amp attached, all loaded with FLAC tunes. I listen to Spotify at work. That's the extent of my musical needs. I have Audio-Technica headphones, and dream of some day owning custom Kaisers. That's my background. I was pretty excited to get these. Right after ordering, I watched a few YouTube videos on them, and read up on Head-Fi. For the price, 1More seems to deliver outstanding products. Needless to say, I was pretty excited. The box finally came and I was found to be very impressed with the presentation. You get a nice, magnetic box housing the IEMs, a leather(ette?) pouch, and multiple choices of ear piece tips. For starters, I found that the ear piece tips pre-attached to the IEMs were the most fitted for me, but I still do not find them perfect. They slide down a bit when in my ear, so there is some loss of sound. I will have to buy some aftermarket ones. The microphone is also sub-par. This is the first time I've used a mic with headphones, and most of my calls could not catch my voice properly. I would get complaints that I sounded muffled or far away, and so I've resorted to using the phone mic most of the time. The mic buttons work flawlessly for playback features, however. As for the sound, it's fantastic. With four drivers, I can hear so much more--and so many more flaws! I usually transfer music files into FLAC, and so I have pretty good sources for music. I've been using both my Samsung Galaxy S5 and Rockboxed iPod Video (equipped with a Fiio E11), and the sounds are great, but I'm noticing some files that weren't transferred correctly. I cannot connect to my computer speakers at work as the speakers do not have enough power to juice up the Quads, so be sure you have a more recent device or one with enough power to drive these IEMs. I also use them on my Wii U's GamePad for Breath of the Wild, and they're actually better than my Audio-Technicas, even with the sliding ear tips. I hear a lot more, and sound is very important in the game. All in all, amazing value for the price. The ear tip issue is more personal as my ears simply don't fit perfectly any of the ones provided, but I do wish the mic worked better.

title: Great Bluetooth headphones, but annoying volume beep.
text: I really like these headphones. The presentation of the setup is done really well, especially considering I've never heard of this brand before. The box comes in a sleeve which removes easily, and the box separates to reveal a lower portion which doubles as a headphone stand. That's really neat! Though I won't use it as I prefer a more dedicated headphone stand, I think it's nice of them to offer it; you can even fish a charging cable through a hole so that it can charge while it's standing. Comfort-wise, the headphones are really comfortable. I was able to find a good height with them on my head and had no discomfort after wearing it for over an hour. I had no issues connecting to my phone right away. I have an S5 and it picked up the headphones almost instantly. I was not able to connect it via my Samsung smart TV, but that may be due to the TV's limitations rather than the headphones'. The sound is very good, and, despite being wireless, there is no noticeable lag. When I say lag, I mean hearing the playback while monitoring the pace of the playback on the screen. Now, for the touch controls. Overall, they work really, really well. I think the design of the track-skip and volume is gaudy and detracts from the overall aesthetic of the headphones (for being black, these headphones are otherwise a real eye-pleaser). However, I did notice on mine that the volume doesn't go very high, and that there's actually a very loud beep whenever I hit max, and it's actually really, really abrasive on my ears. At first I thought it was a one-time thing, but it keeps happening whenever I want to raise the volume and I think it's not loud enough, only to find that I'll reach max pretty quickly. Otherwise, they're great headphones, connect flawlessly, and are very comfortable. I think the right earpiece, which contains the touch area for track navigation and volume, is a bit tacky and detracts from the aesthetic, but that's a personal preference.

title: Not the best
text: These were my first pair of Bluetooth headphones and honestly I wasn't impressed. They didn't work very well and the sound was muffled. Wouldn't spend your money on these.

title: Tough little dudes.
text: These were super easy to install and so far have lasted great on trips to and from Wisconsin (we live in Chicago). They're extremely durable so far, and have held fine in slight rain and regular wind conditions. I usually ride in the city so have easy access to hide from the elements, but it's still nice that these will take a beating every once in the while when I'm on the long expressways. The sound is loud and I'm always able to hear my music, whatever I'm playing. So far so good and at the price I'd say these are a great option for "lower" end bike speakers.

title: PS4 Remote Review
text: After countless times of the ps4 controllers dying on me due to short battery life, media use on the ps4 was beginning to be a bit of an annoyance. Thankfully, the PDP universal ps4 remote has come to the rescue; well, for the most part. First and foremost, let me say that for the price, it does everything it needs to do and does it well. All of the buttons feel solid and are easy to use, the construction is good, the back is nice and grippy, it is lightweight and because it is a universal remote, it also works on your TV and other electronics. When attempting to use it with my TV it quickly synced itself without issue however I should note I have a Sony television. If you are looking for a basic remote for Blu-ray movies and Netflix, this is it. It completely solved the battery issue I had with the ps4 remotes, as it has not died on me once. If you are a Hulu user however, you can stop reading, it simply isn’t good enough for Hulu as it can behave somewhat erratically and will not go out of Hulu menus once in them. Outside of Hulu however I have not had a problem with the controller and it functions great with anything else I may need. There are some minor issues with the remote, for example in order to change the volume you have to switch to the TV controls and then switch back to the ps4 to work with that. It may have just been my controller, and it was easily worked around (use both controllers) but some may find that an issue. When price is factored in, I would say that for the most part, the small annoyances are just that and most users will be able to overlook them. If I had to give a star rating it would be a 4 out of 5 star product. Half a star off for lack of Hulu compatibility and another half off for the little kinks it still has, overall a good product.

title: Works!
text: The main feature we wanted from this was to pull the photos from our iPhone without having to sync all the time. Sometimes our phone gets filled so quickly with photos and videos that we can't take any more and we're not near our syncing computer. That's where this comes in handy. In order to use it fully, you have to download the compatible app (which is free), connect the device, and let the app and device access your photos, contacts, and calendar. We have a few microSD cards lying around, and so far our brands (Kensington and SanDisk) worked fine, even though the packaging is adamant in having you buy their brand of cards. ;) The app itself is pretty easy to use, but I'd rather have the main syncing buttons appear on the first page. When you open it up the app is split into three "pages" that you can swipe through to select. At the top are icons to select the app and card memory (though I'm not sure why you'd back up the phone to the app over the card), and then at the bottom you get features to sync to other apps. Those aren't why we got this product, so when you swipe right you get the buttons to sync the photos, contacts, and calendar. You can sync selected ones or sync them all to the card. We usually just select all, even if we know only pictures and videos have been added since the last sync; we just like to be cautious. Syncing takes only a few minutes. To confirm that all the photos and videos have been synced, I removed the memory card and plugged it in to both my computer and an Android device. I was able to navigate the folders in the card without issue (that is, no restrictions as I thought there might've been since it was an Apple's synced history going into Windows and Google machines) and see all the photos, etc. You can also navigate the folders via the device in the iPhone, but the thumbnails sometimes take a while to load. Initially I didn't think the videos were backed up, but that's because they didn't have that little play icon on them as other videos usually do. When I scoured carefully through the dates, however, I found them all, and no noticeable resolution loss. Perfect! So far this is exactly what we wanted and it works just fine.

title: Flawless with my S5.
