It only took about an hour of reading web forums to find that solution to the Windows app store refusing to work. Two problems I ran into were the sound which is from a single speaker hidden in a slot on one of the short sides of the tablet. If you want to listen to anything other than the default Window's beeps and tones you'll want to pair this with a blue tooth speaker or headphones. The speaker in this tablet is deplorable. The next problem I had was the tablet runs HOT. I was running a program designed for Windows 98, downloading and reading posts un Usenet and viewing a few posted vacation and astronomy images and I had to stop. The tablet was so hot it was uncomfortable to hold and I worried it might overheat and become damaged. While I was impressed to see Windows running on a small tablet I was thoroughly unimpressed with Windows 8.1 the tile system is just terrible. So, it has good video quality on a too small screen with horrible sound and a flaky app store to rely upon, though you can download and install normal Windows programs. I just wasn't that crazy about this tablet. And will definitely be sticking with Android and a much larger screen.

title: Does the Job... Excellent Service
text: Decent cable. About the same thickness as the OEM cable that came with my Samsung tablet. Plug was seriously tight for the first week or so but it's gotten a little easier to plug/unplug since. I worried about the plug getting stuck or coming apart at first but now after quite a bit of use it seems to fit better. Update - 03-09-2017: The cable appears to have developed a short from repeated bending. I contacted the seller and they gladly honored their lifetime warranty on the product and are shipping me a replacement. +1 star for exceptional customer service.

title: An Okay Television
text: Not a bad TV not a great TV. Needed for a bedroom where it's more used for company or background noise than for watching. That being said within the limited viewing angle the picture is reasonably good. For the money this suits our needs.

title: Reliable Power From APC
text: Design changed from the last time I bought one of these. I do like the new placement of the power switch. The battery was a royal pain to remove and connect. They don't give a lot of wiggle room to get the battery out, connected and reinstalled. I've trusted my PC and other electronics to APC products for ages. My last APC battery backup lasted over five years and weathered dozens upon dozens of Florida thunderstorms.

title: Really What I Needed
text: Well made. Reasonably sturdy. Holds dinner a laptop or tablet with plenty of room and next to no wobble. My only complaint is the top could use a bit more texture. Some items like the TV remote soda cans or the cordless phone tend to slide around a bit too easy. Other than that texture issue this is exactly the accessory table that I needed in the living room after my back injury.

title: Love It
text: I've had my X-E2 for a while now and even though it's my all time favorite camera there were times, shooting one handed and with my XF55-200mm zoom attached that the small body bit into the palm of my hand in an uncomfortable way. I had considered the newer MHG-XE hand grip with the opening for the battery/SD card compartment but after seeing the Arca Swiss mount built into the newer grip which looks less that comfortable and realizing that I've never needed to access the battery or SD card when out in the field (I shot over 600 pictures this past Sunday at a motorcycle parade/event with my X-E2 on one battery and still had charge left.) So I decided on this the older HG-XE1. I luckily found a used one here on Amazon for an excellent price. Now with the hand grip plus Lensmate's soft release button and thumb grip my X-E2 is complete. It feels and handles just that much better than 'stock'. Highly recommended.

title: Really Nice Zoom Lens
text: My family got together and picked this up for me during Fuji's sale/promotion in March. This is going to cover Christmas and birthdays for the next few years :) Build quality is top notch. The zoom, focus and aperture rings are all nicely sized and very... grippy. The zoom itself is almost, but not quite, too stiff. I noticed no creep whatsoever. Autofocus is, expectedly, a bit slower than the kit lens but still decent. Image stabilization is impressive enough for hand-held shooting in low light at full zoom. Image quality is impressive. The included hood is huge, seriously huge. It's actually a little hard to get the lens cap on with the hood on. Speaking of the lens hood; my one gripe with this rig is when fully 'on' the lens the hood tends to rattle a little bit. I've found that backing off the connection a 1/4 inch or so keeps the hood from rattling and still keeps it firmly in place. It does make my X-E2 a little front heavy but it's not that horrible. I'm contemplating buying one of the extension grips from Fuji for the camera. A nicely padded neck strap is a definite plus when carrying a camera with this lens mounted on it. One thing I've had to pay attention to is when switching back to my 18-55mm lens I need to be careful of how hard I twist the barrel to zoom in and out this lens is MUCH stiffer to use than the kit 18-55mm that came with my X-E2. I worry I may break the smaller lens after using this lens for an extended period. Highly recommended.

title: Works Well With the Fujifilm X-E2
text: I've used this several times now with my Fujifilm X-E2 and it works great. Simple and easy to understand and set. The only problem I had was the case is a little narrow for my thick hands and setting the controller required a bit of juggling. The addition of a light was a nice feature and even helped getting things connected in pre-dawn light. The case is a little flimsy, possibly easy to break but with care it should last. I found an old mesh pouch, I think I got a pair of promotional ping-pong balls in it, which holds the controller and cable when not in use and is perfect to hang the rig on my tripod when it's being used as an intervalometer which is my main use for this remote.

title: Not as Impressive as I'd Hoped...
text: Beyond bells. More important than whistles. When it comes to a camera, no amount of features are as important as one simple question. And that question is "How well does it take pictures?" And in the case of the Fuji Finepix S1 the answer is "It depends..." It depends on what you're going to do with your pictures. Are you going to look at them on the camera's 3" screen? Are you going to share them with friends who use cell phones? Are you going to post them to Facebook and Twitter and maybe Flickr? Then you will probably be happy with this camera. I have to admit I'm what people, sometimes insultingly, call a pixel peeper. I honestly believe that if the sensor of my camera produces a 4608 x 3456 pixel image that one which is properly composed and shot should look good at its original, 100% magnification, size. The Finepix S1, not so much. I've shot several hundred pictures with the S1 and I believe I've come up with two pictures that look okay (not outstanding, okay) at 100%. That's not saying this won't take a decent picture. Reduce the size to 1920 x 1080 or smaller and the images look much better. Out of the hundreds I've shot I've saved more than a few 'good' pictures. A few drawbacks I'd like to point out about the Finepix S1: This is supposed to be their new 'flagship' big zoom camera but it has a smaller sensor than their HS30EXR and HS50EXR cameras. Why not put the bigger sensor in the (currently) more expensive 'flagship' camera? No external battery charger is included. Charging is done in camera via a USB cable and AC adapter. The camera is not threaded for filters. Seriously? To mount a filter on the camera you need to purchase a relatively expensive adapter. Plus you'll need a lens cap that fits the filter dimensions since the camera's cap cannot be used with the filter adapter. No lens hood is included. An optional and somewhat expensive lens hood is available. The optional lens hood and filter adapter ring cannot be used together. The screen for the EVF is somewhat far inside the camera housing. There is white light coming from the bottom of the EVF enclosure and the EVF screen is significantly smaller than the space it is in. This makes it feel like you're looking around a tiny movie theater. The battery can be inserted wrong way around. I don't see this as doing damage to the camera but I've never seen a battery system that didn't have some kind of notch or tab to keep you from inserting the battery in the wrong way. You can fully latch the battery down and not have power to the camera. When I first read the user's manual I was psyched to find out the camera had the capability to shoot high speed video. This was always something I wanted to play around with. Then I tried it... The fastest the camera will record is 480 fps (frames per second) which is fairly impressive except it only records that fast at a resolution of 240 x 180 pixels. The video quality was good and the slow motion was fairly impressive but even on a 5" cell phone screen that size video is small. It's an unviewable postage stamp on a 23" monitor. Switching to 120 fps results in a 640 x 480 resolution video. This size was viewable and could even been watched (the quality suffered) full screen but the video speed wasn't as exciting as the much faster recording rate. It did make birds in flight an interesting sight but that was about it. Some good things about the Finepix S1: The camera body is weather sealed. It is dust and water resistant (I would not submerge it). If there's a hurricane or thunderstorm and I want to take pictures (and I will) this is the camera I'll be reaching for. The 3" LCD screen is fully articulated which combined with the weather sealing opens lots of opportunities for interesting photography. Super macro mode with ~1cm focal distance. Smooth and quick zooming within the full 50x (24-1200mm) range. The zoom control on the shutter button has two speeds and there is a separate zoom control on the lens barrel which can be set to fast or slow zooming. The camera has a nicely rubberized grip and body. It felt quite secure in my hands. All in all? I like the features and function of this camera but I'm not ecstatic about the image quality. There's significant noise and grain in low light, shots where the ISO is above 400 and at the long end of the zoom. Reducing the size of the images and some post processing work can produce decent pictures. It is an interesting mix of technology and the weather sealing is a plus but the image quality isn't much better than my several years old Kodak Z990 which though not weather sealed has made hundreds of trips to the beach without incident or damage.

title: A Disappointing Camera From Samsung {Edited}
text: My first impression upon unboxing this camera was "Wow, that feels cheap." Everything's made from unattractive plastic. The single dial on the top rear of the camera (oddly blank) feels light, spins too easily and clicking it feels mushy. The other buttons on the camera, power, movie and flash all have the same, cheap, mushy feel. The shutter button has poor tactile feel. The camera is surprisingly heavy; for me uncomfortably, painfully, so.The back is so taken up by the huge 4.8" LCD screen that the thumb rest is too short, more of an afterthought that cause me quite a bit of discomfort during extended use. The DSLR style handgrip is quite large (perhaps too large for small hands) to accommodate the massive 4360 mAh battery. On paper the idea of an Android OS with a 4.8" LCD screen and a big APS-C sensor sounds great but I was sadly less than impressed. Because of the Android OS startup time from fully off to ready to shoot is a very long 23 seconds. In standby mode the camera was ready to shoot in approx. 4 seconds. The camera runs warm, very warm, even just sitting idle on a cool 50 degree day. I would worry about overheating in the summer months. Image quality was unimpressive especially in low light. Early morning, post sunrise, images with sky and clouds were extremely grainy and noisy. Performance in full light was better but not spectacular. Auto focus was run of the mill, often seeking excessively in low light situations. High ISO performance was exceedingly poor. Past ISO 800 images were rather noisier and grainy. In auto mode the camera seemed to make poor choices for ISO and shutter speeds. Controls. Almost every setting is accessed via the large LCD screen. There are over twenty pre-configured shooting modes. I used several of them while checking out this camera. These selections are made from a top to bottom scrolling 'carousel' where you scroll through until you find the option you want. I found it annoying to find and stop on the mode I wanted. You're going to miss shots trying to find the mode you want. Continuous Shooting: burst mode. Surprisingly fast. Kids Shot: the camera plays one of three sounds to attract a child's attention and then bursts five photos. Macro: The Galaxy NX has a surprisingly short minimum focal distance with the kit lens and the macro photos I took were among the best results I was able to get from the camera. Rich Tone: Samsung's HDR mode. Processing time was excessive. Panorama: This is a sweep mode, smoothly move the camera (a tripod helps) to capture up to 180°'s of view. Disappointingly the camera reduces the image size significantly in Panorama mode. Multi Exposure: combines two or more images into one. Drama: combines several images of a moving subject into a single image. The camera was very picky about detecting moving objects. I encountered at least a 50% fail rate trying this mode. Additionally, as with the Panorama mode the image size is greatly reduced. The camera can also be used in manual mode. Samsung calls it 'Expert Mode'. This gives you access to the standard PASM controls. The settings are controlled by three half-circle on screen dials that I found frustratingly hard to use. Try to change one and my thick fingers would spin the wrong dial. Using Shutter Priority mode I found the processing time of 30 second exposures was a disappointing additional 30 seconds. There are some things I did like about this camera. It's not all bad. It can produce decent images and I honestly think the majority of the limitations I experienced were due to the cheap kit lens. The 4.8" LCD is gorgeous, in the right light, I recently went back to a camera with a beautiful 3" screen and it felt small. Some of the included shooting modes are fun to play with. Connectivity via WiFi was rock solid (I wasn't able to test the 3G/4G connectivity) even in parking lots of places that offered free WiFi. There were eleven gigs of free space in internal memory. That was plenty of room for a day's shooting and testing. I never did get around to installing an SD card. In conclusion... I'm not really sure who this camera is aimed at. They seem to be trying to attract smart phone users with the ability to access the internet almost anywhere and instantly share you photos. But do you really need an expensive, heavy and complex large-sensor camera to post photos to Facebook and Twitter? On the flip side I just can't see this camera being attractive to professional photographers or high end photography enthusiasts. While the inclusion of the electronic viewfinder is nice I found the all on-screen controls to be distracting and bothersome and the image quality was for the most part lackluster. A note about durability. As I was finishing up the testing of this camera I bobbled the camera due to nerve damage and it took a spill. The height was not great, less than three feet, and the initial impact was on soil and grass. The lens came apart into numerous pieces. I was able to put the lens back together but it appears to have suffered internal damage and will not focus either automatically or manually. I accept that I caused this damage but I am very unimpressed with the durability of such an expensive camera. I really can't recommend this camera. Three stars but barely. A side note about Samsung's technical support that isn't reflected in my rating of this camera. Calling Samsung's support line was a complete nightmare. Audio quality was atrocious. At the end I was practically screaming to be heard. I spent close to an hour and a half on the phone speaking with seven different people. Each person I spoke to had to be told all my information, the camera's information and the reason for my call. Four times I was transferred to 'the proper department.' In the end I had a supervisor tell me, first that the camera did not exist and then, that it must be a UK version and I'd have to start all over and call their UK support line. I then contacted Samsung through their Facebook support page. It's been almost a week and they still haven't decided what to do about the camera/lens. {Edit} It took nearly a month of back and forth and arguing to get Samsung to agree my camera was a US version, it was under warranty and they would issue a repair ticket for it. It was shipped off at their expense, repaired surprisingly quickly and shipped back. The camera's now in working order. Only one thing marred the process. When they returned the camera and lens the put a cap on the rear of the lens (I'd shipped it with the lens attached) but only put a piece of what looked like a Post-It across the body opening. I found it odd they wouldn't properly cap the body to protect the sensor though on the whole the packing job, bubble wrapped and foam peanuts was well done. Kudos to their repair facility but I'm still very put off by the whole experience with their support people.

title: A decent USB 3.0 Cable
text: I do frequent, manual, backups of my important personal files to a pair of Seagate portable hard drives. This six foot cable gives me a bit more freedom on where I can put my portables, lets me use a rear USB port and keeps my drives away from the edge of the desk where I had to put them when I used the short cables that came with the drives. I was surprised at how heavy duty this cable actually was. It's almost too heavy. I've found it hard to flex and keep in place and while my portable hard drives are weighty enough to stay in place I could see this cable dragging a lighter phone or other device off a desk. I had no problems with fit or connections and while it may be my imagination (I've run my backups hundreds of times over the last couple years so I know how long it normally takes) it seems like data transfer might be just a bit faster with this cable than with the ones Seagate sent out with their drives. This is a well made, possibly too heavy for light devices, cable from AmazonBasics. I have used AmazonBasics cables for quite a while now and never had a problem with any of them.

title: A Rather Decent Monopod
text: The Amazon Basics 67-Inch Monopod is basically (pardon the pun) everything you need in a monopod. It extends to a nice height and even at full extension it feels reasonably sturdy. Collapsing the thinnest section and using just the two thicker sections increases the stability greatly and still gives you a little over 51 inches to work with. Build quality is decent. The locking cams are hard plastic but don't feel cheap and give a positive, tight lock when engaged. The foam grip isn't glued into place. It is just held in place by friction and the three screw heads that hold the camera mount to the monopod. The monopod also includes a wrist strap held in place on the head of the mount by a split ring. A carry bag is supplied. It's enough to protect the monopod though it's not padded and the shoulder strap is short enough to be more of a carry strap. The rubber foot of this monopod can be retracted on its threaded mount to expose a metal spike foot for use in outdoor. The only negatives I've found with this monopod are: The wrist strap is rather small and I cannot fit it over my hand. For reference I wear a size large glove. For me this is more of a palm strap. The soft foot has very little rubber extending past the end of the metal spike. I measured this at just slightly over 1mm. Moderate wear will surely leave the metal foot expose and potentially damage flooring. All in all though this is an affordable and well built monopod and I wouldn't hesitate to recommend it.

title: One Heck of a Camera (Updated}
text: I've only had the Fujifilm X-E2 camera and 18-55mm lens for a short while and I've barely scratched the surface of it's capabilities. This is a camera anyone can use right out of the box but also one that you can spend years learning to master. The retro look and styling are very attractive but they made it, for me at least who was used to an extended grip on the camera body, a little hard to handle. I found myself hitting the AE-L and AF-L buttons often and frequently by accident spun the exposure compensation dial without even realizing I had. I resolved this with the LensMate Thumb Grip designed for the X-E1/E2. It made a good camera great. I also added LensMate's brass soft release button to the shutter release. It does aid in smoother pressing of the shutter button but it also looks great on the camera. The 18-55mm lens that comes with the X-E2 is a real pleasure to use. The zoom is stiff enough to let you feel in control but easy enough that you don't need brute force to use it. Image quality, even at 100%, is outstanding. I've been getting so many 'keepers' that I've had to reevaluate my shooting style. I feel like I'm overshooting. In the past I was shooting three or four hundred images in an outing and getting maybe four or six shots I really want to keep and share. Now, with the X-E2 I'm finding two, three even four times that many shots that are worth keeping. I'm going to need a bigger hard drive! Battery life has been pretty good for me. Even shooting in temperatures down in the 30's and 40's I had no problem taking well over three hundred images and still having battery bars left. In the times I've gone out all day wandering around the county I've yet to have to swap out the battery though I did purchase an extra just to have around. Functionality, configurability and controls are extensive and a bit quirky but easy enough to get used to. As an example the Q button gives you 'Q'uick access to many of the more necessary and often used controls. You navigate around the Q menu with the 5-way controller but you make setting changes with the command dial. One of the features I found most interesting was the ability to constrain the ISO in Auto mode and set a minimum shutter speed. I also liked the ability to configure the four letter prefix for file names. All the 'extra' settings like special effects, double exposure, movie mode and panorama are accessed through the Drive button. I did find a couple small negatives. Nothing to cause me not to want to use it but made me wonder. The odd menu systems. The pop-up flash is a bit anemic and is somewhat blocked by the 18-55mm lens. It's even worse when the hood is attached. The shoulder strap that comes with the camera... I know they're usually bad but this is cheap camera bad not quality camera bad. I put it around my neck, gave a tug, and then threw it away without putting it on the camera. I expected a little more quality there. The tulip lens hood that comes with the 18-55mm feels hard and brittle. It too could have been a bit better quality. I already mentioned the LensMate thumb grip that I think is an absolute must add item (it's really worth the cost). My big clumsy hands desperately needed it to aid in stability and control. Where to start with a conclusion? This is an interesting mix of old school retro styling and modern camera technology. I think Fuji have really blended them together well. I can see myself enjoying this camera for years to come. Very highly recommended. {Update} Not wanting to pile on the negatives but I had intended to and completely forgot to mention the battery door. It's really kind of flimsy and feels like it could easily break. Also, with the way it's hinged I find it rather hard to get the memory card out of the camera because it's so close and parallel to the battery door's hinge.

title: Love It
text: The added height and domed shape of this brass tri-tadpole soft release button adds just enough feel to make shooting with the X-E2 that much better. The brass and black button looks awesome on my all black X-E2 body and the tri-tadpole design is very distinctive. The rubber gasket under the button keeps it from loosening and getting lost. Price wise this is seriously expensive but it's very well made so I guess you get what you pay for.

title: Not as Pictured, Not as Expected
text: Not at all happy with this Kindle cover. All the images on the product information page show the custom image covering the entire cover area. The case I received has a gap more than half an inch wide at both the top and bottom of the cover. It looks terrible. The preview images provided also do not show how clearly the leather cover's texture will show through the image. This just adds to how bad it looks. You can barely make out the image I used. I'm terribly disappointed in this product and am returning it immediately.

title: A Solid Four Star Item
text: This is a review of both the black and blue MarBlue Atlas Kindle Cases. These are decent cases and have some good things going for them. I wouldn't say they're great cases but they do the job with, what I consider, only a few flaws. The system for attaching your Kindle to the cover are four very strong and quite tight rubber reinforced elastic cords. I've had several Kindles and numerous cases over the years and as far as four corner case mounts this is the most secure of that style I've ever seen. I had my PaperWhite mounted in this case and shook it violently, over a pillow and ready to catch it should anything happen, and not only did it stay in place it didn't move a fraction of an inch. I was very impressed with that function of the case. The case exterior is a synthetic leather that truly looks and feels like leather. It is well made, and fairly handsome. Unlike many synthetic products this had no harsh chemical smell. The blue cover looks a little less like leather than the black but it is a very nice shade of blue. The interior is an attractive, and soft, dark grey microfiber that's quite pleasing to the touch. The case is held closed or open with a half inch wide cloth elastic that is well attached to the case. This holds the case closed quite well. The hinge area of the case is a bit too large/tall/wide making the case when folded back a little ungainly and if not strapped down it wanted to flop closed. Inside the case is a nearly three inch wide strap made of the same soft, grey microfiber attached with elastics at both the top and bottom. This comes into use when the case is open you can put your hand or fingers under this strap to read one handed. With my PaperWhite I found this to be slightly uncomfortable making me arch my hand in an odd manner to get my thumb onto the screen. I'm not a fan of the strap, the sections at the top and bottom where it's stitched to the elastic create two lumps that sit directly on the Kindle's screen. They're soft but it's two unnecessary pressure points. This case does not have the magnet that the Amazon brand case does that turns the kindle on and off when you open it. The power button on my PaperWhite was a little hard to reach with the shape of the case and the location of the mounting strap. It wasn't too difficult to use but it's nowhere near as easy as opening the case and having your Kindle come on. In conclusion... The case is decent. It's a little... gappy, the front cover bends when you have your hand in the strap and this creates a gap that will let debris into the case and onto your Kindle. I'm not crazy about the strap but that's more personal preference than anything else. This is a well made decently protective Kindle case.

title: Adequate Cover
text: This is just an adequate cover for the Kindle PaperWhite. I'm not really fond of the pebbled leather texture and would much have preferred a smooth leather cover. Though the pebbling does give a bit of texture to aid in holding onto the thing. The magnetic clasp does an okay job of turning the Kindle on and off with only occasional flubs which require you to open and close it again or push the power button. I've painted the clasp on mine black to match the case as I really didn't care for the silver color that it comes as. The case holds the Kindle INCREDIBLY tight. I've taken my PaperWhite out of the case twice since I received it and both times I was scared to death I was going to damage the Kindle getting it out of the case. So, yeah, it securely holds onto your Kindle... with a death grip. The rubber edges provide adequate protection against bumps and bangs and the back of the case is rock hard. The cover itself is where this fails to be a four or five star item. It's flimsy. You can easily press on the cover and make it tap on the screen. It should have been made as stiff as the material on the back of the case. With the way the hinge is made and the case is put together a very stiff cover would have had little impact on holding and reading your Kindle but would have offered much better protection to the most easily damaged part of any Kindle, the screen. The opening at the bottom provides easy access to the power button and micro-USB connector. I'm going to keep mine, I'm very careful with my devices so I'm not too worried about damaging the screen but if you toss your Kindle in your purse or backpack you might want to think twice about which cover to get to protect your Kindle.

title: Good Sound, Good Fit.
text: ** Note: I received this item free of charge from MEElectronics in exchange for a fair and honest review. ** These in-ear headphones have some really good sound. Decent bass, sharp treble and the mid-range is clean and not muddled. They appear to be well made with soft, supple wires that feel comfortable even when you're sweating like mad. The MEElectronics Sport-Fi M6P Noise Isolating In-Ear Headphones come with several different tips to fit just about anyone's ears. I ended up using the smaller of the two triple-flange tips. Those gave me the best fit and even when sweating profusely the ear buds stayed in place nicely. The memory wire is a nice addition and adds quite a bit to the secureness of the fit. I tested the MEElectronics Sport-Fi M6P Noise Isolating In-Ear Headphone with my home PC, my Samsung Galaxy Tab2 10.1 tablet and a no-name brand portable MP3/video player. The sound was exceptional with all three devices. The control button on the volume tab worked okay with my Samsung tablet. A single click to pause or restart playback and a quick double click to go on to the next track. Noise isolation (not noise canceling) works fairly well. With the ear buds in place but no audio being played back I couldn't hear myself typing on a fairly noisy keyboard and I even missed a phone call when testing at moderate volume on the PC. The only negative things I encountered with these ear buds were... 1) The remote control is a bit small to be using when you're physically active especially the button you need to click, it's somewhat hard to find and press accurately when you're on the go. I also found adjusting the volume in small increments to be a bit hard when moving about. 2) The memory wire is great but I needed to re-bend it to fit my ears each time I used the headphones. These are both minor annoyances and don't really detract from the product in a significant way. I wouldn't hesitate to recommend this product.

title: Good Memory Card
text: I was happy with the Eighteen dollars I spent on this 16 GIG card. Worked fine with both a Panasonic Lumix FZ70 and Kodak Z990. Write speeds were noticeably faster than an older Class 10 Transcend card I had in the Kodak. SanDisk registration took the serial number from the card without a hiccup so it's a genuine SanDisk product. Quite pleased with the card. Recommended.

title: Not Impressed
text: No noticeable difference to photographs with or without the filter on. The claims that "pictures gain brilliance" and "elimination of the unwanted blue cast" didn't happen. As a something to protect your expensive camera lens, fine. Also found it extremely hard to clean. Slight scratches or flubs in the coating could be seen around the edge. Could feel the glass moving about in the frame when cleaning. Returned.

title: Works Very Well
text: Battery life in my Panasonic Lumix FZ70 was astounding. Over 450 pictures and still two out of three battery bars lit (oh, yeah, it does register with the FZ70). Charger worked well. Charge time was similar to that of the Panasonic charger that came with the camera. Build quality was good. All in all this is a top notch product.

title: Mediocre Image Quality
text: I was impressed with the functionality of the camera. Focus was fast, shot to shot recycle time was impressive, battery life was astounding (well over 400 pictures and the battery just dropped by one indicator on the 3-light battery bar). The two speed zoom was nice, easy to control and fairly quiet. I liked that the mode dial appeared on the LCD when you changed settings. Heft and feel were rather nice. And that there's where the plus side ends... I shot over 850 images meticulously testing settings and options in numerous situations and ended up with three pictures I thought were really good. The low light capability even at 20mm wide angle was sub-par. One of my favorite activities is to sit at the beaches here in Florida and watch the sunrise. I've always got a camera with me. Images pre-dawn and at sunrise were... grainy, cluttered, blurry. Post dawn, full light shots of surfers looked like Pointilization art. Even when only zooming out 20x - 30x, far from the extreme limit of the camera, I didn't get one picture I bothered to keep out of well over 150 tries. I also went to a horse show. Full daylight, light fluffy clouds and again shooting well below the full 60x (1,200mm) zoom of the camera and the results were horrid, grainy, full of noise. Many shots looked like badly done art filters in Photoshop rather than photographs from a moderately expensive bridge camera. I also shot a few images at the horse show under the shade of trees and even in iA mode letting the camera pick all the settings and not zooming in at all, images were dark, mottled and grainy. In conclusion... I have an older 30x camera that's getting on in age. I had hoped to retire it and replace it with a new more modern camera. I just wasn't impressed enough with the Panasonic Lumix FZ70. The functionality was great but that's not the most important aspect of a camera, photo quality is and I just wasn't happy enough with the results and returned the camera. For a new $350 camera I expected better. I believe mine may have been one of the rare defective items that occasionally escape quality control.

title: You Get What You Pay For...
text: ...and I paid .04 for this lens cap (+ $2.98 shipping!) I guess if your lens or camera didn't come with a cap or you lost yours this wouldn't be horrible. The lanyard is NOT attached as the photos imply it's just a 21" long piece of cheap nylon string. The cap has a single (why?!) hole to thread the line through to attach the lanyard line. The distance between the back of the hole and the inner wall of the cap is literally 2mm. I tried for over half an hour and could not for the life of me thread the lanyard onto the cap. If I safety line the cap to the camera I really have no use for the product. I had been told this held a little better than the stock lens cap that came with the Panasonic Lumix FZ70 that I just purchased but I didn't see that it had any more holding power on the 55mm Sigma UV filter I have mounted on my camera than the factory lens (which came with an easily attached lanyard). The stock cap is somewhat lower in profile than this. Since the shipping was a several hundred times the cost of the item there's no sense or reason to return this. I guess I'll throw it in my 'spare and old gear' bag and if I somehow lose the Lumix cap that came with and is safely attached by a lanyard to my camera I'll have a spare. Color me completely unimpressed.

title: Not a Great Tripod Head, Not a Horrible Tripod Head
text: This is my 2nd GH-200 tripod head. The first one I received through the Vine program was defective and was returned to Vanguard and exchanged. The replacement I received operates much better than the first. I tested this tripod head with my [[ASIN:B001D60LG8 Dolica AX620B100 62-Inch Proline Tripod]] and my Kodak Z990 camera. At full tension release there is just enough friction to give some confident feedback of movement. It allows responsive and fairly easy tracking of moving objects. The tension knob has approximately ¼ turn of adjustment giving some range of friction preferences. At full lock I found the head to be rock solid with no play or give. The pistol grip has a release handle that allows you to set the tension knob to full lock but have the ability to squeeze the grip and quickly reposition the camera. The spring in the grip is not adjustable and is insanely stiff. After a half hour of testing out this tripod head my hand was aching from the force necessary to squeeze the grip release. In their product description they claim you can track an object "ultra smoothly by pressing the trigger" I did not find this to be the case. You can reposition the camera by squeezing the trigger but at full lock the grip release did not give smooth movement or ease of tracking. The pistol grip has a quick, one hand operation, release collar that allows the grip to be rotated 360 degrees with eight locking points. This collar and release are affected by the friction setting for the ball head. I'm not a fan of their mounting system. First because the screw to attach the plate to the camera does not have a butterfly handle. A coin or screwdriver is required to mount or dismount the plate from or to the camera. Second, while partially released the plate can be adjusted forward or back to get better balance of your rig. There is a pin on the head keeping the plate and camera from falling forward or backward off the mount. Unfortunately there is no positive safety lock. Just a few turns on the tension knob for the camera plate and your camera is completely free of the head. The mounting plate itself can be unlocked to turn 360 degree panoramic shots. There are 72 click points that are 5 degrees of rotation apart. Even with my relatively light Kodak Z990 on this head the clicks became indistinct and hard to notice. Still, it's a nice feature to capture smooth panoramic shots. The tripod mount is threaded for 1/4" or, with an easily removed adapter sleeve, 3/8" screw. This tripod head did not come with the small tool to remove the adapter sleeve that other Vanguard products do but as with the camera plate a screwdriver or coin will do the job. In the end I can't say I'm a complete fan of this tripod head. Itappears to be quite sturdy and should give years of service. Unfortunately, for me, the lack of secure locking of the camera plate and the extreme pressure needed to squeeze the trigger release we enough negatives to make this less than stellar. I can't say that I was wow'd by it.

title: A Well Made Product With Minor Flaws
text: This is my new favorite tripod head. With two controls for setting friction and locking the head in place it's amazingly versatile. The previous ball-head mount I had was either locked or fully loose which made camera control a little scary. With the Vanguard TBH-250 you can have free movement and maintain enough friction to keep your camera from flopping wildly about. You can also lock and unlock the horizontal movement of the head so you can take panoramic shots with ease. The mount is threaded for 1/4" which is a sleeve that fits inside a 3/8" threaded fitting so the TBH-250 will fit on the majority of tripods on the market. The 3/8" thread fit my Dolica AX620B100 tripod perfectly and even fit, separate from the tripod and with a lot of finagling, in the bag that came with my Dolica tripod. A small tool was included to remove the 1/4" sleeve but a flat head screwdriver would also do the job. The only thing I'm not crazy about is the camera mount. It's advertized as a 'quick shoe' mount but it's not that quick and if you're not careful it's not that secure. Slightly loosened you can reposition the mount forward and backward about an inch or thereabouts to get better balance. But loosen the camera mount just a slight bit more and the camera will easily pull free of the tripod head. There is a brass pin which keeps the mount from sliding out front to back and that's great but there's no locking or safety latch keeping your camera attached to the tripod. While we're on the subject of the camera mount the screw holding the mounting plate to the camera requires a screwdriver, coin or in a pinch you can flip the tool for removing the 1/4" thread adapter and tighten the plate to the camera with that. I'm surprised that a tripod head of this quality doesn't include a butterfly nut to hand tighten the plate to the camera. While I do wish it had a more secure mount and an easier way to attach the shoe to the camera I would still recommend this tripod head. It's very smooth, solidly built and feels like it will last for years.

title: Really Somewhere Around 3.5 Stars
text: I've been testing this speaker system with my 10" Samsung Galaxy Tab2 tablet which had no problems connecting to the speakers with and without the app from the Android store. Appearance: Their product description calls this 'fun, trendy and modern'. But to be honest this looks, to me, like an appliance that fell out of my grandmother's 1950's black, white and chrome art-deco kitchen. It's not unpleasant looking but I wouldn't call it modern. When I saw images of the system online I had hopes that the neon green ring around the face would light up. Sadly it doesn't. The handle is also fixed in place and doesn't retract or collapse into the body. It would have been a nice idea so you could stack or store this more easily. Sound: It doesn't sound bad. Especially for being just two 15 watt wide range speakers in a ported (holes to help the bass sound better) enclosure. The bass is a little flat and the high end sounds a little... hollow but it is a lot better than the speakers built into my tablet. I've tried a variety of music; jazz, pop, classical, rock, punk and everything sounded quite good. I found I had to use both the tablet's volume control as well as the speaker systems volume controls to get real volume out of the system. They operate independently of each other. Drawbacks: I don't normally comment on price with items received from the Vine program but at the time I'm writing this review Amazon is currently selling this item for over two hundred dollars. Maybe the Bluetooth equipment is expensive but to me that's a LOT for just two speakers in a box. I didn't pay that much for my four speaker bookshelf system or the subwoofer equipped speaker system connected to my desktop PC. Both of which have far superior sound quality. The battery indicator light only seems to light up when the system is charging. I charged this a week ago and used it for several hours at a time but I have no idea how much charge is left in the battery. The biggest problem I had with this speaker system was when doing anything other than playing music. I thought it would be fun to add big sound to the games I enjoy on my tablet but there's a distinct lag between doing anything and when the speaker plays the sound. I noticed it most of all in my favorite billiards simulator. You would strike a ball...and then hear it happen, even system sounds such as keyboard typing noises, a 'blip' when selecting things played a noticeable time after they happened. The App: I won't say much about the app here. It's completely unnecessary to operate this system with your Android device. It's just poor quality programming that appears to have been slapped together at the last minute. It also doesn't match the documentation and features such as Bass Boost which are in the instructions but don't exist in the app. Speaking of the documentation. I opened the box and found a large booklet and for one, brief, moment I thought this item was fully documented in depth and detail... then I opened the instructions and found there's twelve pages of English instructions which are poorly written and lacking in detail. The rest of the book is comprised of numerous other languages each getting their own few pages. Ah well. Turn it on, turn it up. Enjoy the music.

title: Thin but usable.
text: I wanted an extra cable for my Samsung Galaxy Tab 2 tablet. The original is too short and because it's proprietary I wanted to be sure I could always charge my power hungry tablet. This cable is of somewhat better quality than the one that came with the tablet. Both the connectors fit snug and stay plugged in. For the price you can't go wrong.

title: Belkin Cinema Leather Folio Case
text: This is a reasonably attractive leather case. About a third of the cover on the spine side has a pebbled texture while the rest of the cover is smooth. The Good: I really like Belkin's four corner mounting system. It's very secure and doesn't interfere at all with using the tablet. The inner material is a soft micro-fiber that's gentle on your screen. It doesn't add a lot of weight to an already heavy tablet. There are a plethora of positions the tablet can be stood in. But...(see below) A stylus loop is included. The Not-So Good: If mounted in the case so you can use the rear camera through the camera cut-out all the controls as well as the 3.5mm headphone jack are exposed. This also means that to charge your tablet you have to leave the cover open or pull your tablet out and mount it backwards to access the charging port and protect the screen at the same time. The front cover has 20 very shallow grooves pressed into the micro-fiber material of the lining. These catch the bottom edge of the back cover and hold it in place for viewing. These actually hold the tablet in place reasonably well but because of the soft folding 'hinge' design the table is very bouncy at any angle. Good for viewing not so good for typing or playing games. The case material is thin, 4mm on the front cover and thicker on the back because the stand system. There's also a grooved 'hinge' as part of the front cover which lets the cover flex. This reduces the protection already marginal case material can provide for the screen. Because of the Cinema design the front cover can't be folded over flat against the back for comfortable use while off a table. The elasticized strap that holds the cover closed is flimsy and will certainly stretch out over time. Cover 'creep' happens very easily on this model. When strapped closed the cover can, because it's 'hinged', slide up exposing the screen. There's a notch cut into the back cover that allows you to flip the cover around and stand the tablet up at a high angle. This position is very unstable and I would never use it. I wouldn't recommend this cover. It just doesn't offer enough protection for an expensive tablet.

title: Horribly Uncomfortable & Poorly Designed
text: Horribly Uncomfortable. What's the one thing that makes a good neck strap comfortable for long term wearing? Padding. What's the one thing this strap is completely lacking? Padding! The part of the strap that's supposed to go around your neck is a two inch wide very rough textured bit of nylon webbing. Seat belts are softer than this material. The first time I tried the Joby UltraFit Sling Strap I carried my Kodak Z990 around for about an hour and it was so uncomfortable. Who designs a neck strap with NO padding? This strap attaches to your camera via the ¼" tripod screw mount on the bottom of the camera. It's odd that your camera hangs upside down and I don't like the single point of failure mounting. Also, because of the way it's designed it puts angular force on the mounting threads when hanging and even more when releasing or engaging the quick release latch. Since the threads in my Kodak are plastic I have even more dislike for this mounting system. Additionally, you have to dismount your strap any time you want to use a tripod or monopod. I found in the time I used this that the only time the (non) padded portion of the strap is on your neck is when the rig is retracted when you use the 'Speed Cinch' to bring the camera up for shooting, at least on my extra large frame, the whole strap rotates forward and puts the even more uncomfortable thinner strap around your neck and the 'padded' section down on your chest. To sum it up... it's uncomfortable. It completely lacks any padding. It has an odd mounting system that puts lever like force on your tripod socket and you have to take the strap off to use a tripod or monopod. The only good point to this system is that it is rather well made. Unfortunately it's just well made junk. I wouldn't recommend this to anyone for any application.

title: So Far, So Good!
text: I've had this for a few weeks and have used it numerous times to navigate around Brevard County Florida. So far the maps (which I updated right after getting the GPS) have been spot on except for one time when I was in a wildlife conservation area (that neither Google or Bing maps has either) which wasn't mapped but it's dirt dikes in a swamp and not part of city, county or state roads. Amusingly the Garmin map did show the lakes I was driving around just not the dirt roads. I've downloaded and tried several of the voices offered for the Garmin nüvi 50LM though the only ones I've used have been the TTS voices (those that actually speak the street names). After several trials I've found, oddly enough, that the voice 'British English - Serena' is the clearest and easiest to understand. The 5" screen is great. The display is crisp and clear and can easily be read from a distance. The touch screen is quite responsive. I don't feel like I have to pound on the screen to make selections. I have mine mounted in an [[ASIN:B0015A6YN6 Arkon GN047 Removable Air Vent Mount]] in the passenger side center console air vent to keep it off the windshield and out of the Florida sun. {See uploaded photo.} While this is a basic GPS unit the nüvi 50LM does what a GPS unit is designed to, get you from Point-A to Point-B (options for this are Faster Time, Shorter Distance or Off Road (straight line navigation)) without any extra, distracting, bells and whistles it still has some nice options: * Lifetime free map updates. * Maps can be displayed in 2D or 3D. * You can change the level of map display information shown. * You can turn on or off Map Data Layout information which adds driving direction, time of day, elevation and speed to the main map display. * The icon for your vehicle can be changed. Garmin themselves offer numerous icons to download and there are also places on the internet to download custom vehicle icons. * Automatic switching between day and night display settings. * Lane Assist & Junction View helps you (in some areas) get in the correct lane ahead of time. * Millions of Points of Interest plus the ability to add your own favorite destinations. So far I really like my Garmin nüvi 50LM and enjoy using it. It's made getting out and about a lot easier than paper maps ever did. I'll update this review, if necessary, if any durability issues arise over time. For now, this is one of my favorite pieces of technology.

title: Huge But Flawed
text: What I Like: * It's HUGE! You can fit so much gear in this thing it's crazy. I've got my AE-1 with a 300mm tele/zoom mounted on it and there's more than enough width for it. I have an extra AE-1 body a 55mm lens, two point and shoot digital cameras, a flash for the AE-1 bodies, assorted cables and the kitchen sink in this pack and I think there's still some room left over. * The interior is orange which makes finding things in low light situations much easier than in a dark colored bag. * It comes with a rain cover. * The shoulder straps and backpack are seriously padded. Even fully loaded this thing is comfortable to carry. * It has a chest strap and a waist belt. * Did I mention it's huge? What I Don't Like: *The camera quick-access patch. While it almost certainly won't dump your camera out (it secures at the top with a plastic latch & velcro) the zippers 1) don't completely close off the opening. Dirt, bugs, moisture can easily get inside your backpack. 2) the zippers are attached to each other with a loop of nylon. This is going to catch on things (branches, chairs, doors, etc.) and open. Again, you probably won't lose your camera but if you don't notice the zippers opening and they open VERY easily, you're going to have even bigger openings for problems to get in. You can remedy this somewhat by putting the loop under the latch it still allows the zippers to slide down several inches. * The rain cover comes in a small pouch kept in one of the back pockets. It could easily be lost. * There are only two compression straps on the top 1/3'rd of the backpack. None lower 2/3'rds. * The waist belt has no padding. * There is a pocket for up to a 14" laptop but it's right up against the wearer's back. * The bottom is heavy duty but it should have had feet/rubber runners so it doesn't sit flat on the floor, dirt, puddle, etc. All in all it's an okay backpack but not a great one. There's room for everything you could want to carry but the quick-access patch... that just ruins the backpack for me. My camera gear is expensive and dear to me, I want to protect it the best I can. Having an opening that doesn't seal completely and can easily be opened wider by accident is a poor design. This might work as carry on luggage or getting to and from the car or hotel but I would not recommend using this in the field. I can honestly only give this three stars. I'd love to see them redesign the quick-access patch. That would greatly improve this backpack.

title: Not Ideal for 5" GPS Units
text: My [[ASIN:B005HSDL8S Garmin nüvi 50LM 5-inch GPS]] adhered well to this mount and stayed in place all day even on rough unpaved roads. The Zeikos IR-MAT36 also stayed in place quite well on the dashboard of my 2007 Hyundai Accent. The notch in the ring was a nice feature allowing easy attachment, adjustment and positioning of my GPS. My only problem was that with the larger GPS it sat high on the dashboard and became something of a distraction. I think this would be better suited for use with GPS units smaller than 5". But it does perform as advertized and does it quite well. I'll keep it around in case the vent mount I'm currently using breaks. Recommended.

title: Just About Perfect
text: I bought this as an afterthought when I ordered my [[ASIN:B005HSDL8S Garmin nüvi 50LM 5-inch Portable GPS]]. At that time it was less than $5 so I figured I had little to lose if it didn't work. Then I tried this in my 2007 Hyundai Accent, using the right-hand of the two center console vents, and it worked great! It's better than the stock windshield mount or the beanbag mount I also purchased. I can still easily see and easily read my GPS (the 5" screen really helps) but it's not right out in front of me distracting me. It also doesn't put the GPS in the way of any of the dashboard controls though it's a little close to the radio tuning knob which I never use anyhow. I've driven several hundred miles with my GPS on this mount some of that over unpaved and horribly maintained dirt roads and it just stayed in place without a problem. It's easy to mount. Slightly trickier to remove (requiring two hands). My only worry is it seems a bit fragile but I'm careful with my possessions so I think it'll last. Highly recommended!

title: Not Worth the Cost of Returning
text: This is advertized as a 'hard case.' It is NOT a hard case it is simply formed vinyl with minimal rigidity. You can easily compress the sides with one finger. The description also claims this has a 'padded inner pocket.' The elasticized strip that divides the case in two is no thicker than a heavy-weight T-Shirt. It offers your GPS no real protection at all. The walls, sides, faces of the case have no padding whatsoever. I was forced to improvise padding with a divider taken from one of my camera gear bags. The case does not seal. The zippers come ¾'s of the way up the side and then there's an extra piece of vinyl stitched to both sides of the case. Forming something like a collar. The flap that velcro's over the top does not hold the collar section tightly closed. You can easily slip a finger into the case with it 'closed'. This means dirt and moisture, etc. have an easy path to your GPS. Additionally, I've had this for less than four hours and the velcro patch the flap attaches to is already pulling free of the case! My [[ASIN:B005HSDL8S 5" Garmin nüvi 50LM]] barely fits in the Zeikos IR-CA101 Large Hard Case side to side but there is a lot, too much really, front to back room. Along with the improvised padding I was forced to add to the inner side of the case where to protect my GPS I've also wrapped my 12v car power cable in a piece of towel to keep it from thumping around. I would NOT recommend putting a window or other mounting device in this case with a GPS unit. If it wouldn't cost me half of what I paid for it to ship it back I'd return it in a heartbeat. As far as I'm concerned this product is NOT as described. It's not a hard case. It's not padded. It offers almost no protection AND it's already falling apart just hours after arriving. Do yourself a huge favor and don't buy this, it's overpriced junk.

title: Nice Neck Strap
text: Packaging was a bit mediocre. A cardboard card with the strap through it in a dingy plastic bag. Strap appears to be new/unused and in good condition. This fits my Kodak Z990 digital camera perfectly. A much more comfortable carrying solution than the thin strap Kodak included with the camera. I'm a heavyset guy and with the strap nowhere near as long as it could be adjusted to I have the camera hanging just at arm's length. I can comfortably hold the camera by my side while I walk around. Adjusting the fit isn't easy which is good. This means your strap isn't going to slip (my Kodak loosened up all the time). It make take a little effort and time but it secures the camera well. The padded section of the neck strap could be a little longer. The swivel hinges and spring clips which hold the mounting strap to the padded neck band catch me right in the collarbone. The spring loaded clips feel sturdy and don't seem like they can accidentally be released. The padding itself is very comfortable on my neck. I feel like I could carry my camera for hours without and discomfort. My only complaint, as minor as it may be, is the product labels stitched to the padded section of the strap system. The padding is soft and the labels well stitched in place. They couldn't be ripped out so I had to spend a few minutes carefully trimming them (there are several different tags) away with a pair of scissors. This is a nice update to the basic straps many manufacturers send out with their products. It's comfortable, adjusts to many lengths for whatever carrying style you like and is quite affordable. You can't go wrong with the Kata KT PL-C-STRAP.

title: Four Star Tripod
text: I picked this up in a GoldBox sale from Amazon after I became unhappy with the ultra cheap tripod I had been using. The difference in quality compared to the small difference in price is amazing. The ball head is smooth. The center shaft turns easily for panning when the head is locked. The amazingly adjustable legs are a delight. The lack of a center brace that many tripods have (and which initially worried me) means you can position your camera is SO many ways that a conventional braced tripod would not allow. The camera mount has a safety lock. You cannot accidentally disconnect the camera from the tripod. You need to squeeze the release lever while swinging the mounting arm out of the way. One word of warning. The center shaft can be reversed to place the head closer to the ground for macro photography etc. reversing the shaft is easy, you remove the counter-weight hook and slide the shaft out. Reversing this operation however can be time consuming. There are plastic tabs that ring the opening that go one way they're a bit hard to push out of the way to return the shaft to normal operating position. The ball head is also removable. With the correct adapter you can fit most other tripod heads to this base. In conclusion: You just cannot go wrong with this tripod. From entry level photographers to serious hobbyists this will suit your needs for many years.

title: Kodak's Last Hurrah...
text: Years ago I bought a little 2MP 3X Zoom digital camera. It was a Kodak and it took great pictures. Several years after that I won a Kodak Z650 in an online contest and flat out loved the pictures it took. So when the stars aligned and Amazon had the Kodak Z990 on sale and my gift card balance was enough to afford it I jumped at the opportunity. I really LIKE the Kodak Z990 and I'm sad that it will probably be the last Kodak camera I ever buy... I LIKE this camera... I almost love this camera. While my Z650 almost never came out of Auto mode I find myself accessing the PASM controls and bracketing the exposure compensation when I use this camera. It isn't that the Z990 doesn't take great pictures. It does. It just takes a little work to get them. The camera is hefty, weighing in at 1 LB. 5 OZ. (593g) and feels substantial. To me it feels like what a camera should. The gripping areas on the front handgrip and rear thumb rest are lightly rubberized and the non-movable ring on the lens has a sturdy ribbed rubber covering. The controls are reasonably easy to access and use. I like that you can use either the 5-way controller (similar to a Kindle's) or the clickable toggle wheel next to the thumb rest to access and control many of the camera settings. I like having the zoom controls on a ring around the shutter button. It feels easier to use than those cameras that have this control on the back. It also requires a very light touch as with 30x total optical zoom the lens and controls are very sensitive. At first you will find yourself zooming or going wide-angle past the point you wanted but with a little practice it becomes much easier to control. The Z990 uses AA batteries (4) which, personally, I think is great. You can, in a pinch, get replacements at any convenience store, gas station or mega-mart in the US. It also comes with a serviceable if feature free slow battery charger and four Kodak brand rechargeable NiMH batteries. I've since replaced these with a smart charger and better batteries but out of the box they're enough to get you started. Another great addition is the Optical View Finder. This is incredibly handy when shooting outdoors in bright sunlight. The 3" LCD screen is great but in direct sun it, like all LCD screens, becomes almost impossible to see. I've, as of the time of this review, taken a bit over a thousand images and a handful of videos with my Z990 and I've barely scratched the surface of experiencing all the features and functions it has to offer. Some notable features are: Two panoramic image modes. One has the camera stitching two or three images together to produce the image and the other allows you to hold the shutter button and 'sweep' the camera to produce the panoramic image. Multiple Kodak film time emulations - Kodacolor, Kodachrome, Ektachrome, T-MAX, TRI-X as well as standard B&W and Sepia modes. In camera HDR mode. Multiple burst modes. Full 1080p video in stereo. The camera can even emulates a Photo Booth taking four images in quick succession and stitching them together. Nothing being perfect the Z990 has a few cons I feel need to be mentioned: The memory card is stored in the battery compartment and the battery door is one of the few things I worry about breaking on this camera. It is light plastic and not easy to close with batteries installed. To use a USB cable to transfer images from the camera to a computer the camera needs to be powered up requiring removal of the lens cap (because the cap mounts on the body not the lens). I don't like that it needs to sit with the lens exposed for no reason. The lens isn't threaded so you cannot use any filters with this camera. Preview mode, where the camera shows you the last image taken, cannot be disabled on this model, you can bypass it somewhat by 1/2 pressing the shutter once the preview displays but it would have been nice to be able to turn off this feature. In conclusion: While the Kodak Z990 Max isn't perfect it is an affordable bridge camera that takes excellent pictures day or night with an extremely powerful zoom lens, a host of useful features and controls that can only be topped by DSLR cameras. As Kodak's last hurrah, it's a pretty good note to go out on.

title: Cheap Not Inexpensive
text: I've had several Amazon Basics' items since the line was introduced. Most have been quite good. Unfortunately this tripod wasn't one of them. The feel is cheap and plastic-y. I wasn't expecting bearings in the pan-head but the plastic on plastic mechanisms are terrible. I tested this item with my Kodak Z990 digital camera. It weighs approx. 21 oz. with batteries. The camera mount has a good rubber pad for your camera to sit on and the tightening screw has a butterfly head so no screwdriver or coins are needed to attach/detach the mount from the camera. The mount attaches to the tripod with a spring-loaded release arm. There is actually very little contact area on the tripod itself (only two corners) holding the mount in place, also the release arm does NOT have a safety catch. Pan Functionality - Fully tightened down I can still, with not much effort, swing the head from left to right. Fully loosened the motion is heavy and awkward easily upsetting the tripod's position. Tightening this knob fully actually interferes with the... Tilt Functionality - The action is not much better here. You can lock the tilt angle into place and it does stay there. There's just as much plastic on plastic drag when in motion. The arm is generously long and comfortable to grip. The side-tilt mechanism goes reasonably easily from flat to 90°. It does not lock in place well. Leg Functionality - The legs extend and retract with mild effort. They lock into place firmly. With just the larger leg section extended the tripod is fairly sturdy. Extending the smaller leg sections dramatically increases wobble. There is a weight/gear hook for added stabilization but it is plastic and feels easily broken. The swiveling rubber feet are innovative but only held on by friction and can easily become detached. The center stabilizer locks and unlocks easily with only a quarter turn and holds in place well. There is a serviceable carry handle attached to the leg mount section. The tripod has two bubble levels. The first, a small button level is at the top of one of the leg mounts. The second, a tube level, is just under and inch long and is under and partially obscured by the camera mount. With a camera attached it becomes useless. The center section extends and lowers via a crank mechanisms and locks in place with a plastic collar. There is no positive safety lock. Loosen the collar and your camera comes down rapidly on its own. Extending your camera this way will only increase the instability of this tripod. The included carry bag reflects the quality of it's tripod. Its material is unpadded and thin. It has no extra pockets and the half-inch nylon shoulder strap is also unpadded making it rather uncomfortable to carry. In conclusion... I wouldn't recommend this tripod even as a starter for someone just getting into photography it will only add frustration to the experience. Spend a little more and get a far better tripod or spend a little less and get something of equal quality.

title: Horrible Quality Sound
text: Thankfully I 'won' these in a contest from Marlboro, I would regret having spent ANY money on these earbuds. The fit is acceptable but nothing special. The sound quality is deplorable. title: Somewhat useful...
text: The Gorillapod Video Tripod (Black/Blue) is a good idea on paper but in real life it just doesn't quite measure up. The pan & tilt head is incredibly stiff which leads to jerky motion and bounce in your video. There also, on mine at least, appears to be a good bit of free play or slack in the vertical movement of the control arm. I've tried to tighten this down to no avail. The mounting screw seems to be a bit long. It wasn't bad mounting my RCA Small Wonder video camera but when I mounted my Kodak still camera the screw bottomed out and left the camera loose on the mount. The mount itself seems quite secure tight and sturdily attached to the tripod. I like the adjustability of the legs but if you're not using the tripod on a metal surface for the magnetic feet to cling to it tends to just slide around when adjusting the pan or tilt. The magnets do appear to be strong for their size and will hold my RCA Small Wonder video camera fully horizontal on the 'fridge or door of my car. I tried this with my Kodak Z-650 still camera and it was too heavy for the magnets to support. While on the subject of the magnetic feet I wanted to add a warning that if you're using an older CRT style monitor care should be taken to keep this tripod several feet away from your monitor. Even being more than a foot away from my 19" CRT cause distortion and image warping. There is the potential for damage to CRT monitors. As a stationary camera mount this is a pretty cute product; easy to carry, lightweight with near infinitely adjustable legs. If you just want to plop down your camera so you don't have to hold it this product works fine. When you bring the flaws of the pan and tilt features into play the enjoyment goes downhill fast. All in all it's not bad but it really isn't great.

title: More Than Just a Television
text: The Tivax 3.5-Inch Digital TV is also a multimedia device supporting multiple image, video and audio formats. Audio through the unit's single speaker is a bit tinny and slightly underpowered. At full or nearly full volume it's not all that loud. The unit does have a headphone jack and the addition of a set of decent buds or headphones will improve audio quality quite a bit although there are no bass or treble controls. It comes with a clear plastic screen protector and be warned, if you remove it getting it to lay perfectly flat again is nearly impossible. Along with the headphone connector the TV also has a single Micro-SD memory card slot. I purchased a 2-GIG card to test this device with. I do not know, and the manual does not say, if the TV supports the newer, larger SDHC style cards. The device has NO user accessible internal memory. All input and control are accomplished via two buttons on the face and a four way directional button set. The buttons are stiff and I found, with my thick fingers, that manipulating the directional arrow buttons was a bit hard to do with accuracy. My unit, which is white as opposed to the stated black, arrived with a USB cable (which I have not used) an AC adapter/charger, an external antenna and a peg/tab stand on a lanyard. I found attaching the lanyard to the unit (you'll likely lose the stand otherwise) to be a complete pain and required a bent pin to accomplish. Television Reception: The Tivax 3.5-Inch Digital TV has a built in rod antenna which feels very fragile and easy to bend. The antenna also has a swivel base so care must be exercised when pushing it back into the unit. The included external antenna has a nicely long cord so it can be positioned easily for optimal reception. For the sake of reference I live approximately 80 miles South East of Orlando Florida on the coast. Using the built-in antenna, indoors, upon initial setup the channel scan was unable to find any stations. Plugging the external antenna in resulted in around a dozen channels being found during the setup scan. The 320x240 LCD screen images are crisp and sharp. Colors are vibrant and clear and I was pleasantly surprised at the adjustability of the picture including brightness, contrast, tint and color mode. Moving the television while watching TV should be avoided as the picture will often freeze and breakup. I was quite happy to find that one of the stations I do get is a 24/7 local area weather channel. During Florida's frequent power outages due to severe weather and hurricanes this will be invaluable. Video Playback: I loaded over a GIG of video files onto my Micro-SD card to test the Tivax's ability to playback video files. I chose a mixed batch of AVI, MPG, WMV and MOV file formats. WMV files are not supported at all (oddly the unit DOES support WMA audio files, go figure) and the support for the other formats was hit or miss. Approximately 60% of the fifty or so video clips I've tried to play were supported, but the rest just returned an error. Those that did play did so quite well. Picture quality was good (dependant, of course, on the quality of the videos) as was the audio playback. Perhaps they'll release a firmware update for the unit to add further CODEC support. Audio Playback: As I previously mentioned, the system's speaker is quite tinny. Don't expect great quality sound from it. It's not horrible but it could be better. I tested several dozen MP3 files on my Tivax including low (80 kbps) and very high (320 kbps) bit rate files as well as variable-bit rate encoded files and it played all of them without a problem. Image Playback/Slide show: The Tivax 3.5-Inch Digital TV supports JPEG, PNG, GIF and BMP image formats. Images display crisp and clean with bright and true colors. Landscape oriented images display best and while you can rotate images that are portrait oriented there is a distinct quality loss during rotation. Images can be zoomed in on with multiple levels of zoom. The slide show feature is nicely configurable. The delay between images can be set or turned off for manual page turning. The transition effect done while changing images also has many options. The Tivax will also play any MP3 files in the same location as the images as background music during the slide show. I actually couldn't find a way NOT to have this happen if the audio and video files were mixed together on the memory card although the volume can be set to zero this will surely use more battery power even with the volume down. One feature which I liked, but was not mentioned in the manual, is the ability to set one of your own images as the startup `logo'. Power: The Tivax 3.5-Inch Digital TV comes with a built in Lithium Ion battery which they state can be recharged approximately 500 times. I found that their claimed charge durations were quite accurate. Watching Digital TV with the volume set to around 75% I was twice able to watch for a bit more than three hours before the unit turned off. I loaded several hundred large image files onto the memory card and set the unit to running them as a slide show (silent) and was able to achieve just over six hours of playback before the battery died. MP3 playback resulted in similar results of around five and a half hours of continuous play. When charging there are NO indicator lights showing that the unit is charging nor any way, short of turning it on, to tell if it has fully charged. There is also no on screen low battery warning. When my battery was depleted the unit simply shut itself off. Finally: This is a nice unit and far more than just a digital TV set. A padded case would be a nice option. I'm going to try some of the smartphone cases to see if any fit. I really don't want to scratch or damage the screen. The external antenna while mildly magnetic really needs to be weighted and/or have a clip attached to it as it is rather light and hard to keep in place.

title: Lowepro SlingShot 202 AW
text: The fit and finish of this bag are top notch. I've been camping and backpacking for decades and I have to say the quality of this bag and the workmanship are among the best I've seen. The nylon material is heavy duty and durable. The bag and shoulder strap are well padded for comfort and protection of your gear. The pack includes a built in micro-fiber cloth and two memory card slots in the main compartment. There's even a tuck-away all-weather cover in the bottom of the bag for inclement weather situations. The dividers in the main compartment are infinitely adjustable and all can be removed/repositioned. The pack includes a pull-out tripod holder/foot pocket and strapping system on the side of the bag. There's also a separate compartment at the top of the pack for personal items large enough for wallet, keys, an emergency poncho, etc. Also included are two smaller pockets on the back of the pack suitable for lens pens, notepad, pens, what have you. This bag is huge. Easily as big as most hiking day-packs. There's room for everything and the kitchen sink. Currently I have my old Canon AE-1 with 80-200 mm lens attached. My 55 mm auxiliary lens. A half dozen assorted filters. Cable release. 1:1 reverse adapter AND my Kodak Z-650 point and shoot all in the main compartment. Ease of use is incredible. The shoulder strap and waist belt are widely adjustable for people of almost all sizes. The zippers work flawlessly and fast never catching or hanging. The velcro throughout the pack is quite heavy duty and looks like it will hold up to years of abuse. All you need do is slide the pack from your back to the front of your body and the camera access section is right there. You never have to take the bag off to get at your rig. Those are the pros. Here are just a couple cons: The micro-fiber cloth is not removable. I'm not sure what you could do if it became soiled or stained and needed cleaning. The strap for the tripod is not fixed to the pack and could easily be lost. The all-weather cover fits very tight to the bag (in and of itself this is a good thing, but...) it won't fit over any but the smallest mono-pod or tripod. My [[ASIN:B00005T3TI Ambico 54 Inch Tripod with Quick Release (V-0555)]] just barely fits on the pack. I have no doubt this bag would last years for anyone from amateur to most demanding professional.

title: Perfect Solution for my needs, and of high quality
text: I’m using this cable with the audio out headphone jack on my TV’s HDMI 3 port I use fro streaming stuff from the internet via my laptop.
