title: Excellent Camera
text: I have been shooting Olympus cameras since 1978. I have always loved the lenses. With over 2,000,000 shots on my Olympus E-500 camera, I decided it was time to invest in a new camera. I was reluctant at first to try the EM-1 for three reasons: - The format is Micro-Four Thirds, not Four Thirds. I take 99% of my photos in the telephoto range, and that is what Four Thirds was optimized to use. Micro-Four Thirds is geared more towards wide angle lenses. - The camera is mirrorless and uses an electronic Viewfinder (EVF). - I have to use a converter to mount my existing Four Thirds lenses, and converters have a very bad history. Out of the box: The first thing that you notice when you pull the body out is that it is SOLID. The thing feels like it is built like a tank. I have not tried the "splashproof" and other claims, but just holding this body I can believe them. The camera fits well in my hand. My hands are a little large, and my pinky occasionally slides off the bottom. I may buy the grip/extra battery holder later if this proves to be a problem. YMMV. Using Four Thirds lenses: I have no Micro Four Thirds lenses and a lot invested in Four Thirds lenses, so using them was a key issue. Olympus has 1/17 or 1 MP of the sensor dedicated to phase detection auto focus, the only type of auto focus that will work with these lenses. I find that the system works very well. Focusing is fast and accurate. Mounting the converter is easy, as expected. Once mounted, you use a button on the side to release the lens. This is a learning issue since I still normally hit the lens release button on the camera body. I anticipate little real problems with this since as soon as I try to put the cover on the back of the lens I realize my error. Balance with the 12-60 mm Four Thirds lens is excellent. Holding the lens by the zoom collar, the weight is only slightly behind my left hand. I only have to support the body lightly with my right hand. I personally like that balance. Longer lenses like the 70-300 are also well balanced. EVF: I have used a mirrored SLR since 1978 and a rangefinder 35 mm camera and 126 film P&S cameras before that. As you might guess, I favor a direct view to see what I am shooting. EVF have issues with resolution and lag when moving to a different point of interest or following a subject, especially in low light. The EVF has turned out to be great. I really like Olympus' implementation. There is some lag, but it is generally minimal. The "What You See Is What You Get" is a big plus in my book. Adjust the exposure compensation or manual exposure settings, and the view in the EVF changes to reflect what the image will look like. It is not perfect, but it gets 95%+ of what you will actually get. The display of settings is bright, clear, crisp, large, and surprisingly unobtrusive. The EVF also allows a lot of changes in camera settings to be done without removing the camera from your eye. Use the two dials, and you can see where the focus points that you are using are. Hit the OK button on the back, and you can use the dials to adjust just about every setting while watching the selections you are making in the EVF. Ditto with the other buttons like HDR and auto exposure mode. HDR: I had the opportunity to use in-camera HDR while on a recent trip. The day was cloudy, and there was a lot of shadow against bright grey clouds. The in-camera HDR used a series of shots at different exposures and combined them in the camera. The results were better than HDR Pro in Photoshop CS5.5 IMO. I was much, much happier with the dynamic range and overall look of the images. the 10 fps shooting mode was also great for minimizing camera movement, ghosts and other problems associated with HDR. Image stabilization: The EM-1 has a five axis image stabilization system for the sensor. That means any lens becomes can be used. The fourth and fifth axes are for rotations. One compensates for the slight turn of the camera that often occurs when you press the shutter button. I had good success using IS in low light with my 70-300 mm lens set at 300 mm. Scenes: the EM-1 has many useful scene modes. I used landscape and panorama with great success. The artistic filters and story modes may also interest you. I prefer to do those types of things in post-processing. ISO: The camera has an almost insane 25600 maximum ISO. Yes, you get image quality degradation and noise at that ISO, but the in-camera JPEG processor can actually give you some relief from the problems at higher ISOs. I so far have found shooting up to ISO 1600 produces no discerned degradation. I tried ISO 6400 and found minimal issues. For those who started with film and were in love with the "high ISO" 1000 film for low light shooting, this is a major and welcome advancement. For those newer to photography that have been using higher ISO cameras for a while, the speed may not be much of a gain, but the image quality should be. The low end ISO is 200, which is the new normal. I do not find it to be a problem. I would rather shoot at a faster shutter speed than have an ISO 100 setting in most cases. There is an ISO LOW setting, but I do not plan to use it. If you regularly shoot in bright light and want lower f-stops, invest in a neutral density filter. Back display: The back display is slightly disappointing. It can only tilt up and down, not rotate so that you can see your composition when you are getting into the shot. It works well for shooting over crowds or getting a low angle shot. On the plus side, the display is clear, bright and a touchscreen that can be used to select a point of interest for focusing and can be used to take the shot in live view mode. You can also use it to select settings to change. The next generation should be even better, and hopefully it will have a screen that rotates. SD card: One change from the E-500 that I do not like is the use of SD rather than CF cards. CF cards are nearly indestructible, and a good Sansdisk Extreme card works virtually anywhere, anytime and is virtually impossible to physically break. The xD card slot disappearing is no loss, but not having a second card slot is somewhat surprising given the high-end prosumer/professional positioning of this camera. Controls and customization: The controls are pretty well placed for me with the exception of the auto exposure lock button. That is right beside the viewfinder and too far to the left for my liking. You can do a lot of customization with the control buttons and dials, but there are limits. I have not made any changes yet because I am still learning the camera. Overall the defaults seem logical and useful. This camera has two dials, one on the front and one on the back. The E-500 only had a back dial, so I am learning to use the two dial system. They work well for adjusting and selecting options. I think the second dial was a good addition. Both are conveniently located for my fingers. Image quality: All of this is meaningless if the image you get out is bad. The EM-1 does not disappoint. I know that there are people who insist that they need 48 MP or some other ridiculously large number. The reality is that 16 MP is a great size for printing full-size 300 dpi images on your printer or using a commercial photo printing service. If all you do is screen displays, it is about eight times more pixels than you need for a typical 2 MP monitor. The quality of the EM-1 pixels is very high, and you get excellent out-of-the-camera RAW and JPEG images. I have no problems seeing fine detail at 100% and higher magnifications. Summary: This camera is a winner, and it works with my existing Four Thirds lenses so I do not have to invest another $3000+ in lenses to use it. I have a lot to learn, and it will take some time to get the most out of the camera, but out-of-the-box, using my E-500 techniques, it is already doing great work.

title: Works relatively well
text: The camcorder was bought to record some interviews and later to be used for general videos. It worked very well for the interviews with excellent image quality and color balance. The audio was good but not great with the built-in microphone, something that I expected. I have tried to use it for other general videos with a fair number of action shots of animals, planes and other moving targets. I find the screen to be difficult to see in direct sunlight, one of the main reasons I strongly prefer an optical viewfinder over a screen. The audio is okay, and the video quality is very good in bright and moderate light. In very low light, it starts to suffer as most camcorders in this price range do until it eventually becomes almost unusable. I am not enamored with the controls. I find that they do not fall where I need them. The still camera is only okay, though it does give a 12 MP image. Get a DSLR or quality P&S if you are serious about still images. If you want a very good, moderate cost camcorder for moderate to bright lighting and can live with the controls, this is a good choice.

title: Good concept, not so good device
text: I bought and installed the Pogoplug on my LAN for the purpose of sharing photos over the Internet. Right out of the box I had misgivings. There is no documentation or technical specifications. That immediately raised serious questions in my mind about it being vulnerable to hacking or opening access to my computer and personal information. You have to attach it to your modem/router and allow it to go out on the Internet without knowing what it is doing. I decided to take it on faith that the company was legitimate and not going to install a backdoor into my system. I attached a Seagate USB external hard drive as my main memory device. I have also used USB memory sticks for temporary storage. All are USB 2.0. Initially I had issues with people accessing my files. The Web access used by outsiders does not show any indication of activity. If you have a couple of hundred photos like me, it can take a couple of minutes for anything to appear. I have also had people report 404 and other errors fairly frequently. My workaround was to create more folders to compartmentalize everything. They load quickly enough for people to see something happening and know that they are connected. Once you get inside the folders, people see a filmstrip and a large image like they would see in Windows. It is a serviceable but not glamorous interface. It is also not customizable. Once I established that people could access my photos over the Internet, the next step was to fill up the hard drive. To do so, my plan was to push the files over my 10/100 MBps LAN. The Pogoplug shows up as a drive, so all I have to do is drag-and-drop. The problem is that it is incredibly slow. I normally get about 30 kBps. That is dial-up modem slow. This exposed the second big problem. Remember the total lack of documentation? I had no FAQ, troubleshooting guide, technical specifications or other information to go on. I had to contact technical support via the Pogoplug web site. The Web site is slow and not always working, but I did get to someone, and they gave me the obvious suggestions like turning everything off and back on, dismounting and remounting the drive, trying a different drive, etc. After several iterations, I still had a slow connection that was now unreliable, a bunch of tech talk gibberish on ports and processes to open and close, and a closed out support ticket. Doing more research, this appears to be a known and frequent problem. It is a deal breaker for me. I am going to be looking for a replacement. As an interim solution, I will attach the USB HD directly and transfer my files on an as-needed basis. However, I am looking for an alternative now. So, to summarize, the concept is great, the implementation is okay, but the tech support and the LAN connection are not good. If you are serious about file sharing, this is not the device for you.

title: Good sound not so good connectivity
text: I got this wireless buds cause I lost my previous pair of tws buds. It comes in a cheap box with minimal packaging. As soon as you take it out of the box you question the quality of the product. It feels light and made of cheap plastic. But as long as it performs it's good right? Well let's start with the positives. The sound quality is excellent. Not too bass-y which is what I like. It is clear and the sound separation is quite nice. I noticed instruments in some songs which I haven't heard in my previous wireless earbuds. All in all this is a great sounding earbuds. You can also use it mono or one at a time. But that is where the qualities end. The ANC is bare minimum. There's no app support. And whenever you try to switch the noise cancelling mode it goes to ambient sound first then you have to change it again. Sometimes the taps doesn't register properly. The mics on it are ok. It picks up a lot of noise but in a quieter environment the calls are good. But I dont know if it's my product or in general, the mic only seems to work properly on the right earbud. The left earbud barely picks up my voice. The main issue I had with this earbud is the Bluetooth connectivity. It would disconnect randomly in the middle of calls. One time it kept disconnecting and reconnecting a few times in the same call. When listening to something the track sometimes skip randomly. And there is no clear indication or it doesn't let you know that it's low on battery. It just dies when the buds run out of juice. The battery life is average. Not bad but not outstanding either. Around 5 hrs on the earbuds itself and with the case it lasts me around 2.5days I'd say. (On average I use the buds 3.5-4 hrs daily)

title: Great discreet bodycam…Kind of
text: [[VIDEOID:bc06b38f85cb90428ede7cda6c1d5f8f]] I picked this up as a “discreet” way to document my daily commute. Where I live I either commute by bike or transit. As of late our transit system hasn’t been the safest way to get around the city. I opted to try out getting a body cam in thre event anything unfortunately occurred I’d at least have some way of documenting the event while keeping my hands free. I picked this up and while it took me a bit to figure out how to navigate the menu once I did the cam was amazing. I can articulate the lens to point forward straight up or back towards me (vlogger style). It’s small enough that it’s relatively noticeable. The screen while small allows for playback on the device itself which it’s a welcome addition. The ONLY strike against this cam is the gold screw point on the clip. It sticks out against the black body of the cam and draws peoples eyes to the cam. Now to be clear I’m not recording people for nefarious purposes however I would prefer that part be blacked out so as to allow more discreet carrying options. Other than that this cam is great decent photo/video/night vision. And the sound on playback is surprisingly loud for such a small cam. All in all definitely worth a buy if you can get over the gold screw point.

title: You don’t need to be a cop to use body cams!
text: [[VIDEOID:ee99d8a345601f7d7ea29edf87624595]] I got myself a bodycam because I believe it’s a useful too for Civilians as well as LEO’s. This particular body cam is GREAT quality has good sound and some extra little features such as password locks and badge # (LEO’s specific but you can assign yourself a number through the menus). Now this cam is a FULL-SIZE body cam meaning it’s about the same size as LEO’s wear. If you’ve seen LE wearing a body cam they’re VERY Obvious. So if you’re looking for a discreet cam this isn’t it. Now with that said the options allow you to use a “stealth” mode where there’s no sound from menus, key entry or power on/off. It has incredible night vision mode as well as a flashlight and emergency mode. At this point I suppose you’re wonder what the hell does a Civilian need with those functions. Well…I can’t speak for everyone but what I can speak to is life happens car accidents , random drunks etc. having a way to document these things could be a life safer because memory isn’t the greatest when something wild occurs. I’ve used this for a hiking trip to help remember which path I’ve taken. As a dash cam (there’s a mode for that also). And as an additional part to my plate carrier. Bottom life it’s an amazing cam and I will likely order a few more for other purposes.

title: Ditch Cable
text: I debated getting rid of my $95 cable bill for months. After receiving a free month trial to Netflix, I realized how many movies and TV shows were now available. Coupled with free trials to Hulu and Amazon Prime, the savings from the first month of canceling cable practically paid for the Roku. As for the device, it has a quick retrieval time when accessing your queue. The remote is small and uses radio waves, not infrared. This means you do not need to point the remote at the device, like most TV remotes, and the box can be hidden with the rest of your entertainment center wires. All of this, and a free app called Twonky, which allows you to beam videos from your tablet/smartphone to your Roku, makes this device a must have for your entertainment needs.

title: Great TV / Great Price
text: This is a great TV! Don't waste money on a 1080p picture. The 720p/1080i picture of this TV is indistinguishable from 1080p. The SCREEN BURN is slightly annoying, but nothing to get into a stink over. You'll only notice ghost images if you look for them, and they are not permanent. The REFLECTION for the plasma was also a concern for me, given that my TV is in a room with six foot by six foot plate glass windows. I hardly notice reflection unless the images on the screen are pitch black. Other reviews speak of the infamous PLASMA HUM; I don't hear it. The SPEAKERS on this TV are perfectly acceptable. For additional research on plasmas, I found a great link: Benefits & Misconceptions about Plasma [...]

Not with the enclosed battery. The red light on the bottom of the mouse went on for just about long enough for me to point & click, see the mouse working that one first moment, then .....poof....the battery died. Wow, I didn't expect that or I'd have ordered batteries too..So, as for the mouse, I'm sure it's as good as it should be. As for the "new" battery, not so much. I've always had the best luck with purchases from Amazon, & there's no way they can be faulted for the dead battery, but for anyone else looking to buy this product, please make sure you have fresh & functional batteries on hand.

title: Poor battery life, feature rich
text: If only the battery life was better... I have the GPS turned off and I only measure my blood oxygen level when I'm asleep yet it is nearly impossible for the watch to last a little more than 24 hours. My next Garmin will be the one with a solar powered assist. That being said for the negatives this watch has the features I wanted at a good price: - Sleep quality/quantity - Blood oxygen level - Steps counter - Flight of stairs counting - Water intake recording ) manual input) - Multiple activities recording (it can detect when I'm running, bike riding, etc.) It has been durable and the screen is still scratch free. However when it came to buying a premium tablet I had been nothing but disappointed with Android tablets (I have Google and Samsung versions at home). Neither seemed user friendly and were always terrible on battery life and speed. After much research I bought an iPad Pro 11... this is a great piece of technical engineering! From the outstanding battery life, beautiful screen, app integration, picture quality, LTE connectivity and speedy performance I have never used any Android tablet that comes close to how great this iPad is! From the small footprint of iOS on the hard drive to its graceful line this is a well thought out workhorse that is equally at ease for fun! My only quibble is the lack of a scrolling screen however everything I’ve thrown set it so far it has handled with ease! I’m installing Office 365 on it today- Apple, I may not like your phones yet I love your iPad Pro 11!

title: Simple is good.
text: I am not the target demographic for this device: middle-aged empty nester who loves to watch sci-fi, thrillers, and horror. I have a number of these brilliantly simple, highly configurable lights. They are perfect in the bedroom where, depending on our intended mood, a variety of different colors or modes might be appropriate. I have two in the living room, hiding behind tropical plants at a 3' height, on either side of the big screen, about 5 feet away on each side. I have a routine set up to turn off all the lights in the room and engage campfire mode in both lights at 45% brightness with a single keyword. Voila--instant torchlight in the jungle (or romantic candlelight - take your pick). I am a colossal LOST fan, and this lighting is perfect for watching LOST, or anything scary or dark. And if I need a different effect, that's only a few words away. The simplicity with which these set up and configure themselves is so good it makes Apple products jealous. If you have an Alexa on your Wi-Fi network, simply plug the Glow in to a power source, open the Alexa app on your phone, and the light will auto-connect to your network and add itself to Alexa. It will then prompt you to configure it with a name and add it to any groups, etc. Utterly simple. If the setup fails, it might ask you to scan the barcode on the back of the booklet it came with to get it going, but this has not been my experience - they have all self-configured and join the network seamlessly. For those of you complaining this does not have a mic and speaker - folks, it works WITH an Echo device. It is a light - that's it. If Amazon built Alexa mics and speakers into this it would cost double--and I am positive they are developing just such a light ...for which you will pay $60+. Normally, these are $30/ea, but they were 45% off on Prime Day, so I added a few more. There are indeed cheaper (and much more expensive) smart mood lights on the market, but if you run Alexa at home, this is hands down the best way to do it. Seamless. It baffles me that Amazon does not have a whole range of lighting products which work exactly like this. They easily could. Give me one of these on a larger scale (12-15") and make it weatherproof for outside on the patio, please.

title: Decent dashcam for the price, a pain to configure, not the image quality I expected
text: For the price this is hard to beat. It has lots of great features, including a Wifi app, but resolution/quality even on the highest settings are slightly disappointing. I have everything configured to provide the sharpest possible image (highest resolution and bit rate, etc.), and if a car is more than 30' away, zooming in on a screenshot of a license plate is iffy at best, even if the footage was taken in bright daylight (screencaps taken in VLC). Something seems off to me. Yes, I removed the protective films, and yes, my window is reasonably clean (normal conditions). I have attached two photos: one of the unit in a fantastic little case I found for it (see below), and a screencap showing the problem I described. The van in front of me is semi-readable, and was about 25 feet away. The car 15-20 feet further away on the left is unreadable, as is the plate close to me on the left. And yes, I have the CPL filter installed on the lens. Configuring this was a bit of a hassle. The Wi-Fi app is not intuitive, and some quick googling led me to discover you have to temporarily disable your cellular data the first time you use it to get the camera to connect. Once configured, the camera itself acts as the network your phone connects to. This means your phone cannot be connected to any other Wi-Fi network while you are connected to the camera. I have no idea why they don't just allow you to use Bluetooth for this--it would be simpler to set up, that's for sure. Honestly, having integrated security video will be a factor in the next car I purchase. This is all way too much work. Many PCs will not play the default file format this records in as they lack the correct video codec (H.265) or enough processing power. I think there must be a way to change the format it records in, but I was unable to find the configuration setting to change in either the app or the camera itself. To get this to play files on your PC, I suggest using VLC Player. It is free, and if you are running the latest version (check for updates in the application), it will run them just fine if your PC has the juice for HD at this level. If you experience dropped frames or choppy video when playing back on your computer, this is probably because your computer is not equipped with a GPU to support this high resolution of video (many aren't; if you don't have a dedicated video card in your PC, you may experience this). My office desktop does not have a dedicated video card and the video is a bit choppy if other things are running--expected. If you are interested, the case is the "Mchoi Hard EVA Travel Case for Garmin inReach Mini GPS", (ASIN: B08F9QV1BQ), which is very sturdy and cost me $13.49 in Feb 2021. I looked for EVER for a case for this, and this was the best fit I found.

title: Great laptop in the 4/32 configuration: excellent keyboard, great battery life, fast and silent
text: Fantastic Chromebook. I tried a number of Chromebooks before settling on this one, and the #1 reason is the keyboard. This has a great keyboard that feels much better than most others. The typical Chromebook keyboard has very little travel/feedback from the keys, and most feel very cheap with a zero-feedback key action. Don't get me wrong, this is not as good as a full-sized keyboard, but it is surprisingly easy to type on. In fact, I understand Google themselves designed this keyboard for Acer. Anyway, it feels good. The display is great, but be warned--it is highly reflective. Using it outdoors or in rooms with lots of bright overhead lights is challenging. in the 4GB/32GB configuration with the faster processor, this is a very fast Chromebook. The screen flipping trick is a nice feature if you occasionally need to use it to watch a video, do a presentation, or as a tablet, but it is too thick (3/4") and heavy to use as a tablet regularly (feels like it weighs more than twice as much as my iPad Air). I am very pleased with my purchase though--I needed a small and light laptop for work use with browser-based apps. Perfect. Also, the 10+ hours of battery life is awesome. Paid $240 new from Amazon (I personally would not buy a laptop from a third-party seller).

title: A great value, love the SFF chassis, needs better packaging
text: *UPDATED* Update after living with this PC for half a year: Zero problems, fast, and works perfectly for my application (business use). And excellent value. VERY pleased with this purchase. --- The PC itself seems to be a great value, and is working fine thus far. The system is plenty fast. The HDD is a bit busy/noisy, and spins a bit more than it should, as though the system is caching to disk constantly. I'm not doing anything demanding with it at all--just light MS Office use and surfing. That's it. No gaming, no video editing, nothing heavy. Note this system is intended for business use, and could not handle much in the way of gaming or video editing, as it has no video card. The on-board graphics use the system's RAM, so anything asking a lot from the system's limited graphics capabilities will slow the entire system down immensely. Luckily, I outgrew DOOM years ago. The SFF case is heavy, but oddly a bit flimsy, with more flex than I had expected for the weight--especially the back panel--mine was oddly bent outward. I pushed it back in/straightened it (I had to in order to plug things in--the plugs were deeply recessed due to the bent real panel--very odd). The chassis itself is a joy to work with though, as the case pops open on hinges without turning a single screw--not even a thumbscrew, and everything is very accessible. The HDD's working vibrations and sounds are amplified by the plastic subframe the drive is mounted in, which acts like an amplifier for the vibrations. I worry a bit that the system's small case will have cooling issues. There just isn't much room in there, and there is only one small 3" system ventilation fan (+ the power supply's fan, and a fan over the CPU). There are vents on the front and rear of the system, but I would like a lot more ventilation--I would have appreciated a perforated lid. Heat is the enemy of all electronics, and my other systems all have more ventilation than this box. Of course, this is an off-lease corporate desktop workstation, and is not designed to have the long life of other systems. The components in the box are the cheapest possible variants thereof, and I do not expect this system to last more than 3-4 years at the most. That said, $269 for a branded Lenovo PC with a 3.2GHz Intel Core i5, 12GB of RAM and a 2TB HDD is a fantastic value. If it dies in 3 years, I will have gotten my money's worth. Important note about the packaging: it simply was not enough protection. I guarantee the system took some hard knocks on its way to me. The UPS driver actually dropped it at my feet from a height of 1'--not kidding! The system is not packaged in an inner box within the shipping carton--the carton IS the box. The small Styrofoam corner blocks used to float the system inside the box are unusually rigid, so much so that they provide little in the way of cushioning, and one of them had cracked in half--meaning the PC wobbled around in the box during shipping. Also, the carton was sealed with "Microsoft Certified Refurbisher" packing tape, making it clear to all it contained a PC. They need to change the packaging--a desktop system simply needs more/better protection than this. I half expected it to be DOA due to the abuse it took on the way here from Arizona.

title: Looks and feels like a very high quality cable--vastly superior to OEM, and all other competitors
text: This was a gift for a teenager who is VERY hard on their phones and cables, and keeps shredding their cables. This is the king of all cables, and should last forever. I have a dozen other Anker products, mostly cables, and all have performed flawlessly. This looks and feels like a high quality product. So far so good. I spent a decade in IT, and I believe in buying top-quality cables. This cable is vastly superior to OEM Apple cables (anything is better than Apple's terrible cables), and seems much sturdier and rugged than any other cable I have seen.

title: Vastly superior sound (compared to Echo Dot)
text: Alexa now has a deeper, fuller voice! The bigger speaker (compared to the Dot) makes a huge difference. Also, the mics seem to work better, even though they are supposed to be the same(?). Music however, is what it's all about. This little gadget fills the room with rich, full sound. Love it.

title: Perfect: fits my GoPro clone perfectly
text: Love it. Exactly what I needed to hold the GoPro clone I use (without a case). Great price too.

title: This product should be included with every camera. It is that good.
text: Everyone with a camera needs one of these. Seriously. Brilliant product. I love mine, and gave one as a gift, and the user loves it. :)

title: Very happy: OEM Apple Smart Case for iPad Air
text: Ordered this hoping it would be authentic OEM Apple, not a knock-off. It is! Very pleased with this purchase. The case looks great and fits like a glove--exactly like the worn OEM Apple Smart Case it is replacing. Thank you!

title: Much more speaker for your money than others in this price range
text: Initial impressions: I have had this for about two weeks and have used it only a few times. Very impressed with it thus far. Got it in a lightening deal for $15.99. Fantastic speaker for the money. Loud as hell--seriously, twice the volume (with less distortion than expected) of other $20-ish bluetooth speakers. I love that it also has a radio in it and a handle, and can accept aux, MicroSD and USB input. Looks and feels like something more substantial than just a plain little box. Also, has a massive battery. Overall, very pleased thus far with this purchase. Will update later when I see how well the battery performs over time.

title: Anker = high quality
text: Love these cables. I have recently started using several Anker products, and I am very impressed with their product quality. This appears to be a very well-made cable.

title: A perfect fit for my Microsoft Wedge Mouse
text: So far so good. I just got this, and was worried it would be too small. I did not buy it to hold my headphones, but instead, my Microsoft Wedge Mouse. It is a perfect, snug fit. Very pleased. :)

title: A heavy-duty cable for a regular-duty price?
text: This is a very good entry-level HDMI cable. Better than everything out there for anywhere near this price. This feels like a heavy-duty cable, for a regular-duty cable price. Note that it is somewhat stiffer/less flexible than many cables. If you have a tight space scenario, this cable does not bend easily. Otherwise extremely pleased with this purchase. Highly recommend.

title: Serious (and odd) design flaw makes it uncomfortable to hold in your hand - not a good case for reading
text: I looked at a lot of cases before selecting this one, and I am sad to say I am very disappointed in this purchase. I have an Omoton case for my Kindle PaperWhite. I really like the design of the shell--the way Kindle fits into on it, so I was trying to find something similar, where the entire unit is enclosed all the way around. This was the only case I found which appeared to fit this way, so I ordered it. Build quality is fine, and the Kindle does fit snugly in the case, providing the fit I was looking for. Unfortunately, there is a serious (and odd) design flaw in this case: a small lip that protrudes outwards and runs all the way around the edge of the unit. This lip serves no purpose, and I do not understand why it was built into the design. I don't know why the lip did not register as a potential problem when I was making the decision to buy the unit--I suppose I thought it would be too small to matter. I was wrong. It matters. It is not an issue when you are not holding it: for example, using the tablet to watch movies and it is supported by the folded case on a flat surface (although this feels somewhat precarious/barely balanced). The issue is when you are holding the case in your hand and trying to read with your Kindle: the lip digs into your palm or fingers and after a few minutes becomes uncomfortable. You end up shifting the kindle to your other hand every couple of minutes. This is uncool, and makes what would otherwise be a great case almost unusable as a hand-held device. I thought about returning it, but given the hassle involved, I decided not to bother for a $12 unit. I cannot recommend this case. If you plan on reading with this case (i,.e. holding it in your hand for any length of time), it will be uncomfortable (sure is for me anyway).

title: *UPDATED REVIEW* Will not automatically pair, on-board microphone disables the mics in my phone, and charges phone VERY slowly
text: *UPDATED REVIEW* A seller replaced a different defective FM transmitter unit with this one for me (mine has the Kollea brand name on it, but this is the identical unit, private-labeled). This is a better product than what it replaced, but is not without it's flaws. I have three (*UPDATE: now four, and the fourth one is a deal-breaker--see below) complaints with this unit: 1) It will not automatically reconnect to my phone about 75% of the time. I have to manually shut Bluetooth off and turn it back on on the phone, sometimes a few times before it pairs successfully. This is a hassle--a PITA. Every time I get in the car, I have to go through this process--every time power is cut from the transmitter, actually, so if your passenger knocks it and it pops out of the 12V socket, it will have to be re-paired, which is supposed to happen automatically, but does not, and you then have to go through the process. Frustrating. 2) Charge output is only 1.0A. this is why I returned the first one--phone gives a "slow charging" warning when charging from this unit, regardless of what USB cable I use (I tried four different cables, all of which I know for certain can carry 2.1A). 3) Callers have occasionally complained they cannot hear me well when using this unit, and I occasionally (but not often) encounter FM interference. I believe Bluetooth itself is part of the problem, and anyone who has used a few Bluetooth headsets or units like this knows audio quality is terrible. Period. We just deal with it. Add to that the burden of having to transmit your signal via FM to a car stereo and the user-side audio (what you will hear in your car) is always going to be craptastic. 4) (*UPDATE) When paired, voice recognition on my phone, which is usually quite good, becomes severely impaired. This is also likely the culprit for complaint #3, above. I suspect this is because when paired, it tries to use the built-in microphone for voice recognition instead of the microphones on my phone (of which there are 4). It is disabling the extremely good microphones in my phone (Nokia lumia Icon which is well known for having incredible audio input) and using the unit's crappy microphone instead. This microphone is located in the unit, which is attached to the center console of my car near the shifter, and thus picks up all the vibrations and related road and engine noise transmitted through the structure of the car as I drive. This approach is terrible. I have stopped using the unit for anything requiring voice input, including telephone calls. In other words, this is just a big awkward charger now, and one that charges painfully slowly (see complaint #2). If it were possible to disable the onboard mic, and use the mics in my phone instead for calls and voice recognition, this would be a much more serviceable unit As it is now, it is just a piece of junk. Cannot recommend this item. There are definitely worse products out there. I have not tried them all, but of those I have used, this is the best one so far. I will likely keep using it until the lack of automatic pairing pushes me over the edge with it one day and I get something else. (*UPDATE: this thing just does not work well, and I am now looking for something else.)

title: If you are looking for a good AM radio, keep looking. Not well-made and performed poorly. Expected better from Sangean.
text: I returned this radio--it simply was not very good at the job I bought it to do (picking up AM radio) and was poorly made. I bought it to listen to Los Angeles Dodgers ballgames on AM570. Simply put, this radio could not hold the station. AM570 is strong and clear on most other devices, but the Sangean, despite the other reviews, seemed to have terrible reception in my apartment, even near a window (I live in an interior unit in an apartment building--windows on the courtyard). It could not hold the station well, and there was a lot of interference no matter what I tried. At no time was I able to tune into AM570 with a clear signal--far too much noise. This is the only reason I bought the radio and it's inability to pick up AM570 rendered it useless. I replaced it with the [[ASIN:B012F0DGYE Sony ICFP26 Portable AM/FM Radio (Black)]], which performs a lot better and costs about $3 more. The Sony picks up and holds AM570 in my apartment perfectly, with no noise/hiss. The Sony is clearly the better product. It also looks much nicer--the Sangean SR-35 looks and feels like a cheap piece of crap. The Sony is actually a far more appealing, sleeker-looking device (I wish it were a bit smaller). The second flaw was that the battery door would not stay closed. the little tab that clicks to hold it closed seemed too small or something (it was not bent). It just did not stay closed. Even if it had worked well (which it did not), this would have beeen enough to return it. it would literally have required a rubber band to stay closed. I was really disappointed with this radio--I had expected better, given Sangean's reputation. I cannot recommend this radio for AM use--get the Sony instead and save yourself the headache of returning it. (*I would like to thank Amazon for making the returns process so painless though!)

title: Better reception than the Sangean SR-35 for the same price
text: Got this little guy to replace the Sangean SR-35, which I returned because it got terrible reception. This is a much better piece of hardware. I live in a large building and my interior unit faces into the courtyard on the ground floor. This means reception can be an issue with some devices. I bought the Sangean (and replaced it with this) to listen to Dodger's radio (because you cannot listen to games online at all--terrible! Thanks for nothing iHeart Radio, and to the Dodgers for selling out--again). An AM radio was literally the only solution. Unlike the Sangean, the Sony is able to provide consistently good reception of AM570 without a fuss. The Sangean simply couldn't--there was too much interference and the reception seemed poorer. One can only conclude the radio itself on the board is superior in the Sony. Bonus: The Sony is a much better-looking unit (but neither looks like it would survive much of a fall). would be 5 stars if it were slightly smaller and a bit more durable.

title: Fantastic--best eReader I have tried (I've tried a lot). Text-to-speech capability from previous Kindles notably missing (why?).
text: OK, so the Kindle Paperwhite is pretty much the greatest thing ever. Seriously. Now I can sit outside in the dark on my patio at night and read without a big bright light which also attract insects. I wish the bezel surrounding the screen were a couple millimeters wider (I keep turning pages by accident), but otherwise this is an absolutely brilliant piece of gadgetry. I own three kindles, and this is my favorite by far. HOWEVER, there is one feature sorely missing from it, which is why I am hanging on to my Kindle Keyboard and Kindle DX: it will not do the text-to-speech trick. Why not?? This seems like the simplest thing ever to integrate, and if adding the speakers is too expensive, just give us a headphones port. Anyhow, I love this thing and I wish I had bought one ages ago. Oh--and I purchased it used (like new) from a seller on Amazon for $50, which makes it an excellent value.

title: Did my homework - decided on this one - great decision so far
text: Did a lot of homework before selecting this case for my Paperwhite. The professional reviews out there placed the OMOTION case firmly at the head of the class in terms of build, features, and functionality. I bought it and have been extremely happy with the purchase. If this changes, I will update this review, but for now, I'm happy.

title: Love these--great sound and value, but what's with the flimsy cord?
text: I got these on sale for under $30. Love them. but I admit I hesitate to expect a long, healthy life for them. They sound genuinely excellent (unbelievably good for the price!) and are actually very comfortable (love the fabric for the ear pieces), but the cord is super-thin and flimsy-feeling. Unless it is a lot stronger then it looks & feels, I fully expect to accidentally get up one day with it plugged into my PC and accidentally rip it out of the headphones (at this price point you do not get removeable cords). This cord is only about 1.5mm in diameter and does not inspire confidence. Cord length is fine for most uses, despite other reviews stating the contrary--it's shortish, but at about 5' it's fine for me--I use it either sitting stationary, or connected to a device I am holding or carrying in my pocket. If these headphones had a tougher/removable cord, I would be perfectly happy. Note: Sennheiser really does conquer all--these were $26 (I think) and sound better than anything else I have tried lately (including Beats--terrible), including many sets costing much, much more.

title: Perfect
text: Bought this to protect my MS Surface RT. Love the feel of it, and it does a wonderful job. Lots of padding and is very soft. Interesting note: there was a water leak from the apartment above mine and this was laying on the counter with the Surface in it. The counter was flooded. The case absorbed water, leaving the Surface inside it only slightly damp. After leaving the Surface out with the kickstand open for two days, just to make sure it was dry, it booted up and worked fine with no indication of damage. The case took three days to dry and is now fine too. If the Surface had not been in the case, I am sure it would have been soaked and may not have survived. Also, I have another one of these cases I use for an Android tablet, and it works beautifully.

title: Love this case - exactly what I wanted.
text: This case is exactly what I wanted: extremely durable shock-absorbing (read: drop-proof) protection without screen protection. Let me qualify that statement: I did *not* want screen protection. I love the pearl eink display on my graphite Kindle Keyboard, and it now has a big brother. I do not want a screen cover, as this would greatly reduce the screen's otherwise remarkable clarity, adding unwanted elements such as bubbles, surface scratches, and glare to the mix--no thank you. There is a reason I disliked reading on the iPad so much I gave it back (very reflective!). In fact, this OtterBox defender case came with a stick-on screen protector--no way. It would ruin that big, glorious pearl eink display. A screen cover serves no purpose once you remove the device from your backpack/messenger/tote/briefcase for use. Assuming you transport your Kindle device safely in an appropriate sleeve (you put your other expensive electronic equipment--your laptop/tablet in one; your Kindle deserves the same amount of respect), the screen protector is completely unnecessary--the sleeve protects the screen during travel. THAT is when the screen needs protecting--when you are not using it, from the other goodies in your messenger bag/backpack (keys, pens, earbuds, and anything else rattling around in there). Yes, that's right--I'm talking about a Kindle in an Otterbox Inside a sleeve inside your briefcase. ...Inception-level protection. You got it. Better safe than sorry, right? What if they once again stop producing our beloved Kindle DX and something happens to yours? I do not want to have to replace my DX--especially if it has to be with a Fire device (5% the battery life, reflective, heavy, expensive--no thanks!). When you are holding your Kindle in your hand, reading, a screen cover only detracts from the experience. What you see in my pictures is exactly what you get: a beefy, black rubber (not silicone--too easily torn; rubber is much stronger) form-fitting sleeve with an equally form-fitting outer plastic shell. Science geeks like me understand how this works, and just in case you are not one, here is the idea: if you drop your device onto the floor, the outer shell absorbs some of the impact energy generated by the device hitting the floor. It then disburses the remaining energy of the impact broadly into the rubber inner lining. The rubber lining then in turn disburses the now greatly-reduced impact energy into the device. In other words, by the time the force of the impact is filtered through two layers of protection, the second of which is very absorbent and resilient (rubber) the device inside absorbs little if anything of the original impact. I feel very good about having my Kindle DX in an Otterbox Commuter. If I ever had one of those incredibly poorly-designed (read: seriously fragile) apple devices, such as an iPad or iPhone (which I do not, and am not ever likely to), it too would live in an OtterBox Commuter case. OtterBox = the best protection a device can get. I paid $18 including shipping for this. A great price, and worth much more in terms of peace of mind.

title: Returned immediately - should have read the reviews first
text: I have gotten in the habit of checking the low-star reviews of items and because Amazon makes this product for use with their own Kindle DX device, I (lazily) did not bother. I foolishly assumed it would work just fine. So ...while I was waiting for my order to be delivered, curiosity got the best of me, and I checked out the 1 & 2-star reviews. *Whoops.* Turns out that this cover, which hooks directly into the Kindle DX on the left side with little metal hooks, puts a lot of strain on the front plastic shell of the Kindle DX, especially if you mistakenly open it up from the wrong side, which I am sure everyone does from time to time. Lots of users have reported the stress caused by the way this cover connects to the Kindle DX actually causing the Kindle DX shell to crack. No thank you. Not even willing to risk it. Returned, unopened. Bought another case. (*Note/alternative suggestion: if you are lucky you might still be able to get one of the few remaining Otterbox Commuter cases for it here on Amazon. Otterbox no longer makes them, but if you hunt, you can find them around in small quantities. I got one for $12 + $5 shipping.)

title: This has an odd design flaw
text: Looks and feels very nice in the hand. Seems of decent quality, but the Kindle is held in with elastic which will eventually lose elasticity. The flaw I mention is the clasp: when there is no Kindle in it, an invisible magnetic clasp (as in embedded inside the product) holds it closed, making the front "stick" to the back. However, when the Kindle is in it, this clasp does nothing, and the unit does not stay closed. Not sure how wise it is to have a magnet in such close proximity to the Kindle either, but that is another story. Glad I got this for 50% off on a promo. Was a gift. So far so good.

title: Great strap, wish it were a little longer
text: I really like this strap a lot. Use it with my Panasonic Lumix DMC-LX7. I just wish it were a little longer (possibly adjustable?). The little pockets are exactly the right size to hold spare batteries! This is a super-tough strap, and may be overkill for my little compact-system camera, but I love it. The back is rubberized (three strips), and it holds the strap in place. If everything else in the world were made this well, I would be a happy camper. Worth every penny.

title: Much too large
text: This dust cover is much too large for the Brother HL-2270DW Laser Printer, with several inches of room on each side and in extra height as well. It fits like a an XL sweater on a medium-sized kid: baggy, wrinkly, and just sloppy everywhere. It is made for something considerably larger. (Note: the printer in the picture above is not a Brother HL-2270 series--it is larger and taller.) It also smelled quite repulsive when it arrived, so I aired it out outdoors for a couple days--helped. Then, of course, when I tried to use it on the printer it did not fit. Returned. May make my own.

title: Exactly what I expected--maybe a little better, even.
text: I spent a long time hmmming and hawing over this purchase. I really wanted the OEM Panasonic case for my LX7, but at $65 here on Amazon, it was just too expensive. I compared the aftermarket cases for this camera and examined photographs closely. This was the winner for apparent quality and design. And it lived up to expectations. I was worried that it would block some of the screen or controls in the back, but this is not an issue at all. This case fits almost perfectly (screw mount is slightly out of alignment with the hole on the bottom of the camera--but it works), and is of as high-quality materials as one can imagine, given that this is *not* a leather case. The prospective purchaser should be aware that the vast majority of the cases on Amazon for the LX7 are not real leather. You can tell a case is real leather on here if it costs a fortune. The real leather cases on Amazon are all >$50, and some are $100+. For $15, this case represents an excellent value, as it fits pretty well, is well-made (sturdier than I expected!), and looks very nice. (I have the white LX7 and I bought the light brown case--the color of a well-worn baseball glove). One thing: as expected, the strap is made of vinyl, and looks it. I will likely be upgrading to a proper, padded camera strap though, so this is of little import, at least to me. If you are on the fence, take my advice and go for it. This is a good value, and a decent case--especially for this price. I did, and I have no regrets. Note: you will have to remove the case to access the battery/SD card compartment and the ports, as is the norm with all cases of this type for this camera (I was unable to find one that did not require this). --- UPDATE: After several months of hard use, this case has held up remarkably well. No evidence of wear. I get compliments on it, as well. Note: Do not attach the camera to a tripod with the bottom of the case on. The knob on the case is threaded to allow you to do this, but getting it off the tripod mount afterwards is a nightmare. Just take it out of the case--trust me.

title: Excellent value laptop
text: So , a while back (<1 yr) I did a whole bunch of research for a friend who needed a new laptop. Everything I read pointed to Asus, so we went that route. Everything worked out just fine, so when it came time for me to upgrade, I followed suit. I got this box, with a slightly faster processor and a 500GB HDD for $299 on sale elsewhere two weeks ago. Happy with it thus far. The keyboard layout is a little unusual, and definitely takes some getting used to. Battery life is excellent, and even at the dimmest setting, the screen is totally fine indoors. I wish it had another USB port, and the lack of Bluetooth seems silly (I miss it though). Built-in cameras is not great, but for Skype, its just fine. Love how quiet this thing is. Yet to feel any heat from it. Happy camper. --- UPDATE: After using this for a while now, I can safely say it is a great laptop except for one, glaring fault: the keyboard is terrible. Worst layout I have ever had on a laptop. Makes me want to replace the laptop. If only this was not a problem... *sigh*

title: My world is forever changed; or how I learned to relax and love the box.
text: This is ridiculous. Never before have I ever gotten so much joy from an electronic gadget (and I'm a gadget NUT). After renting from Netflix for YEARS, I finally got a Roku box for Xmakkah from my girlfriend, who shall henceforth be worshiped as a god. I LOVE it (and yes, her too!). I have only two complaints, neither of which has anything to do with the Roku box itself, but rather the service I receive from Netflix. 1) Netflix desperately needs to step up the selection of available streaming content. The vast majority of the 20K titles currently available are old, unloved, and largely undesirable. Sure there is some decent content, but nowhere near enough of it. A good example of this is TV: I can Watch Dexter, LOST, and Heroes, but not Survivor, X-Files, or The Sopranos. I can watch the Old Battlestar Galactica, but not the new one. I can watch Masters of Horror, but not The Twilight Zone. You get the idea. 2) Video quality degrades when other devices are used that eat up bandwidth. I use my broadband cable connection for everything except my microwave oven. Seriously: telephony (Vonage), Internet access, online backup, and Roku. If I am watching something on the Roku box and I answer the phone, the resolution on the screen drops dramatically and the audio quality on the call is terrible. You get the picture (pun intended)... Oh, and I have one more issue, although this is not really an issue--more of a request: Roku needs to greatly expand the channel store!!! YES PLEASE!! Setup was a breeze and I was watching a movie in less then 10 minutes (and 9 of those minutes were the Roku box connecting to Roku itself and registering/updating firmware). :o) Get one of these. Trust me. Best thing I got for Christmas by a mile.

title: Buyer beware--lens mechanism problems
text: This camera was highly recommended from a very trusted source, and the reviews were mostly positive. I expected a lot from it, and for a brief period, (maybe 4 months) it worked well. Then the problems began. Lens errors. Yes, despite Canon's insistence that this sort of thing "never" happens, the mechanical lens error you will read about in other people's reviews (known issue with this camera) of this camera happened to me. I bought it hoping they wouldn't, but alas, I am apparently a sucker. Next time, I shall heed the warnings of my fellow Amazonites. No more Canon products for me.... As time wore on, the lens error became more and more of a problem. After another three months, I called Canon. The (arrogant) tech support guy just said, "Oh, this happens when the batteries are weak." "Oh really?" I said, unwrapping a new set of Energizer AA's. "Let me just stick these puppies in here and see what happens... Huh. Well, would you look at that. So much for your battery theory pal." After embarrassing him thusly, his only "solution" was to send the camera in for Canon to look at it (at my expense). This would take a minimum of six weeks, after which there was no guarantee I would not continue to have the same problem with the camera. I mean, come on--a design defect is a design defect, after all. I was certainly not the first person to have this problem with this camera. Not only that, but no camera for SIX WEEKS?? I would not have survived. Sadly, before I could pack the thing up and send it in, I dropped it from the staggering height of three feet. You guessed it, end of camera. Canon makes cheap crap with poor durability and cheap lens mechanisms. So guess what I did? Yup, I bought myself a Nikon. I've had three of them with ZERO problems over the years. This is number four. My replacement is working beautifully, and is smaller to boot. Excellent image quality too. I will not buy a Canon again. Fool me once, it's your fault. Fool me twice, it's mine. Buyer beware.

title: If it sounds to good to be true...
text: ...it probably is. I would be well served to remember that before buying stuff next time. This thing was just so tiny I had to have it. And for the first 2 weeks it worked ok. Not great, just OK. Then the talk time began slipping... then the static began... then people started telling me they couldn't understand me. Then it stopped working completely. Less than 3 weeks old and already headed to the trash. What a waste. I've made up my mind: with bluetooth headphones, you get what you pay for. I'm going for a Jawbone 2, spending the extra cash on it, and I have no doubt in my mind it will be everything the reviews say it is. Enough Samsung garbage. Should have known. There are no other Samsung products in my home, and nor will there ever be. Matt

title: Quick & dirty
text: This is going to be quick--I only have a minute. However, as an avid point & shoot hobbyist, I wanted to contribute my $0.02 worth in on this magnificent little gem. Small, simple, and almost goof-proof, this is an ideal inexpensive camera for anyone just getting started. No optical viewfinder, managable file sizes, and the typical unbeatable Nikon lens mean you get serious bang for your buck with this camera. Full auto works well, and easy access to simple manual control over the basic parameters of the capture process mean it is easy for anyone to make minor adjustments. Also, there are (I think) 16 or 20 custom auto modes, including fireworks, black & white, etc. HUGE plus: this camera runs on AA batteries. Spend about $25 once on a charger and two sets of high-capacity rechargables (2600miAh), and you will be all set. Regular Energizers are good for 100+ shots with the flash. The rechargables I bought are good for easily 250+ on a charge. MOney VERY well spent. For your dollar, this is a hard camera to beat--and what makes it great is that it's a Nikon--these people know lenses... and TRUST ME, it's all about the optics. Nikon simply rules in that dept, IMHO.

title: Nice but very fragile
text: I got one of these for the holidays last year (12/06) and I was totally stoked. This was my first iPod--what a shame that it turned out to be such a fragile, poorly engineered device. I mean, this thing got dropped once from about 2.5 feet (it was only 2 months old) and it was TOAST (and it was in a plastic hardshell case!). I have had Laptops that survived worse. Come to think of it, I've had a lot of (far cheaper) devices that are better able to take abuse than this $400 item--including TV remotes, cell phones, Nintendo Game Boys (designed to be nearly indestructible), OTHER MP3 PLAYERS, etc. It seems that a physically appealing design does not necessarily equate to superior engineering--quite the opposite in this case. I do like it, and the replacement I got from Apple works very well. It's great looking and it does the job well. Too bad I'm so terrified of dropping it that I had to buy a big, bulky silicone case to improve its chances of survival. Let me tell ya, in its crash-test-dummy outfit, it no longer looks even the slightest bit sleek. Have you ever dropped your keys when getting out of the car? Your cell phone? If you answered yes to either of the above, then you can probably expect to drop your iPod one day. I hope you have a (thickly) carpeted garage--or that it lands on your foot. Bottom line: If I were thinking of getting an MP3 player, iPod or another brand, it would have zero moving parts; on other words, I would buy a flash-based device instead of one with a hard drive. I also cannot help but wonder why Nintendo does not take what they have learned about building child-proof, nearly indestructible portable gaming devices and apply this to a worthy competitor to the iPod. I would be the first in line... I gave this product 3 stars because it does a good job of what it is touted to do: play MP3s & video/images. In fact, the user interface, including the GUI and the click wheel is one of the nicest, most intuitive designs I have ever seen on a piece of consumer electronics equipment. Too bad it's put together so cheaply. Grossly overpriced? Most definitely. I hope the iPhone turns out to be a higher quality piece. --- UPDATE: 8/2013: still working fine... :)

title: My 4x4 iPod
text: This thing is genuinely neat. I got the black one for my black 80GB video iPod. I had to laugh when I (finally) got my iPod into this thing (no easy feat, let me tell you!): it looks like an iPod wearing a piece of an offroad 4x4 tire--which is just fine with me. It also makes me think of something you might see in Doom3 or Halo... totally rugged and "futuristic". This is a sci-fi fan's iPod case. I have not dropped it (yet), so I cannot attest to any protective qualities it may have, but the silicone is very thick and (reassuringly) strong. Do not try this at home, but I am reasonably sure it would bounce around if I dropped it. I removed the beltclip anchor as I would never use it (I cannot imagine myslf hanging a $[...] piece of hardware on my hip attached by a flimsy piece of plastic that reportedly breaks anyway. Nope, my ipod's travel plans will consist strictly of into and out of the briefcase (or jeans pocket). Incidentally, you may be interested to know that I bought this case to replace one of those clear acrylic hinged ones that did nothing for my last iPod when I dropped it (may it rest in pieces). No kidding--my friends, you do NOT want to drop an unprotected iPod, and the form-fitting clear case I had for my last iPod may have protected it from scratches, but it offered zero crash protection. I learned my lesson, and this one should do a nice job of both.

title: Easy plug and play. Excellent audio quality
text: I have had the Topping D10s DAC for about 3 weeks. It has proven to be a high quality DAC . This is my current configuration: PC -> DAC via usb DAC -> headphone amp or AV receiver via RCA cable, or to second DAC via Digital COAX or Optical Toslink The resulting audio is far superior using this DAC, compared with plugging my PC audio out directly into either my headphone amplifier or AV amplifier. When using a DAC, the audio is much cleaner and there seems to be better channel separation. The DAC does not enhance the audio signal at all. There is no high, mid, or low end over amplification. The audio out is the same as the audio in, and that's the way it should be. I have used other DACs and the Topping D10s is a good as the others I highly recommend this product.

title: Excellent headphones for those who know what they're looking for
text: It's "almost" (see my edit below) impossible to find a negative review of the Audio-Technica ATH-M50x Closed Back Headphones. And I have to agree. Probably the best headphones I've ever owned. They've been available now for 10 or so years. You can't get this high end quality audio anywhere else for this price point. I got an excellent deal. The headphone purchase also included 3 high quality extra items for just about the same price as the headphones alone. My package included an extra cable, a solid hard plastic carrying case, and a FiiO A1 headphone amplifier. The headphones live up to all the positive reviews, and the extras included made for a very good total price. I would definitely recommend this product. Updated 2/4/2021, 4 months later. I still love these headphones. I have to laugh when I occasionally check the customer reviews and find that most of the criticisms are based on how these headphones were purposely engineered. Let me be more specific. Some of the negative comments include: -others around you can hear what you're listening to. Oh well. Too bad. They should probably put on their own noise cancelling headphones. Which brings me to my next point: -they're not noise cancelling. Yup, that's right. When I did my search for headphones, I specifically did NOT want noise cancelling OR Bluetooth. Much prefer putting the money saved when not buying these options and putting it toward better cans. -there is no microphone on the cables. Correct again. These headphones were not necessarily intended for those who want a set of cans primarily to support their cell phone addiction. -they must be used with the company's proprietary cables to attach to the headphones. I'll take that and love it. Why? Because they twist and lock into the bottom of the can. How many times, with other headphones, have I moved too far, or stood up or whatever, and the cord would be ripped out of the cans!! -too much bass, not enough base. Midrange too pronounced, or not enough. And they go on and on and on. -the "best" (tongue in cheek) criticism stated that none of the included cables, nor the included adapters fit his computer. I don't know what kind of a computer this person has, but, if Bill Cosby appears in TV commercials for your computer, headphones should not be your #1 focus right now -and finally, and I quote, "I needed to add an EQ to make them sound like I wanted them to". Precisely! These cans were designed and manufactured specifically for those who are looking for an accurate, unadulterated representation of the original recording. The way the musicians and the recording engineers intended it to sound. If one doesn't find that acceptable, and that's fine, include an EQ somewhere in the mix. As a matter of fact, I have more than my share of sound shaping hardware and software all over my system in order to tailor the music to my liking. You need to like the sound quality reproduced through headphones and speaker systems alike. And this is very subjective. One person's likes are another person's hates, especially when it comes from those who love to sound like they "might" know what they are talking about.. I bought and returned a number of headphones because I didn't care for how they sounded. I kept these. I do agree with one common complaint. The earpads do get uncomfortable after a while. I checked for aftermarket replacements, but many included their own negative reviews that they changed the sound quality from the originals. That's the last thing I want.

title: A very nice keyboard with many connection options.
text: Typically I stick to higher end gaming keyboards. Mechanical and optical switches are generally my go to. I had never used a keyboard from this brand before so when I was given the chance to grab one, I figured I would see how it stacks up. So far I'm fairly impressed. I've used some tournament edition keyboards with the smaller form factor from other brands so I knew what I was getting into when it came to the size of the keyboard. All in all, sizing is fine. They key placement and distance between keys works fine. I do run into issues at times where my fingers get lost on the right side of the keyboard. Getting used to that will come in time though. The key response is quick. They are mechanical switches but they do manage to deaden the sound a bit which is nice. The RGB features are basic at best. You have a few settings you can select from and all of it is done directly on the keyboard itself. It has your normal basic modes. It illuminates well though and you can increase/decrease the brightness. The build quality is nice. For being a 75% keyboard, it has some weight to it. I like the fact the keys are labeled for both Mac and PC. I primarily use it on my PC though. The place where it seems to shine is in the connectivity department. I can connect it by bluetooth to numerous devices or I can have it wired. I generally run wired to my main PC and if I need to use it on my MacBook or other devices, I just unplug it from the PC and connect by BT to the other device. It works out nicely. From a gaming standpoint (which I do a lot of), I'm not certain that I like it as much yet. Emphasis on the "yet". I know it takes some time to become accustomed to a new keyboard. The response and feel. I'm going to continue gaming on it for a while to see if I become more adapted to it. It just feels different than what I'm used to. It most likely has to do with the key spacing more so than anything else. This is definitely a nice keyboard and I recommend it. I will most likely continue to use it as my daily keyboard for a while longer to see how it holds up over time.

title: Nice band but could be better
text: I've always leaned more towards this style band and this one is decent. It's definitely worth the price point, however there are some minor issues compared to other bands of this style that I have. The cuts in the metal, particularly on the sides, are not rounded off or smoothed. On my wrist, this makes it feel a little rough at times. It's not something I pay much mind to, but I do notice it occasionally. Other bands of this style, that I have, seem a little more rounded or smoothed out. They feel a bit more comfortable in that regard. The band does fit the watch face perfectly. Installation was a breeze. I did not have to adjust the length of my band so I can't speak to how easy/hard that is. The locking clasp works fine. Again, you can see/feel the difference between this clasp and pricier versions of these bands, but it gets the job done. All in all, this is a decent band that's well worth what it costs. I'd definitely recommend it to someone looking for a replacement band for this watch if they were trying to stay more budget conscious.

title: Works but not for what I was hoping...
text: This product is very easy to use. Setup is simple and in most cases I'm sure it works great. Particularly with remotely playing videos and whatnot. Or using it as a means of a screen share. My intent was a little more involved and I wanted to use it for gaming on my TV from my laptop. Everything was going smooth until I actually attempted to play a game. That's when you notice the deficiency in the product. I had attempted a few different games and the results were the same for all. The video lag was atrocious. The motion blur made games impossible to play effectively. The delay between actions and response on the screen was pretty long. If you're looking for a means to cut out the HDMI wires to a display, and you have no intent of doing anything graphically intense, such as gaming, this product works great. If your intent is to use it for gaming purposes, you may want to stick to wired.

title: Does what I need it to with no issue
text: So I'll first start by saying I've yet to actually plug this into my PC. So I can't review it based on it's connectivity there. I've used other USB hubs and generally they're "okay" at best because you're obviously sharing the full speed of one USB port across multiple ports. The more ports the hub has and devices you have plugged into those ports, the more degradation you're going to see. I prefer USB hubs that also have their own power supply. This one does not. It has a neat little feature where you can turn on/off each port by a switch next to the port. Not entirely sure how useful that would be since typically if you have something plugged in, you'd most likely want it on, but maybe in the case of a webcam or something you may want that ability to just turn it on/off vs unplugging it. I personally use this USB hub more as charging hub. I basically have it plugged into a wall outlet with an adapter just charge multiple devices off of it. Saves me from having multiple wall adapters and power strips. For that purpose I love this hub.

title: Great little watch...but...
text: I love this watch but I do have some issues which usually sway me from wearing it all the time. When I first got it and saw the band style, I knew right off the bat I was probably going to have a couple issues. I was right. These bands (silicone maybe) typically cause my skin to get a rash. Not every watch band like this will but when things cost less, I find it typically does. I like that it continually reads your body metrics so I don't want to take it off. I'll wear it all the time, including in the shower, until the rash starts. Then I have to take it off for a few days. The bands do look replaceable but they don't say what other bands they're compatible with. The other gripe I have with it is the accelerometer (I assume) being used to determine when you raise the watch to look at it. It's spotty at best. Often times I'll raise my wrist to look at the screen and it will not turn on. I will have to turn it on by the button. Other times it will be overly sensitive and turn on whenever it feels like it. Maybe it's just my device but I was really hoping that feature would work better. I like the idea of raising my wrist and the watch face turning on. The app connectivity is nice and the tracking of all your stats is nice. The ability to customize what shows on the main screen as well as changing your watch faces is great as well. It really is a nice watch. If I can find a band that is better, I would wear this thing all the time but I get so irritated by the rash that develops. If you don't have that issue with silicone bands, then by all means, this is a great little watch.

title: Wish it worked better
text: I've had nothing but problems with this extender. I'll first start off by saying I do work in an IT field, so it's not lack of expertise in the area. The device just fails to deliver. I've mainly used it as a repeater in attempts to give a better signal to an outdoor camera but all too often the camera will lose connection to the device. I've tried numerous devices through it and the connection / speeds have always been spotty. Granted I could try running an ethernet cable to the device in attempts to create a better environment for it to succeed in but that was not the intent of it's use from the beginning. All of these devices, including the outdoor camera, maintain better signals and connections to my WiFi router without the extender in the mix. I, personally, would steer clear of this device unless I'm just unlucky and have a poor performing unit.
