title: Amazing flexibility, serious value.
text: I've got some experience with soundbars having been an early adopter in them along with the first generation plasma televisions. The thought then was to hide the wires and hang everything on the wall as if it were art - the modus operandi hasn't changed, it's just improved and become much more affordable. First, the flexibility of this system makes it great for anyone. You can connect the speakers and create a large soundbar you can place on a shelf or hang up on the wall. This is ingenious - it looks great as one piece and you don't have to worry about multiple speakers. Or, you can keep the speakers separate and still either place them on a table or shelf or whatever, or hang them on the wall. So if you prefer the speakers vertical to the left and right of your TV, or if you prefer them horizontal under the TV, you have the freedom to do either with this system. Next are the features. I found the Dialog settings to be superb. With my previous speaker setup I was always adjusting the volume between quiet monologue scenes and action scenes to hear what was being said. This system adjust everything on the fly automatically so you can hear the dialog without making any other changes. I connected it right up to my cable box with HDMI and it was done. No complicated wires to hook up, one and done. The subwoofer included is WIRELESS! That is terrific. I put it behind my seating and it was just perfect. I tested the Bluetooth feature from my phone - I turned on Pandora and beautiful clear music came instantly through the speakers. Nothing to really setup, it was playing tunes in seconds. All in all I'm really happy with this system. With the flexible speaker setup, the great features, and the price so low you can't even buy a subwoofer for that kind of money, it's a no brainer.

title: Excellent Tivo Killer!
text: With features like built-in ethernet networking (no more relying on a phone line!), the ability to send shows to your friends (and receieve shows too! Missed Friends last week? title: Home Made Might Be Better
text: So it’s 2014 and I finally entered the world of touch screen computing and like a good sucker, I dished out $28 for the Kensington Virtuoso Pro Pen 39526 WW (Stylus and Pen combo). It arrived before the computer, but I decided to examine it nonetheless to see what makes a stylus a stylus. First of all, I didn’t like the feel and weight of this item and the pen leaked on my finger. The pen’s tip is a heavy weight metal, which makes it good for writing, but when it’s flipped for screen use, the heaviness is on the top of the stylus (where the pen is) instead of at the bottom. I don’t like that type of imbalance for drawing. I discovered that this item is an overpriced do-hickey that anyone can make at home from practically anything that you have lying around the house. For the how-to video instructions on how to make your own stylus to suit your personal taste and/or needs you can check out the websites that I’ve listed below and/or read the summary that follows. Our smartphone, computer, or tablet’s touch screen senses touch because our fingers produce electrons, hence sending an electrical message to the screen that allows us to write or draw. Therefore to make a stylus, we need something that will behave as a conductor between our finger and the screen. Metal is a conductor. Inexpensive good metal conductors include aluminum, a metal rod (such as an antenna barrel or metal pen), a paper clip, a naked copper wire, or the metal spring that’s inside an old pen. A wet sponge or Q-Tip can also conduct electricity and neither of them scratches the screen. To design a scratch-free stylus, insert a strip of sponge or Q-Tip into a metal casing (such as an old pen or a slender antenna tube that you’ve cut to size). Each should fit tightly into the barrel in order to make a good contact and connection with your finger and the metal casing. Wet the tip of that sponge or Q-Tip and use it on your touch screen. If you don’t have a metal barrel available, you can use a cheap plastic pen. Drill two holes, one on either side of the plastic barrel. If you don’t have a small drill handy, you can burn the holes through the pen using a heated ice pick or paper clip. Insert the sponge (make sure it protrudes through the pen’s tip and that it also makes contact with the holes that you drilled). The final step is to insert a paper clip or a stripped copper wire through the holes and the sponge that you packed into the pen’s barrel. Next, wrap the wire tightly around the pen’s barrel. When you write, make sure your finger(s) touch the wire, which will transmit your electronic touch to the sponge and your tablet’s screen. For the visual instructions, watch the following You Tube videos: Make a stylus with practically any gadget that you have at home or office: [...] [...] Design a fancy one from scratch: [...]

title: Watch the Edges
text: I ordered this USB coupler from Tiny Deal (China) through Amazon on January 20th and it arrvied February 20th. I should have paid careful attention to the edges that are clearly visible in the photo. Evidently a poor design, the edges are raised, appearing like metal burrs. In my opinion that design was unnecessary and potentially dangerous as the edges could have been rolled or not folded at all. Although the reliefs aren't razor sharp, they can still pose a hazard for young hands or for anyone who has pronounced arthritis. When I inserted the male USB cable, it doesn't go all the way into the coupler, but it does appear to make a connection with the electrodes that are inside the unit. However, at this point, I haven't given it a trial run for continuity, since I have purchased numerous cables and connectors to keep in stock rather than for immediate use. In time, I suspect that I'll eventually find a coupler without burrs that will be less hazardous to connect and disconnect.

title: Great Educational Item
text: I believe this microscope may be for teens and older students, but I ordered two of these microscopes as gifts for families with young children, three are age seven, in Puerto Rico and Florida. Last year, I decided to spend my money on true educational "toys" instead of computer games or other ridiculously expensive gadgets for kids. The two scopes went to my siblings, grandparents who spend a lot of time with their grandkids and who would hopefully put them to good use. I also sent them a lab manual and several Golden Book nature books. The microscopes have proven to be such a hit with most of the family, namely three generations who have been collecting leaves and all manner of specimens to view with the children, photograph, and upload to the computers. One seven-year-old is using it to do his school's science presentation. I'm so delighted with their enthusiasm that I'm ordering a third scope for a family in Virginia that home schools there four children who range in age from two to ten. Spring will soon be here and it's the perfect time to enjoy and learn about their environment. By the way, if I had more time, I would love this science tool for myself.

title: A Major Disappointment
text: This product was designed for portability - it's small and takes up little space in a traveler's bag. The compactness is what also contributes to its uselessness. Most devices come with cube shaped plugs or three prong plugs that will overlap the neighboring socket, so instead of having three sockets, you're lucky if you get two. The holes are also so small and tight that it's difficult to insert and remove a plug, especially if you have arthritis as I do. Pulling at a plug on this device will loosen the surge suppressor from the host socket and I fear that I might accidentally electrocute myself. Final analysis: Poorly designed unit that's unfriendly to large or broad adapter plugs.

title: Good for the Price
text: UPDATE (03.20.14): The original review (Nov. 20,2012) is below. A couple of times, I tried to use the radio with the so called back up battery that had been more than charged, but the radio doesn't operate with it. I therefore dropped the rating from 5 stars to 3 because what's the use of having a back-up battery if it isn't going to work? The radio works fine with the AC/DC adapter that costs extra. I haven't tried the crank and have told myself that I will resort to such labor only in an emergency, which I haven't yet had. Also: You get static on the radio if your cordless phone activation is too close to the radio, but any microwave or radio wave (including flourescent lights) affect all radios, not just this one (that's the nature of transmission). ORIGINAL REVIEW: Yes, you do have to buy the AC/DC adapter separately, but if you have a Radio Shack universal adapter, you can use that. I paid $10 for the Kaito one, which is a fair price. I bought six of these little radios for myself, a relative, and friends. We get a good signal in both NYC and Alexandria, VA. I bought the green model from Amazon, which is fine for me because I'm not fashion conscious about most things. After purchasing them, I discovered that Acorn sells them in different colors: red, yellow, etc. I prefer analog to digital because digital electronics has to be reset every time the power drops to zero, so the analog tuner on this radio is perfect for me. I wish the little front knobs were a little larger, but the fact that they are not totally round compensates for the lack of size, especially for people like me, who have arthritis. If you have vision problems though, you might need a magnifying glass or good glasses to read the markings along those front buttons. In summation, I like this radio and all the little connections that come with it for the cellphone or computer tablet.

title: It's a chore to communicate with manufacturer
text: Keyboard keys stuck or did not respond, and manufacturer suggested that I download their new keyboard driver. So, I selected an Asus driver site from the Bing list, and unfortunately ended up at an alleged Norton phisher site and downloaded the alleged driver, which in turn disabled the computer. I called Asus and they reconfigured the computer to the factory setting. The upper cover is rubbery on the outside - perhaps designed as a shock absorber, but it attracts a lot of dust that doesn't wipe off easily. Bottom line, I didn't like this laptop, so I gave it to my brother. Let him deal with downloading a new driver while I stick to my old 2002 Toshiba.

title: Belkin Easy Transfer Does Not Transfer Programs
text: If you're looking for a cable that will transfer your programs as well as your files, this isn't it. I didn't expect it to do that when I bought it, but I hoped that it would. Shame on me, because I bought it without doing the research first. There are two products on the market that will migrate your programs as well as your files: one is Zinstall, which offers two versions, and the better of the two (XP7) is presently on sale - you can view a nice video on their website; the other is LapLink, which has received lukewarm or not so warm reviews. If you have all your old programs on CD's as well as their product keys on hand, however, you might be able to install the programs manually and still use the Belkin Transfer Cable to transfer your files from the old computer. When I tried to manually install my MS Office 2007, which was an upgrade that I could use on up to two computers and for which I had the product key, the Windows 7 on the new computer would not accept it because it couldn't detect a previous copy on the new computer. The new computer came with an incomplete version of MS OFfice 2010, which isn't a PREVIOUS copy, but a more advanced copy, so it appeared that I was out of luck. I solved the problem with Zinstall XP7, which cost me $89 and allowed me to transfer files, settngs, and programs without needing any special cables. With Zinstall, you can use any type of computer cable- DSL, USB, whatever you have available. When the files are transfered, you're actually placing fresh copies of them onto the new computer; the original files remain on the old computer. So, if you plan to toss that old computer or donate it, and don't want anyone to inherit your personal business, you still need to delete those files from the old machine. The Belkin Easy Transfer Cable for Windows 7 allows you to transfer the files from an XP, Vista, or 7 computer to a Windows 7. It comes with a CD that, similar to Znstall, you have to install onto the old computer and the target computer. You then follow very easy steps before you connect the cable. After you're instructed to connect the cable, you do just that and follow a few more steps. Because I used Zinstall, the Belkin software and cable were of no use to me. UPDATE: On Windows Vista, I recently noticed an entry for transferring files and settings in the Control Panel. I haven't tried it, but I mention it in case readers are interested in following that link.

title: Medical Practice Applications
text: This is an Asus Eee Slate EP 121-1A010 update; we've changed the rating from "Like it" to "Love it" and we're adding a couple more to the office. I chose it for a gastroenterologist friend who needed it for her medical practice. Now that patient records need to be digitized, she uses this tablet to keep track of all her business's management needs, which include patient vitals, records, and billing. In the doctor's own words: "I log into Athena, which is our electronic medical record and practice management, and then all the info regarding a patient gets put in. So, the girls will use the tablet to populate BP, pulse, etc, past medical history, chief complaint, etc. Some of it is clicking onto specific fields and it will auto-populate with a touch. I think the ASUS Eee Slate is the perfect size screen by the way. I really like that one. The Acer (an alternate tablet which we tested) is good but, screen is small so it's difficult to maneuver over fields." The doctor had been advised to get a Windows tablet and the ASUS fits the bill. She tried it and an Acer tablet so that she and her staff could get the feel of two different products. The Acer is considerably less expensive, has less memory, and lacks a few features that the Asus has. We had hoped to get tablets with the anticipated Windows 8 that MS announced around March 2011, but by August 8th, the anticipated release date was 2012. Failure to comply with new federal laws for digitized medical records means incurring penalties, so she wanted to have everything by September, hence these two touch tablets seemed to be the best choice as of August 2011. After nearly three months of use, it became clear that the Acer couldn't meet her needs, but the ASUS has been wonderful. The doctor and her staff can download medical templates and macros directly from her provider, Athena Health, onto a main computer or the tablet. While her medical staff handles the initial patient consultations, the info can be transfered to or from a tablet into the office's mainframe computer, athenahealth.com, and to the doctor's own tablet via e-file or e-mail. They no longer need to transcribe handwritten information into the office's computer; it can now be done on the spot, saving time. The tablets can also be used to read Kindle books. The ASUS has the added advantage of a wireless Bluetooth keyboard and a digital pen, which I believe can be an asset for anything that requires a signature, e.g. a prescription or an MS Office Word business letter. It also interfaces well with a wireless printer, but it does have USB ports. The ASUS also comes with a mediocre MS Office program that can be upgraded for a better version. My initial favorites were the Apple iPad2 or a Toshiba tablet. However, neither of them comes with a Windows operating system (OS). Toshiba uses Google's Android (aka Droid) and Apple uses its own system. While you can change Toshiba's OS to a Windows OS, I wouldn't recommend it if you're not technically savvy.

text: After about 24 hours of apparently normal use, it started freaking out. It uninstalls our clock faces and the ECG app. When we re-install them, they work fine for about two minutes, then disappear. In the Fitbit app, it gives us the option to re-install them, but only after showing a screen saying that there is no internet access (this house has almost a dozen other wireless devices that do not suffer this problem). We will be returning this cursed thing at the earliest opportunity. 0/5, would not recommend.

title: Received used item instead. Stopped working in three weeks. Replacement Stopped Working.
text: Took a coffee break and left the computer idle. When I returned fifteen minutes later, the monitor no longer worked. It's been in use for about three weeks, and now reports that it has no signal. Windows can see when the monitor is plugged in, but the monitor still reports no signal. Plugging in other monitors which continue to work proves that the problem is not the graphics card or ports. To say I'm disappointed is a massive understatement. I'll be asking for a refund as soon as I finish posting this review :-( [Edited to add] I've received a replacement for the broken monitor, and it was immediately obvious that the monitor they sent me the first time had been used and returned. The tape on this box was new, the interior packaging was different, and there were items in the replacement such as decals and the like that were not present in the first one. Shame on you for selling me used equipment as new :-( [SECOND EDIT] The replacement stopped working three months to the day after I started using it. It would appear that the problem wasn't one bad used device, as I'm fairly confident the replacement was new. It seems like this line of monitors is just garbage unfortunately, and that malfunctions are common. I'm so extremely disappointed.

title: Wheel Tilt functionality is too sensitive, only works for about 8 months before breaking.
text: This trackball is a bit small for my hands, and it is difficult to use the "middle mouse click" functionality, but other than that I quite like this trackball. Clicking the scroll wheel is a quite common user action these days, so I'm quite surprised that it's so difficult to do with this mouse without unwanted scrolling in the process ("Wheel tilt" is too sensitive). I regularly use programs like 3DS Max where the middle mouse button is an absolutely integral part of the functionality. Even in the web browser, where clicking the scroll wheel will open a link in a new tab, or clicking the scroll wheel on a tab will close that tab, I'm constantly being faced with this irritating limitation. {EDIT] This trackball started acting wonky about six months in, and become almost unusable by eight months. It finally became completely unusable at almost exactly eleven months after purchase.

title: Didn't even last nine months
text: After approximately nine months of light usage (it mostly just sits on my desk until I need it to test software, which takes ten minutes then it goes back on the desk) it simply refuses to turn back on. There are all kinds of complaints that I have about this device, but none are more indicative of the quality of this piece of garbage than the fact that it broke after nine months of very light usage.

title: Works great on PC, completely useless on Surface RT
text: This sweet little USB Ethernet adapter gets five stars for working like a champ on my PC, even though my PC already has a built-in Ethernet adapter. If you are looking at this item because of the many articles out there suggesting that it works on the Surface RT, however, save your money. It's completely useless on the Surface RT, and will not work. There are no "official" drivers available for it, and even the ones that several sites have made available for download will not work because they are not MS-certified and therefore Microsoft won't allow them to run on the Surface RT. I wish I had known this before spending money on it, since I have absolutely no other use for it. Can't knock the product though, it appears to work quite well for any other purpose.

title: Possibly the worst tablet ever made
text: I've been a professional software developer for more than twenty years, and in that time I've used a very large variety of computing devices for both personal and professional use. I don't think I've ever hated a computing device more than I hate this abomination. Actually, I can't remember actually hating any device prior to this. The touch-screen is terrible and inconsistent, and I frequently need to tap things multiple times in order to get a response. Windows 8 might be okay if it weren't so completely locked down on the Surface RT. For instance, you cannot install any other browser; you're stuck with Internet Explorer, the worst browser available on any device, and cannot even install plugins to block spam ads and malware. The web browsing experience is truly terrible, and the design of the browser is sufficiently different from *every other browser* to make it as counter-intuitive as possible. There is almost no software that will run on the device except what can be obtained through Microsoft's online store, which is a fresh hell that deserves it's own product review. At least with my Android devices I have broad compatibility and a wide variety of software available for just about every purpose. The on-screen touch keyboard is clunky and poorly designed, and is at times incredibly difficult to use. For instance, trying to compile an email in GMail is pathologically difficult, since the keyboard takes up literally 75% of the screen, leaving almost no space to see what you're typing and making it incredibly difficult to scroll down to the "Send" button to actually send the email. There appears to be no support for swapping the built-in touch-screen keyboard with a better version like Swype, which is incredibly disappointing. Attempting to connect USB devices is extremely hit or miss, and many I've tried simply do not work due to lack of "official" driver support. For instance, I purchased a "Belkin F4U047-RS USB 2.0 Ethernet Adapter" on the advice of several websites saying that they'd been able to use that specific adapter to add an Ethernet adapter to the Surface RT. Unfortunately, Microsoft has asked those websites to no longer distribute the drivers that made the device work, and have disabled the use of such drivers on the Surface RT since they are not Microsoft certified drivers, leaving me with no Ethernet and twenty dollars wasted. I could go on for several more paragraphs, but I've wasted enough of my life on this piece of offal. If I didn't require this device to be physically present to test software builds on, I would have sent it back almost immediately.

So far they work really well in these gadgets and the charger surprisingly charges them faster than I thought. Definitely worth the money because they last much longer than the non rechargeable disposable batteries and better for the environment. As for fit they seem to fit fine in everything so far without any problems which is really nice especially on expensive devices. I can tell you that they get a little warmer in the charger than I am comfortable with which concerns me. Because from personal experience fast charging getting batteries hot is not good for any rechargeable batteries it runis them plus its not safe I wish they had a slow or low charging setting. I can honestly say these easily out perform the Rayovac, Energizer, and Duracell rechargable batteries that discarge quickly saving you money and headaches. For just normal homeowners use for remote controls and around the household these should work perfectly fine. I have bought other batteries from EBL off Amazon and absolutely love them. I will have to keep taking notes on discharge, charging, and start measuring voltage on these to see how consistent they are and update this review. Stay tuned. Truthfully the only reason why I bought these is they do not offer the red EBL 1.5v AA Li-Ion rechargeable 3000mWh batteries in any quantity greater than four with a charger on Amazon which is why for value for my money I only rate the "value for the money" partpurchase at 3 stars. EBL needs to make those available here just like these batteries why they do not is a mystery to me. If you need an honest to goodness AA 1.5v battery for something sensitive to voltage read my review on those batteries they sell.

title: Vast improvement over previous model
text: I am impressed with the improvements in this newer model. The headband is softer, more bendable and comfortable. They now include a sizing band that holds it against your head (like a ring sizer). Slightly better battery life too. And they have added a little padding where the vibrators hit near your ears. The controls are still really user-friendly even while wearing it. As always, it is easy to load/change music. What hasn't improved? Well it still digs in a little at the sides. And the battery life is still not as great as the competition. I miss the bright yellow color of my old one. Hard to see/find in my bag. The carrying case is not useful for watersport equipment. It shouldn't get wet. Which is dumb for a swimming headset. It is just as heavy as before.

title: Love these more than I expected to!
text: Pros: It is hard to find a really good swimming headset. This is it. (I have tried many other types, and this is the winner for me.) SO easy to charge. So easy to load music. Allows for folders (my other headphones don't). Weighs NOTHING. You don't know you have it on! Doesn't press to hard or hurt anywhere. A lot of bone conduction headsets are uncomfortable but this one is not. Has a huge battery life. Also it TELLS you every time you turn it on how much battery is left. (If you want to check after you are done, turn it off and on again and it will tell you.) Controls make sense. Mostly. A few features require long push and hold to activate, but the stuff you use daily is intuitive. Volume is good. Not super loud, but also you can adjust the placement around your ear to be louder/softer. Cons: The band is longer than I need. So there is a gap at the back of my head. I wish it were a little smaller. The buttons are a little fidgety. They are so small and all feel alike so it takes a while to feel your way around and figure out which button is which. I wish they would put the power and mode buttons on one side and the Plus/minus buttons on the other ear. Or put the plus minus on the outside rather than under edge. That said, I put my 400 songs on it and just let it play while I workout. This one is petty but there are 2 modes - water and regular. It changes the EQ to supposedly sound better underwater vs. on land. But I find the on land mode sounds better in water. BUT I don't use earplugs. So maybe that is why.

title: Fits fantastically. Only get the clear version though if you have a light-up Mac keyboard
text: I prefer these keyboard covers to others because they really fit better and are easy to type on. They hug the sides of the keys and don't slide. They also don't get all oily underneath like the cheap ones. However I ONLY get the clear version for keyboards where the letters light up. (like my macbook) The colorful ones not only don't let the light through properly, but they are hard to read. (see Photos 1 and 2) The light only shines through the letters and the only clear part of the color covers is the letters - so unless they line up perfectly, it doesn't work. With the clear ones it is no problem! Now fair warning - the clear ones are not crystal clear. The keys will not look shiny black. They will look matte and slightly greyed. (See Photo 3) But they are perfectly easy to read. And you can see how much dust and dirt is already on mine after 2 days - it is totally worth it to protect your laptop!!!

title: Gorgeous color. Works well. Sturdy. Great venting. Feet can't fall off. LASTS.
text: I have had mine nearly a year. I love it. Best case I have ever had. (EDIT: going on 2 years now and I STILL love it. I am really pretty rough with my laptop and it gets abused regularly. But the case is going strong) Pros: Gorgeous teal color (not plain blue). Works well. Provides ample corner protection, which I need. (see Photo 1) Once you get it on properly, it stays put. The 4 feet can't fall off because they aren't separate pieces stuck on like most cases. The venting is fantastic. In addition to the bottom vents, the way top and bottom meet in the back allows for full venting open or closed. This is rare. But it still manages to protect the back corners well. It's a fairly clever design. (see photo 2). I like the way the kickstands gently lock in place when open. Also the case is not heavy or bulky but is very protective. Cons: The biggest problem is that in order to take it off you pretty much have to break it. If you have a reason to need to take the case off and on again this is not for you. If you want it to never come off, this is great. It is also very (physically) hard to get on. The last clip just wouldn't clip (and I have a lot of experience with laptop covers). So I had to take it off and start over (doing the problem clip first). Even partially on, the thing did NOT want to come off! It was quite a challenge. Plus the instruction sheet is translated into such poor English it makes no sense. The two clips on either side of the trackpad might scrape your wrists a little, depending on your angle. (see Photo 3) Luckily the angle of my wrists misses the tabs and I have never had a problem. Most people wouldn't have an issue. As to how it holds up: I don't use the little tabs underneath that tilt the keyboard up. But they haven't broken off. I needlessly worried about the little bits that protect the back corners on the bottom cover. (See photo 4). They also remain unbroken. (EDIT: STILL unbroken after 2 years including dropping it) A tiny portion on one of the many tabs holding the case did break off. (EDIT: 2 years in and I am now missing 3 of the tabs. STILL doesn't change the effectiveness at all) There is one tiny crack in the case near the bottom right of the keyboard. I think it actually happened putting it on in the first place. (Or rather when I had to pry it off to start over.) However it is very small and in a place where there are two layers. And the bottom layer has no crack. Therefore it can't really spread or get worse. And again, it doesn't affect anything. (EDIT: 2 years in and the crack has not worsened and case is still secure) I may need to buy a replacement because it's a work laptop and we have to turn it in once a year for maintenance. They will destroy the cover when they remove it. (EDIT: they didn't take the case off so yay! That is how I am on my 2nd year. If I ever need to buy a new one I am getting the same case. I love this case)

title: Not perfect. Love them anyway.
text: I have had these for a year now and use them daily for watching TV, so I can say I have given them an exhaustive workout. I love them, and can't imagine how I lived without them. BUT they do have their issues. Pros: They recharge easily and hold the charge for many hours. I have used them for 8+ hours straight without having to recharge. They are comfortable and cushioned, and adjust for my son's Charlie Brown-like huge head and my small one. They are comfortable when worn over just one ear (If I have to keep the other ear free to hear sound in the room) They are in range even outside the house, so I can use while gardening, going to the laundry room, cleaning the garage... The sound is clear. The recharge station is compact and effortless. Easily cleanable Cons: They slip off your head if you lean forward. If they don't receive audio signal for a few minutes, such as when a show is paused, they play painfully loud static If the volume is loud, others around you can hear. When there is only a low sound signal, such as a very quiet moment in a film, or when you pause, you can hear a pulsing sort of hissing noise. Like any wireless system, you need to be 5 feet away from the base for it to work properly. Anyone needing to be closer can use wired headphones anyway. When you turn them on, they take a couple seconds to connect. So you don't get sound instantly. It isn't easy to have multiple pairs so people can share. Charge station can only charge one. You either have to set up 2 separate units or take turns charging multiple headsets. I wish there were a way to daisy chain the sound output or there were more room on the charging rack.

The previous tenant obviously didn't care about anything and let an incredible amount of stuff get down in the cracks. I cleaned as much as I could without pulling out the stove which is beyond what this elderly handicapped woman can do. And this product fits nice and looks just fine for my purposes. It is really flexible. Even in this freezing apartment with an unheated kitchen it is really flexible. It is a little longer than I need, probably because the stove is not as close to the wall as it should be. Although this would be quite easy to cut, I am sure, I don't want to cut it as I may have a decent kitchen someday where I can use the length. All plastic and vinyl things are stiff in this place, but this silicone is really great.Not sure if the other will fit on the other side where the gap is narrower but since I don't often cook on that side it won't be a problem if it cannot get it in the space. I have previously had a hard white plastic strip which melted and then I had white (vinyl maybe?) strips I lost in a move. They didn't melt but they did get yellowish. I think these are an improvement on both. Would definitely buy again.

text: This is a decently made caddy, aluminum not all plastic like one I had purchased for an older Dell (never worked but too cheap to send back). Two issues for my particular hardware, the Satellite and a OCZ Agility. First there is a small bracket in my laptop that secures the optical housing to the machine with one screw underneath the memory bay. There are two screws from the laptop of adequate length to reach the original equipment optical housing though this bracket. These screws cannot reach down to the thread portion located deeper inside this caddy. Although I have probably hundreds of screws, none were both long enough and thin enough to get through the holes in the Satellite's hold down bracket to the caddy. I ended up using electrical tape to secure the bracket to the caddy. I think it will be fine. Second, the Agility did not appear in the bios or in windows when laptop was booted. After much messing around with other drives in the caddy I finally realized that the Agility was not shoving up tight enough to the connectors. I had to push it from behind with a thick screwdriver. Success. A Vertex was not a problem nor was the mechanical drive. Just the Agility. I believe it is just a problem with this drive, probably connector board a little off but not noticeable when regular SATA and power cables are applied to it. Last is I guess a non-issue from function but not from form. The bezel or lack thereof. Yes, it will look a little funny without a bezel. I had quite the time removing the Satellite's bezel from the optical drive but did manage it in the end. And I can still pop the optical in when needed (like when I was troubleshooting) and run it without its bezel in a pinch. YMMV Overall OK certainly for the price. They might want to look into how deep those threads are where a hold down bracket is applied. My mfr screws certainly were not long enough. Would be nice if they could supply two in addition to the HD screws they already do. And the lack of even some sort of generic-ish bezel were the only reasons for the one star off.

"Quick" shoe isn't that quick as you have to find a coin or screwdriver to attach it to your camera. 2. It's not easy to use if you have small hands - it isn't physically possible for me to use the Grip Position Release System with one hand. 3. The trigger action is very stiff and makes my hands tired very quickly 4. Adds significantly to the weight of the tripod I use this mostly for motor sports events and panoramas because of the smooth panning action, where I don't need to move around much or pull the trigger very often. This would probably work a lot better in the hands of a stronger person with bigger hands. Amanda Richards, October 17, 2013

title: Strong enough for a man, but doesn't understand women.
text: Pros: 1. The 102 is small enough for everyday toting - great size for everyday working folk who always keep their camera close at hand. 2. Enough space in the main compartment for a DSLR with medium telephoto/standard zoom lens attached, plus an off camera flash and one more lens. 3. Easy zippers allow quick access to the camera, and support straps keep it secure. 4. Comes with an all weather cover neatly tucked away in a pocket and a built in microfiber cloth. 5. Two external compartments and a pocket for small accessories. Handy memory card pockets in main compartment. 6. Includes a tripod holder and strap 7. Nicely padded with customizable dividers Cons: 1. The 102 is a lot smaller than it looks on-line. A Nikon SB900 flash can't stand upright as illustrated, but has to be pivoted over the DSLR compartment. 2. The upper compartment can't hold a change of clothes, or anything other than small accessories, keys, a wallet and a couple of calling cards. It can hold filters, a small lens or a point and shoot camera. 3. Can only hold compact tripods or monopods, and even then, it becomes unwieldy. 4. If you sling the strap over one shoulder, the bag isn't balanced and keeps slipping off your shoulder, especially if you're doing anything with your other hand. 5. If you sling it over your head and across your back as illustrated, it's stable, but not comfortable for the female anatomy, and certainly not aesthetically pleasing for frontal views. 6. If you use the additional support strap, it doesn't fit around your waist as it should, but across your chest, hence even more problems for female photographers with curves. 7. No place for water bottle, no cell phone pouch on strap I bought this to use for everyday toting of my DSLR. Size wise it works for this purpose, but is not comfortable to walk around with. It's not big enough for travel or comfortable enough for nature shoots, or weddings, or suitable for anywhere you'll need extra gear, water or clothes. Definitely not for a theme park or hiking expedition. I would recommend this to male urban or street photographers (or non-zaftig female photographers). Amanda Richards July 22, 2013

title: For those times when you need a little something to steady yourself
text: First and foremost, this is a monopod, and should not be expected to perform the duties of a tripod. The two are not on the same playing field, especially if said field is not level, and the monopod's job is simply to hold the fort when a tripod can't go into battle. Pros: 1. This monopod comes with its own little stand, and is perfectly capable of standing on its own three feet. 2. It can easily support a DSLR with a medium telephoto lens. 3. Set up is simple, requiring only unscrewing the bottom section, opening the legs and screwing the base back on securely. 4. Extends over six feet tall with two adjustable sections 5. Perfect for concert and theatre events in low or changing light, when a tripod either isn't allowed or is impractical. 6. Great for weddings and museum visits 7. You can sit with the monopod braced against your chair and your feet anchoring the legs for extra stability. (I also use a cable release) 8. Padded grip 9. Handy against attacks by stray animals in the wild. Cons: 1. At the shortest it's still more than two feet long, and doesn't fit well in the external tripod section of smaller camera bags. 2. It's very heavy for all-day trekking around theme parks, museums, big city tours and the like. 3. No carrying case (but has a strap to fasten it on to stuff) 4. Little legs make a lot of noise when concealed (but see below) 5. A bit tricky on uneven ground if you want to use the legs Things you can fix: 1. Needs a Quick Release head (albeit adding extra weight and cost) 2. Rattling feet can be muffled with a rubber band Overall, I'm happy with this monopod, except perhaps for the length and weight. It does a great job when you're rushing around in crowded places where tripods fear to tread. Amanda Richards, June 19, 2013

title: Great for walkabouts
text: Point of View: Hobby/Amateur Cameras: Nikon D7000/D600 I would not have purchased this lens if it hadn't come with the D600 as a kit lens, but I am SO glad that Nikon knows best. As a medium telephoto zoom lens, I use it on the D600 most of the time for capturing landscapes and street photography. At 24mm it's wide enough to capture everything from foreground elements to distant landmarks, and at f/3.5 it's fast enough to get the wedding party in a church (if the lights aren't too dim) without using a flash. When it comes to festivals and carnivals, I use this on the D600 for the big picture, and a 50mm f/1.8 on the D7000 for street portraits. It is light and unobtrusive enough to take into crowded places for extended periods, something I would never do with a 70-200mm f/2.8. What it's not good at is wildlife photography and sports photography, but there are other lenses for those purposes. The only thing I don't like is the lens hood, which when inverted over the lens completely blocks the zoom ring. It also gets in the way when you're trying to remove the lens from the camera. If I don't need to use the hood, it's easier to take it off completely than keep it on-camera. Overall, a compact, convenient and affordable lens for general purpose and vacation photography. Note: Uses a 72mm screw-on filter Amanda Richards, February 3, 2013

title: A cinch for a strap
text: Pros: 1. Easy to set up - no tools required. Just attach the stainless steel/aluminum mount to the tripod socket at the bottom of the camera and tighten the thumbscrew. (And recheck ever so often that it's tightened) 2. Fits a lot more comfortably than a regular neck strap. All DSLRs should come with this type of strap. No neck burn or awkward carrying positions. 3. Can be tightened against the body by pulling on the pivot ring and camera (in opposite directions) for when you need to go hands free across some difficult terrain (or when your hands are otherwise occupied) 4. Can be worn on either shoulder or even behind your back as needed. 5. There's a locking mechanism to hold the strap in place when you're not shooting. 6. Strap adjusts itself and extends when you raise the camera to take a shot (when the locking mechanism is disengaged of course) 7. This strap is built for a man, (the women's strap has a small curve for the zaftig photographer) but it's still comfortable (and strong enough) regardless. Cons: 1. Dangling an expensive camera and even more expensive lens upside down, from ONE screw, in ONE spot, on the bottom of the camera, is a bit nerve-wracking. (But regular straps can malfunction also) 2. Strap could have been improved with a bit more padding. 3. Strap takes up quite a bit of space in a camera bag (but you can't have everything) For smaller bags you can detach the strap and reattach when needed in a couple of seconds. 4. Obviously you have to detach the strap when you want to use a tripod 5. No fault of the strap, but the models in the video on the product page need some instruction on how to hold a DSLR properly (LOL) Overall, this has solved a big problem for me, as this is a much more comfortable way to carry around a heavy camera and lens for hours at a time. Amanda Richards, January 8, 2013 Note: I recently bought the women's version of this strap. The only difference is that the strap is a little bit narrower at the top, and has a clever little bend for negotiating feminine curves.

title: Best bokeh for your buck
text: I bought this because when you can't afford Nikon glass, you choose Sigma. One of three (arguably) most recommended wedding lenses, the others being a 50mm f/1.4 or f/1.8 prime and a 24-70 f/2.8, my experience with this is creamy dreamy soft backgrounds with perfectly focused subjects. Please note that this is an amateur point of view, and I shoot weddings when the bride or groom asks whether I'm going to walk with my camera, because the camera takes really good pictures. I love it for details like the decorations, cake and candles, for far off shots of the ceremony without getting in the way, and for those cool shots where the bride/groom is in focus and the groom/bride beside her/him is out of focus (but very recognizable) What I don't like is the weight (but I can suck that up) and that you can't work the group shots without changing the lens (until I get a second camera) unless you're standing way back, which isn't always possible. I also love it for portraits, especially of toddlers, and will be trying it next at a field hockey game, as I understand it to be aces at sports. I bought the [[ASIN:B000CDA7Y4 Sigma APO Teleconverter 2x EX DG for Nikon Mount Lenses]] which works fine with this lens, and plan to go stalking hummingbirds as soon as they discover my [[ASIN:B0019Y0YCA Aspects 153 Mini Hummzinger Hummingbird Feeder]]. If you need to shoot in low light, and prefer ambience instead of the brightness of flash, this fast lens and some ISO pumping can really do the job. (Note: I'm currently using a Nikon D7000 and hope to upgrade to a full frame in the near future) Amanda Richards, January 2, 2013

title: Sound boost for your computer
text: Pros: 1. It's a Bose 2. Relatively easy to set up even for a non-technical person 3. As would be expected, great sound 4. I didn't expect the ear buds to be comfortable with that funny looking rubbery plastic thingy that fits into your outer ear, but I was wrong (using the smallest size - it comes with three sizes) Plus, they don't fall out of your ears if you make sudden movements. 5. Control for volume and the audio jack are on the same speaker, so easily kept within reach 6. Sleek modern look 7. Not designed for noise reduction, so you can still be aware of what's going on around you. Cons: 1. No "off" position - the volume can only be turned down, but not off 2. Speakers are a little on the large side if you're limited for space on your desk - just over 7" tall, 3" wide and just about 6" deep 3. Ear bud case is nice, padded and zippered, with Bose logo, but is too big to fit in your pocket. My iPhone actually fits comfortably inside the case. 4. Ear bud packaging requires a chainsaw and jaws of life to open Overall, a good acquisition for me as my computer speakers went kaput some time ago, and this is way better. Amanda Richards, January 1, 2013

title: A lot of bag to like
text: Pros: 1. Light 2. Durable 3. Well thought out and constructed, aesthetically pleasing 4. Back mesh prevents overheating against your body 5. Adjustable straps around the chest and waist for extra support and portability 6. Can hold a DSLR with a 70-200 lens attached, plus 3 or 4 more lenses in the bottom compartment. 7. Three way access to the bottom compartment, plus customizable padding makes it easily adaptable 8. Padded lap top sleeve holds a 15" laptop 9. Top compartment and side pockets hold tons of extra gear such as memory cards, spare batteries, filters, remotes, lens cloths et al, plus a change of clothes and other personal stuff 10. Comes with a rain hood that covers the bag and your gear in inclement weather 11. Can fit on airplanes for travel 12. Bright orange interior makes it easy to find gear in a hurry Cons: 1. Holds so much stuff that you tend to overpack, and THAT's when it weighs a ton 2. 9.6 x 8.1 x 16.5 inches sounds much smaller than it actually is. This bag is pretty big, but then of course it holds lots of stuff. Too big for everyday toting, but fine for photo shoots. 3. No compartment on strap for cell phone - not essential, but really handy 4. One external strap can possibly hold a tripod, but not very securely. 5. No water bottle pocket, but I guess you can attach one with a carabiner 6. Nice canvas zipper pulls, but I can see the pull tab breaking off from the slider, as that part is pretty thin. I wouldn't recommend grabbing the bag by the zipper pulls (if that's all you can reach without getting up.) This is now the biggest camera bag of the three that I own, and probably the one I will be using for travel in the future. Amanda Richards, January 1, 2013

title: Unsafe text
text: The look of this is very cool Retro-chic and so old-school Great for teacher/boss misleading "Wow! She made notes - and she's reading!!" The problem with the Verso Trends Is that the cover twists and bends Because it's mostly pliant plastic With corner straps made of elastic If by chance it takes a fall There's no protection there at all Without a strap to keep it shut Your Kindle may just go kaput In short, this cover's just for looks To stash your Kindle with your books A talking point, I will admit But otherwise, it's just a nostalgic gimmick that's really cute, but not terribly durable*. *(Not the last line you were expecting) Amanda Richards, December 27, 2012

title: Great for storage, tough to tote
text: This external hard drive is very easy to install and use, with no additional software required. Just plug in and you're ready to start using it. For those who may need it, a very brief Quick Start Guide is included in the box. I have been using this drive to supplement the meager 160GB on my aging laptop to store my ever-growing photo, music and video collections. When I bought the laptop, even 1 TB was unheard of, but in this digital age, 2TB of storage is never too much. Of course, as was mentioned by another reviewer, (and which I think is very good advice,) you should always keep at least two copies of your important files on different drives in case of hardware failure. This drive has a large enough capacity to back up the computers in my household for now. I would not use this drive as a portable device as mentioned in the product description. The product is described as a Desktop external drive, and in my opinion it is too bulky to carry around in addition to a power supply cord, since it uses external power. There are smaller external drives, albeit with less storage capacity, that are better designed for portability. Users should note that even though it might be plugged into a power outlet, it only powers up when it is connected to a computer. Once disconnected, or if the computer is shut down, the drive powers off. Amanda Richards, November 10, 2012

title: Like a bug in a rug
text: The problem with My Passport is It comes without a case And toting it with all my stuff Gets scratches on the face My Passport doesn't seem to mind It handles wear and tear But I prefer to treat my stuff With tender, loving care The cable's in the mesh pocket I think I got that right My Passport goes under the strap This holds it nice and tight The case seems rather sturdy But the pull tab's kind of "iffy" The loop looks rather scrawny Like it'll break off in a jiffy For now My Passport's safe and sound In its faux leather house Asleep in Lycra bedding Like a rug-snug bug or mouse Amanda Richards, May 26, 2012

title: iStorage
text: Anyone who doesn't own an iPod or iPad probably won't see the utility of this device. However, for those who know the limitations of a 16GB iDevice, this can come in very handy to extend your storage. One caveat is that given the cost of the Airstash at the time of writing, if you haven't yet taken the iPlunge, it might be better to go with the 64GB iPad 3 or 2 in the first place. However, if you already own the 16GB, then getting this device becomes an economical option. The tech specs are covered in the product description, so below are some of my observations based on my experiences using the Airstash with an iPad 2. Once the Airstash is powered up (by holding down the power button until the green indicator light turns on, then releasing it to see the light flash rapidly three times), you can connect your device to it wirelessly. However, in order to take full advantage of the Airstash, you will need to install the Airstash+ app which you can download from the Apple AppStore for free. This app allows you to access the files that you have copied to the Airstash. Alternatively, you can use a browser and browse to airstash.net for the same functionality. While it may look like a flash drive on steroids, and works in a similar fashion when you plug it into your computer's USB port, I found it was not as straight-forward a matter when being used to save files. Accessing the files you have placed there is simple enough, but in order to save stuff to it using your iPad/iPod, your app needs to be WebDAV compatible. The Quick Start Guide supplied with the device briefly mentions that once connected you `launch the WebDAV compatible app of your choice'. Now, if you're like me, then you probably have no idea what this means. What I've discovered is that WebDAV is some kind of `format/protocol' that allows you to save your files to the Airstash. The problem is, not all apps are WebDAV compatible. Apple's Pages, Numbers and Keynote are, but QuickOffice isn't. So if you're a Microsoft Office user like I am, accustomed to QuickOffice, then this device might not be for you. You can read your Office files from the Airstash, but you wouldn't be able to edit them and save them back to the device. Other observations... Without installing additional software/apps, mp4 (movie) files on the Airstash played easily on my iPad, but not avi files. (I didn't try digital movies but the product description says that you can play movies loaded on it on your device.) I couldn't figure out how to save stuff directly onto it that I had downloaded to my iPad, like apps, attachments, books, etc. Maybe there is an easier way, but I had to sync my iPad with my computer first, then copy the files over to the Airstash from the computer. The iPad could open epub books (in iBooks) and pdf files saved on the Airstash. Presumably there shouldn't be any problems with music and photo files, but I didn't test these either. It took about 8 minutes to transfer 366MB from my (old) laptop to the Airstash using USB 1.0. With newer computers this should be faster. Some pros, some cons - consider this is you have an iDevice that needs more storage space. Amanda Richards April 20, 2012

title: Fast and furious
text: This is an ideal memory card for amateur photographers who typically take more than 400 photos on a regular photo shoot whether enjoying nature's bounty or just covering the good old family reunion. Professional photographers would generally step up to the 32GB cards, but for the serious hobbyist, this will do just fine. This card will hold more than 4,000 JPEG images at approx 3 MB each, or about 960 RAW images at around 14MB, so there's lots of room for you to take repeated shots of Uncle Carl and Cousin Luke until they get their smiles in sync, or keep shooting that beautiful sunset until the green flash. I have used two of these in a Nikon D7000 for almost a year without a problem or a lost photo. The 10 speed means that you can shoot continuous sequences without delays, so you'll never miss the kiss after the cake is cut, or the cute moment on the swing as your child soars in the air. Two tips to note are that your memory card will last longer and perform better if you delete your photos using the computer after you've saved them, rather than trashing them one by one through the camera. Secondly, format your cards through the camera before each new shoot so you start off fresh and clear each time. It's also recommended to change your cards after a reasonable period of use, so keep the page bookmarked. Highly recommended for serious hobby or amateur photographers. Amanda Richards, April 19, 2012

title: Going the distance
text: This is my current go-to lens. I wish I could afford one of the more fancy-schmancy professional telephotos, but until then, this one is the one parked on my Nikon D7000. Uses: 1. Birds, bugs and other critters from a safe distance or on the fly/run 2. Portraits of one or two people (gives excellent bokeh) 3. Landscapes and seascapes, especially in vertical/portrait mode. Limitations: 1. Buildings from across-the-street distance 2. Large groups of people 3. Macro shots from thisclose Depending on the type of photography you enjoy, this may or may not be the lens for you. It works fine for me for the uses above, especially when the subjects are a respectable distance away, but it doesn't have a wide enough angle for limitations 1 and 2, and if you're closer than a couple of feet it won't focus properly. It's also pretty heavy, but makes up for this by making you look like a pro who knows what they're about, especially when you use the lens hood (included and highly recommended for use) The auto-focus is not as smooth as it should be, and you can sometimes hear the mechanism moving around trying to do its job, but image stabilization and the tripod detection mode are huge pluses. (It also attaches/detaches from the camera in the opposite direction to my other (Sigma) lens) For the type of photography I'm doing at the moment. even if it's not on the camera, this lens goes with me wherever I roam. Amanda Richards, March 30, 2012

title: Must-have for GP3 Gorillapod
text: This ball head is a must-have if you're considering using a Gorillapod. Mine is attached to the GP3, but apparently it can be used with most tripods. Pros: 1. Convenient. An easy way to get shots requiring portrait formats or odd angles. Pans 360 degrees and tilts 90 degrees. 2. Quick release clip allows you to get the camera on and off quickly. 3. Looks sturdy, and holds the camera securely with an adjustment knob. 4. The clip comes with a bubble level Cons: 1. Attaching the quick release clip to the camera is a bit of a pain, requiring a coin (any currency) or a strong fingernail. Better to attach the clip to your camera beforehand, and just leave it on the camera. 2. The quick release requires pulling a knob at the front while sliding the clip out of the groove. Maybe a spring release would have been better. Strongly recommended for Gorillapod users. Amanda Richards, January 10, 2012

title: For monkeying around
text: This weird little tripod is a useful addition to the gear of any amateur or hobby photographer with a DSLR and the inspiration to take breath-taking and/or unusual photographs. (I'm using it with a Nikon D7000) Pros: 1. Light and portable. If you don't have a side pocket on your camera bag, just wrap it around a strap or loop. 2. Flexible. As advertised, the legs can be bent into loops and angles for getting shots from weird angles. It can also be wrapped around posts, tree branches, bench rails etc. 3. Convenient. An easy way to get shots requiring a stable camera almost level with ledges or sideways attached to a tree. However, you can only shoot in landscape format unless you get the accessory BH1 ball head. Naturally, with its little legs, you'll be pretty close to the ground if there's nothing available for wrapping around, but you'll be sure to get great camera angles from a worm's eye view. Cons: 1. Attaching your camera to the tripod is a bit of a pain, requiring a coin (any currency) or a strong fingernail. A better bet is to get the accessory Joby BH1 Ball Head with Bubble Level and attach the quick release clip to your camera beforehand. 2. You need to practice with it a bit to get the stability right, and if you have the legs in an unbalanced position, or on a smooth surface, you can get sagging and camera movement. 3. Trying to get the camera level without the ball head can be quite challenging, and you may well miss the shot. (Of course you can always do the straightening with software, but it's better to get it right the first time.) 4. Can't shoot in portrait format unless you get the ball head. 5. Hard to get the legs back straight with all the segments in line. Note: It comes with a 1/4-to-3/8-inch adapter attached to the mounting screw, so you have to remove this to attach the camera or accessory ball head. Recommended (with the [[ASIN:B002CVU4G0 Joby BH1 Ball Head with Bubble Level for Joby GP3 SLR-Zoom Gorillapods]]) for photo walks, theme parks or general walk-abouts where that prize-winning shot may be just a Gorillapod away. Amanda Richards, January 10, 2012

title: Big fat bass
text: Being a lady approaching that certain age, my ears are not of the necessary construction to accommodate ear buds with any degree of comfort. Indeed, even the increasingly complicated act of bending at the waist can cause regular buds to become dislodged, so I approached these with some measure of reservation. The memory foam did not feel much different to regular buds, but were not as reluctant to stay put as rubber buds. The construction is good, and the aesthetics are good, but still, they tend to hurt my ears after using them for a while. I like the cloth covered cord, which feels a whole lot tougher than regular cords; and also the anti-tangle slider which works fine for me, but can be reduced in seconds to a tangled mess in the pocket of my ten year old son. The big fat bass tends to overpower the higher frequencies a bit, but is still an improvement on other similarly priced models, especially as I prefer heavier bass over tinny trebly sound. One minor improvement would have been if it had shipped with a case to store the extra buds which tend to get misplaced, and help with my son's tangling issues. Amanda Richards, January 3, 2012

title: Up close and personal
text: I bought this lens to do portraits and general low-light photography, and don't regret it for a minute. It looks a little stunted on the Nikon D7000 after taking off the telephoto, but is a dream to carry around and a snap to use. Paired with the [[ASIN:B001BTG3OQ Nikon SB-900 AF Speedlight Flash for Nikon Digital SLR Cameras]], anyone can take a picture perfect portrait, and you can capture gorgeous bokeh and snap away in low light situations thanks to the large 1.8 aperture. For the beginner, this lens can autofocus, but you can also switch to manual if preferred. As it is a prime lens, you have to move around to compose your shots (no lazy zooming in) but if you want full body shots, you'll have to move back quite a bit so as not to cut off heads or feet. Same goes for group shots - this isn't an ideal lens for large groups of people. Included is a lens hood, manual and sturdy drawstring carrying case. For the price, weight and what it can do, this lens is highly recommended for portraits, low-light, general and street photography. Amanda Richards, December 28, 2011

title: A pocketful of everything
text: Pros: 1. A bag big enough to carry all your camera bits and pieces. There's a padded lower compartment with customizable Velcro edged dividers for camera and lenses, a drawstring upper compartment for your what-nots that can be converted to one big compartment with the lower one; five smaller external zippered or Velcro-closing compartments; two pull-out side pouches for water bottles or tripod; a rain cover, and a lot of hooks, straps and loops for attaching gear outside of the bag. 2. The bottom compartment can easily hold a DSLR camera with two or three lenses, or one lens and a flash, or a combination thereof. 3. Smaller pockets have zips &/or Velcro closures for securing lens cleaners, filters, diffusers, spare batteries, chargers, memory cards, remotes or shutter cables etc. 4. Sturdy construction and nicely padded adjustable straps. 5. Cool National Geographic logo to give the impression that you may actually have something to do with the magazine. Cons: 1. It's a big bag to lug around, especially if you're not built like a rugby player. 2. Even though it's a big bag, and has many pockets, it's still not ideal as a carry-on travel bag, as the upper drawstring compartment is too small to hold a change of clothes and toiletries, and the sideways slit pocket is awkwardly designed to fit a full-sized laptop. 3. It's not possible (or very difficult) to whip out the camera at short notice without taking off the backpack. 4. Too many external loops and fasteners add to the weight. 5. You may have a hard time remembering which pocket you put specific items in. I use this bag for events or outdoor shoots where I may need more than the basic equipment. For daily use, the [[ASIN:B000YIWNUS Lowepro Fastpack 100 (Red)]]is much more convenient to fetch around. Amanda Richards, December 28, 2011

title: So-so in the tropics
text: I'm beginning to believe that there's no anti-fog product that will work when you're living on the edge of the Amazon rainforest. Based on the reviews, this one seemed to be my best bet to prevent my spectacles and camera lens from fogging when leaving an air-conditioned area for the hot and humid outside air. Unfortunately, it does not work at all for spectacles and with limited success on the camera lens. However, I will continue to use this product until something better comes along, as instead of the whole lens fogging up after being treated, there were only random patches of fog on the camera lens, and these cleared up a lot faster than with the untreated lens. (I gave up on the spectacle lenses) If anyone can suggest what I may be doing wrong, I'll be more than pleased to revisit this review through fog-free lenses. Amanda Richards, December 15, 2011

title: Idiot proof (Using on Nikon D7000)
text: Using this shutter release is so easy that even a beginner like me had it up and running in less than one minute. I've never used one before. I'm using it on a Nikon D7000 to shoot long exposures, and hope one day to capture a heavenly lightning show without getting electrocuted in the process. This product has only four components - shutter release button, shutter release button lock, cord and plug. You simply make sure that the camera is turned off, insert the plug end into your camera's accessory terminal and turn on the camera. Remember to turn off the camera when you're done before disconnecting the plug. Pressing the button (there's only one) is just like pressing the shutter button on your camera, except that you can slide the button to the locked position, go have a cup of tea, and come back and release it to complete the photo. (I exaggerate, but I guess you COULD have a cup of tea if you were doing an extra-long exposure.) The D7000 offers exposures up to 30 seconds, but if you use this handy gizmo, you can scroll past that to "bulb" mode and keep that sucker open to your heart's content. You can also use it for portraits, self-portraits and for those times when you really want to minimize camera shake. The only problem with the self-portraits is that the cord isn't that long, so you'll probably only get extreme close-ups. If self-portraits are your thing, better get a wireless remote. The one made by Amazon is pretty darned good. So, camera, tripod, LED flashlight and this wired remote, and I'm all set for some light painting. This is definitely an essential part of any camera gear collection. Amanda Richards, December 8, 2011

title: Not a whole lotta shaking going on
text: This remote works perfectly with a Nikon D7000, and reportedly will also work with Nikon models D40, D40X, D50, D60, D70, D70S, D80, D90, D3000, D5000 AND D9000 Digital SLR cameras. It comes with frustration free packaging (albeit too much packing material) and once you remove the plastic tab to make the battery connection, you're good to go. The remote itself is a one-button deal, so there's no need for complicated manuals, at least for the remote. Getting the camera set up for remote shooting is the major challenge, as the Nikon manuals are not easy to follow. It's much easier to do a search on YouTube and follow the videos there. If you are using the remote to include yourself in family photos, take sneak pics of unsuspecting wildlife or minimize camera shake while taking lights at night or portraits by day, this can be done simply by rotating the camera's release mode dial (on model D7000) which is below the mode dial (the one that says P, A, S, M, scene, U1, U2 etc.) to the second to last setting, putting your camera (and tripod if necessary) where you want it, setting up the shot, and beetling off within a 16 foot radius, pressing the single button when you are ready. That's it. For long exposures, rotate the release mode dial one more place to the last setting, which is called Mup, or Mirror Up. One press raises the reflex mirror and the second press releases the shutter and resets the mirror. Of course shooting fancy stuff like lightning, star trails and the craters of the moon requires a full knowledge of the manual setting on your camera, a sturdy tripod and a lot of patience, but this remote will do its part of the job with just one button. If only the manual camera settings were as easy to use as this remote, I'd be a pro in no time flat. Amanda Richards, November 13, 2011

title: Day tripper
text: "She was a day tripper, a Sunday driver yeah It took me so long to find out, and I found out" (The Beatles) The Fastpack 100 is the smallest camera bag in this range, and is excellent for day trips and daily toting of your DSLR camera and accessories. Normal camera bags are like big boxy handbags, and I was looking for something less clunky so I could always have my camera on hand just in case a "Breaking News" Pulitzer opportunity came by. I carry a Nikon D7000 with a Sigma 18-250mm lens. The video on the product page is very helpful in identifying all the features, but it also includes the larger models. This model includes: 1. Padded compartment for DSLR camera and a couple of extra lenses, accessible from the side without having to take off the backpack. 2. Slots for memory cards 3. Lots of padding for customizable packing. 4. Separate upper compartment for small camera or personal items. 5. Two external accessory pockets 6. Water bottle holder 7. Cell phone case on strap 8. Slot for attaching other small accessory bags, if needed. 9. Padding and waterproof breathable material for comfortable fit 10. Adjustable straps This bag will not hold a notebook computer or any large personal items. It can't tote a change of clothes or a tripod, and is not big enough to function as a carry-on bag on an airplane. It is however perfect for daily use, especially if you also have to carry a handbag/briefcase for your real job. It is also the ideal bag for a walk in the park, zoo, gardens or theme park, while keeping an eagle eye out for that Pulitzer shot. Amanda Richards, September 3, 2011

title: Hot flash
text: What looks like a flash, acts like a flash, but is much more than your average flash? This gadget provides a painless backup solution for businesspersons and students who can't survive without their trusty laptop/netbook/notebook and the information therein. Even for users unfamiliar with backup software, the Echo software included on the drive is a snap to use. Once the backup drive is inserted into a USB port on your computer, it will take you through some simple steps to configure the backup. You can choose the easy predefined Automatic plan or you can choose the more advanced Custom backup plan. There is a Quick Start Guide, also included on the drive, which provides a brief explanation of the options that are available. When configuring your Custom backup profile, you can specify which file types you want backed-up. You can select ALL files, or there are some basic ones such as text, spreadsheet, presentation, music, videos, photos et al that you can select. There is also an OTHER category where you can define other file types that may be important to you, for example, zip, rar, pdf, etc. In addition, you select which folder(s) you want backed-up, set filters if required, and set the number of versions of files to keep, a useful option if you accidentally delete or modify a file. There is also the option to select an Automatic backup which activates every time you plug in your flash drive, and Live which continuously backs up your modified files to the flash drive without your intervention. Restoring files is just a matter of clicking on the Restore menu button, selecting the files and/or folders you want restored and setting the location where to restore the files, then hit RESTORE. Alternatively, if when creating your profile, you had decided not to password protect it and encrypt it, the files can be accessed quite easily from directly on the root of the backup drive in the My Backup folder. To backup another computer, you would have to install the software on that computer and set up another backup profile. This version of the Lexar Echo has only 16GB of storage capacity, and is really too small to back up more than one home computer with music and video files; it can barely back up one computer, much less two or more. On the other hand, it would certainly be good for business people on the road since they will generally be using smaller files and the backup is a no-brainer. While it has a good feel to it and the retractable connector saves losing caps, it is a bit on the `chunky' side and competes for space with other USB devices. It can also get damaged if you're not careful when moving the laptop around and it gets hit during the process, as it sticks out quite a bit. I did not check for backup/restore speeds nor did I follow up on the 2GB of free online backup space which was offered in the setup. It appears this is no longer available at DMAILER, the backup software manufacturer; but instead I was guided to check YuuWaa online backup services. Extremely handy for business or school use, and especially for people who have senior moments and accidentally delete or write over important files on a regular basis. Amanda Richards, July 8, 2011

title: Not quite spy-gear
text: First of all, the D-Link camera is relatively easy to set up - always the one to play with techie stuff first, my husband had it up and running in a flash (well almost a flash). Just attach the supplied cable to your computer, run the CD and follow the simple instructions and you're good to go. According to the instructions, you have two options to set up the camera: wirelessly or wired. Naturally, my husband tried the wireless option first, which didn't work because it claimed (spuriously, we believe) that it couldn't find the network, so he had to resort to the other method, which worked right away. We're using a Linksys wireless router. The camera works quite well indoors where the intensity of the ambient light is generally much lower than outdoors. However, in the brighter outdoor light it is difficult to discern what you're looking at (is it a bird, is it a plane?). The colour is not the best, but then again, it ain't a Nikon 7000. There is some amount of adjustment that can be done online to change the settings, but you'll need to create an online account/register your camera first with D-Link at [...] This is also necessary if you want to view your camera remotely. Strange enough, whenever I try to access the camera online, I get a message telling me that the application needs an earlier version of Java. However, after hitting for the next three dialogue boxes or so that pop up, it will display the picture. I tried accessing the camera from outside my home network but was unable to do so. Maybe firewall issues?? (Too much effort required to check this). There is also an iPod app that is quite good, minus sound. Night vision was surprisingly good too. In the dark, the images were shades of grey, but in brighter conditions, the colour returned. Four LED lights lit up whenever the night vision was activated (could be an issue if you wanted to place it somewhere discrete). On the down side, the camera has to be plugged into an electrical socket to work, and the cord it came with is very short. This means you have to either place it near an electrical outlet or use an extension cord. This would obviously have limitations on where you can place it. It also has to be connected to your home network whether wired or wireless. While in theory it could be used as a security camera, it has to be powered 24/7, so if you live in a country or area prone to an uneven power supply which could damage sensitive equipment, then you may want to consider that before getting it or you may need to install additional equipment such as line conditioners/UPS to protect your equipment. The sound is not very good. In fact, after a few hours use it started to make a clicking sound in an endless loop. Recommended for limited applications such as keeping an eye on kids (or pets, or pesky guests), or when you're avoiding (hiding from) certain people who come calling at your gate, but not as a dedicated security system. Amanda Richards, June 29, 2011

title: iLike
text: This review deals with the performance of the iLuv iMM747 Audio Cube using an iPod Touch and an iPad 2. Pros: 1. Easy to open packaging, easy to set up, easy on the eyes. 2. Slightly big for a bedside table, but a good size for a desk. 3. Convenient controls on the top if using it at a desk. 4. Charges device while in operation. 5. Good quality sound, reasonable bass and volume without distortion. 6. Syncs with iTunes when connected to a network. 7. Easy to dock the iPod Touch. 8. You can watch videos or TV shows using it as a base with big speakers for your tiny touch screen television. 9. Small enough to tote around for big sound at sleepovers or small gatherings. 10. Cooler looking and lighter than a boom box. Cons: 1. No remote control. 2. No remote control. 3. No remote control. 4. Power cord is too short, and the wall adapter is a bit large for outlets that are close behind bedside tables or other furniture. 5. The iPad 2 is hard to dock due to the angle and placement of the port. 6. The back support is not tall enough to hold the iPad 2 securely, or at least it seems that way to me. Other: 1. You need to take the device out of the case before placing in the docking station. 2. A message saying "Application not installed" pops up when you power it up, even though all apps are up to date. 3. If you can play Angry Birds sideways, you can get the sound effects at high volume (this may be considered a bad thing) Conclusion: Good value for the price, and high quality sound for the size. Amanda Richards June 10, 2011

title: Love/Hate Relationship
text: As a general rule, I hate hands-free handsets. I hate it when I begin speaking with someone, and I think they're agreeing with everything I say, and then it turns out they're actually talking to someone else using their dratted ear extension with the flashing blue light. I hate the fact that my ears are the wrong size and shape for the majority of headsets. I hate it when my untrained (clumsy) fingers hit the wrong part of the headset when I'm simply trying to stop it from falling to its death from a height of just over 5 feet, and I either redial the last number or hang up on the one person who hates being hung up on. Plus, they're UGLY, and don't accessorise well with any wardrobe!! HOWEVER, I hate it even more when I have to pull over and park to take or make a call. And I especially hate it if I DON'T pull over, and then get busted by the only policeman on the entire empty highway who has insomnia and a full book of blank tickets waiting to be filled in.
